chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: Sing, Heavenly Muse, of the first disobedience of Man, and of the fruit of that forbidden tree whose deadly taste brought death into the World and all our woe, with the loss of Eden — until one greater Man shall restore us and regain the blissful seat. Sing, O Muse who, upon the secret summit of Oreb or of Sinai, once inspired that shepherd who first taught the chosen people how the heavens and the earth rose out of Chaos in the beginning. Or, if Sion hill delights you more, and Siloa's brook that flowed close by the oracle of God, it is from there that I call upon your aid for my adventurous song — a song that intends no middle flight, but to soar above the Aonian mount, pursuing things not yet attempted in prose or rhyme.

And above all, you, O Spirit, who prefer before all temples the upright and pure heart — instruct me, for you know. You were there from the first, and with mighty wings outspread you sat dove-like, brooding upon the vast Abyss, and made it pregnant with life. What is dark in me, illuminate; what is low, raise up and support.
So that, rising to the height of this great argument, I may vindicate Eternal Providence and justify the ways of God to men.

Say first — for Heaven hides nothing from your view, nor the deep region of Hell — say first, what cause moved our first parents, in that happy state, so highly favoured by Heaven, to fall away from their Creator and break his will over one single prohibition, when they were lords of all the rest of the World? Who first seduced them to that foul revolt?

It was the infernal Serpent. His guile, stirred up by envy and revenge, deceived the mother of mankind — at the time when his own pride had cast him out from Heaven with all his host of rebel Angels. With their aid, aspiring to set himself in glory above his peers, he had trusted to equal the Most High if he opposed him. With ambitious aim, against the throne and monarchy of God, he raised impious war in Heaven and proud battle — but the attempt was vain. The Almighty Power hurled him headlong, flaming, from the ethereal sky, with hideous ruin and combustion, down to bottomless perdition, there to dwell in adamantine chains and penal fire — he who had dared to defy the Omnipotent in arms.

Nine times the span that measures day and night for mortal men he lay vanquished with his horrid crew, rolling in the fiery gulf, confounded, though immortal. But his doom reserved him for greater wrath. For now the thought both of his lost happiness and of his everlasting pain tormented him. He threw his baleful eyes all around — eyes that witnessed vast affliction and dismay mixed with obdurate pride and steadfast hatred.

At once, as far as an Angel's sight can reach, he surveyed the dismal scene, waste and wild — a horrible dungeon, blazing on every side like one great furnace. Yet from those flames came no light; rather, a visible darkness served only to disclose sights of woe, regions of sorrow, doleful shades, where peace and rest can never dwell, where hope, which comes to all, never comes. Only endless torture presses on, and a fiery deluge fed by ever-burning sulphur that is never consumed.

Such is the place Eternal Justice has prepared for those rebellious spirits — their prison ordained in utter darkness, their portion set as far removed from God and the light of Heaven as three times the distance from the centre of the earth to the utmost pole.

Oh, how unlike the place from which they had fallen! There he soon discerns the companions of his fall, overwhelmed with floods and whirlwinds of tempestuous fire. Weltering by his side is one next to him in power, and next in crime, known long after in Palestine and named Beelzebub. To him the Arch-Enemy — thence called Satan in Heaven — spoke with bold words, breaking the horrid silence thus: "If you are he — but how fallen! how changed from him who, in the happy realms of light and clothed in transcendent brightness, outshone myriads of the bright! — if you are he whom mutual league, united thoughts and counsels, equal hope and hazard in the glorious enterprise once joined with me, and whom misery has now joined in equal ruin: into what a pit you see we have fallen from what a height. So much the stronger has he proved with his thunder; and who until then knew the force of those dreadful arms? Yet not for those, nor for anything else the potent Victor in his rage can inflict, will I repent or change — though I am changed in outward lustre — that fixed mind, and that high disdain arising from a sense of injured merit, which raised me to contend with the Mightiest, and brought to the fierce contentions innumerable armed Spirits who dared to dislike his reign and, preferring me, opposed his utmost power with adverse power in doubtful battle on the plains of Heaven, and shook his throne. What though the field is lost?

All is not lost. The unconquerable will, the study of revenge, immortal hatred, and courage never to submit or yield — and what else is it not to be overcome? That glory his wrath or might shall never wrest from me. To bow and sue for grace on suppliant knee, and deify the power of one who, from the terror of this arm of mine, had so lately doubted his own empire — that indeed would be low.

That would be an ignominy and a shame beneath this very downfall. Since by fate the strength of Gods and this heavenly substance cannot fail; and since, through the experience of this great event, with arms no weaker and foresight much improved, we may resolve with more successful hope to wage eternal war, by force or guile, irreconcilable against our grand Foe, who now triumphs and, in his excess of joy, reigns alone, holding the tyranny of Heaven."

So spoke the apostate Angel, though in pain, boasting aloud, yet racked with deep despair. And his bold comrade soon answered him: "O Prince, O Chief of many enthroned Powers, who led the embattled Seraphim to war under your command, and in dreadful deeds, fearless, endangered Heaven's eternal King and put his high supremacy to the test — whether it was upheld by strength, or chance, or fate — too well I see and lament the dire event that, with sad overthrow and foul defeat, has lost us Heaven, and laid this mighty host so low in horrible destruction, as far as Gods and heavenly Essences can perish. For the mind and spirit remain invincible, and vigour soon returns, though all our glory is extinguished and our happy state is here swallowed up in endless misery.

But what if our Conqueror — whom I must now believe almighty, since no less than almighty could have overpowered such force as ours — has left us this spirit and strength of ours intact, so that we may strongly suffer and support our pains, and thus satisfy his vengeful anger? Or perhaps do him mightier service as his slaves by right of war, whatever his business may be — whether here in the heart of Hell to labour in fire, or to do his errands in the gloomy Deep?
What then does it matter if we still feel strength undiminished, or eternal being, if we must undergo eternal punishment?"

To which the Arch-Fiend swiftly replied: "Fallen Cherub, to be weak is miserable, whether doing or suffering. But of this be sure — to do any good will never be our task, but always to do ill our sole delight, being the contrary of his high will whom we resist. If then his providence seeks to draw good out of our evil, our labour must be to pervert that end, and out of good still to find the means of evil.

Which often may succeed in such a way, perhaps, that it shall grieve him — if I do not fail — and disturb his inmost counsels from their destined aim. But look! the angry Victor has recalled his ministers of vengeance and pursuit back to the gates of Heaven. The sulphurous hail, shot at us in the storm, has been blown over and has settled the fiery surge that received us as we fell from the precipice of Heaven. And the thunder, winged with red lightning and impetuous rage, has perhaps spent its shafts and now ceases to bellow through the vast and boundless Deep.

Let us not miss the opportunity, whether it is scorn or satiated fury that gives it from our Foe. Do you see that dreary plain, forlorn and wild, the seat of desolation, void of light except for the pale and dreadful gleam of these livid flames? Let us head there, away from the tossing of these fiery waves.

There let us rest, if any rest can be had there, and, reassembling our afflicted powers, consult how we may henceforth best offend our enemy, how to repair our own loss, how to overcome this dire calamity, what reinforcement we may gain from hope, or, if not, what resolution we may draw from despair."

Thus Satan spoke to his nearest comrade, with his head lifted above the wave and his eyes blazing with sparks. The rest of him lay prone on the flood, stretched long and large, floating for many a rood — as huge in bulk as those whom fables name of monstrous size: the Titanian or Earth-born giants that warred on Jove, Briareos or Typhon, whom the den near ancient Tarsus held, or that sea-beast Leviathan, the hugest of all God's works that swim the ocean-stream.

Him, perhaps, slumbering on the Norway foam, the pilot of some small night-foundered skiff, thinking him an island, often — as seamen tell — moors beside under his lee with fixed anchor in his scaly rind, while night invests the sea and the longed-for morning delays.

So stretched out in length the Arch-fiend lay, chained on the burning lake. Nor would he ever have risen from there, nor lifted his head, except that the will and high permission of all-ruling Heaven left him at large to his own dark designs, so that with repeated crimes he might heap damnation upon himself, while he sought evil against others; and, in rage, he might see how all his malice served only to bring forth infinite goodness, grace, and mercy, shown upon Man whom he seduced — but upon himself threefold confusion, wrath, and vengeance poured out.

At once he rears his mighty stature upright from the pool. On either hand the flames, driven back, slope their pointing spires and, rolled up in billows, leave in the midst a horrid vale. Then with expanded wings he steers his flight aloft, lying heavily upon the dusky air, which felt the unusual weight, until he alights on dry land — if it could be called land, that burned with solid fire as the lake burned with liquid fire. It appeared the colour of that soil which, when the force of subterranean wind transports a hill torn from Pelorus, or the shattered side of thundering Etna (whose combustible and fuel-filled entrails there conceive fire, sublimed with mineral fury, aid the winds), is left a singed bottom all wrapped in stench and smoke. Such resting-place his unblest feet found. Beelzebub, his next companion, followed him.

Both gloried that they had escaped the Stygian flood as gods, by their own recovered strength, and not by the sufferance of supernal Power. "Is this the region, this the soil, the climate," said the lost Archangel then, "this the seat that we must exchange for Heaven? — this mournful gloom for that celestial light? So be it. Since he who is now sovereign can decree and command what shall be right, the farthest from him is best — from him whom reason had made equal, but whom force has made supreme above his equals. Farewell, happy fields, where joy dwells forever! Hail, horrors! Hail, infernal world! And you, profoundest Hell — receive your new possessor, one who brings a mind not to be changed by place or time.

The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven. What does it matter where I am, if I am still the same — and what I ought to be, all but less than he whom thunder has made greater? Here at least we shall be free. The Almighty has not built here for his envy, and will not drive us out.

Here we may reign secure; and, by my choice, to reign is worth ambition, even in Hell — better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven. But why then do we let our faithful friends, the associates and co-partners of our loss, lie thus astonished on that oblivious pool, and not call on them to share their part with us in this unhappy mansion, or once more, with rallied arms, try what may yet be regained in Heaven, or what more may be lost in Hell?"

So Satan spoke; and Beelzebub answered him thus: "Leader of those bright armies, whom none but the Omnipotent could have foiled! If once they hear that voice — their liveliest pledge of hope in fears and dangers, heard so often in the worst extremes and on the perilous edge of battle when it raged, their surest signal in every assault — they will soon resume new courage and revive, though they now lie grovelling and prostrate on that lake of fire, as we lately did, astounded and amazed. No wonder, after falling from such a ruinous height!"

He had scarcely ceased before the superior Fiend was moving toward the shore. His ponderous shield, of ethereal temper, massive, large, and round, he cast behind him. Its broad circumference hung on his shoulders like the moon, whose orb the Tuscan artist — Galileo — views through an optic glass at evening, from the top of Fesole or in Valdarno, to discover new lands, rivers, or mountains in her spotty globe.

His spear — to equal which the tallest pine hewn on Norwegian hills to be the mast of some great admiral's ship would be but a wand — he used as a staff to support his uneasy steps over the burning marl, so unlike those steps on Heaven's azure. The torrid climate, vaulted over with fire, beat on him sorely besides.

Nevertheless, he endured, until he stood on the beach of that inflamed sea and called his legions — Angel Forms, who lay entranced, thick as autumnal leaves that strew the brooks in Vallombrosa, where the Etrurian shades high-arched above form a bower; or like scattered sedge afloat, when Orion armed with fierce winds has vexed the Red-Sea coast, whose waves overthrew Busiris and his Memphian chivalry, while with perfidious hatred they pursued the sojourners of Goshen, who beheld from the safe shore their floating corpses and broken chariot-wheels. So thick strewn, abject and lost, lay these, covering the flood, under amazement at their hideous change.

He called so loud that all the hollow deep of Hell resounded: "Princes, Potentates, Warriors — the Flower of Heaven, once yours, now lost — if such astonishment as this can seize Eternal Spirits! Or have you chosen this place, after the toil of battle, to repose your wearied valour, for the ease you find to slumber here, as in the vales of Heaven?

Or in this abject posture have you sworn to adore the Conqueror, who now beholds Cherub and Seraph rolling in the flood with scattered arms and ensigns — until presently his swift pursuers from Heaven-gates discern the advantage, and, descending, trample us down as we droop, or with linked thunderbolts transfix us to the bottom of this gulf? Awake, arise, or be forever fallen!"

They heard, and were abashed, and up they sprang upon the wing, like soldiers accustomed to watch on duty who, when found sleeping by whom they dread, rouse and bestir themselves before they are fully awake. They did not fail to perceive the evil plight they were in, or to feel the fierce pains.

Yet to their General's voice they soon obeyed, innumerable. As when the potent rod of Amram's son, in Egypt's evil day, waved along the coast and called up a pitchy cloud of locusts, warping on the eastern wind, that hung like Night over the realm of impious Pharaoh and darkened all the land of Nile —

so numberless were those bad Angels seen hovering on wing under the roof of Hell, amid upper, nether, and surrounding fires, until, at a given signal, the uplifted spear of their great Sultan waved to direct their course, and in even balance they alighted on the firm brimstone and filled all the plain:

a multitude such as the populous North never poured from her frozen loins to cross the Rhine or the Danube, when her barbarous sons came like a deluge upon the South and spread below Gibraltar to the Libyan sands.

At once, from every squadron and every band, the heads and leaders hastened to where their great Commander stood — godlike Shapes and Forms surpassing human, princely Dignities, Powers that once sat on thrones in Heaven, though their names are no longer recorded in the Heavenly records, blotted out and erased by their rebellion from the Books of Life.

Nor had they yet gained new names among the sons of Eve, until, wandering over the earth through God's high sufferance to try mankind, they corrupted the greatest part of humanity by falsehoods and lies to forsake God their Creator and the invisible Glory of him who made them, to transform him into the image of a brute, adorned with gay religions full of pomp and gold, and adoring devils as deities. Then were they known to men by various names, as various idols throughout the heathen world.

Say, Muse, their names as they were known then — who, first and who last, were roused from the slumber on that fiery couch at their great Emperor's call, and came singly, next in worth, to where he stood on the bare strand, while the promiscuous crowd still stood apart?

The chief were those who, roaming from the pit of Hell to seek their prey on Earth, dared to fix their seats long afterward next to the seat of God, with their altars beside his altar — gods adored among the surrounding nations, who dared to endure Jehovah thundering out of Sion, enthroned between the Cherubim. Yes, they often placed their shrines, abominations, within his sanctuary itself; and with cursed things profaned his holy rites and solemn feasts, and with their darkness dared to affront his light.

First, Moloch — horrid king, besmeared with the blood of human sacrifice and parents' tears, though the noise of loud drums and timbrels drowned out the cries of the children who passed through fire to his grim idol. The Ammonites worshipped him in Rabba and her watery plain, in Argob and in Basan, as far as the stream of utmost Arnon. Nor content with such audacious neighbourhood, he led the wisest heart of Solomon by fraud to build his temple directly opposite the temple of God on that opprobrious hill, and made his grove the pleasant valley of Hinnom, from which it was called Tophet and black Gehenna — the very type of Hell.

Next, Chemos — the obscene dread of Moab's sons, from Aroar to Nebo and the wild of southernmost Abarim; in Hesebon and Horonaim, the kingdom of Seon, beyond the flowery dale of Sibma clad with vines, and Eleale down to the Asphaltic Pool.

Peor was his other name, when he enticed Israel at Sittim, on their march from the Nile, to do him lewd rites — which cost them dearly. Yet from there he extended his lustful orgies even to that hill of scandal, by the grove of Moloch the homicide — lust set hard beside hatred — until good Josiah drove them from there to Hell.

With these came those who, from the bordering flood of old Euphrates to the brook that separates Egypt from Syrian ground, had the general names of Baalim and Ashtaroth — the former male, the latter feminine. For Spirits, when they please, can assume either sex, or both; so soft and uncompounded is their pure essence, not constrained or manacled by joint or limb, nor founded on the brittle strength of bones like cumbrous flesh. But in whatever shape they choose, dilated or condensed, bright or obscure, they can execute their airy purposes and fulfil works of love or enmity.

For the sake of these, the race of Israel often forsook their Living Strength, and left his righteous altar unfrequented, bowing lowly to bestial gods — for which their heads bowed as low in battle, sinking before the spears of despicable foes. With these in troop came Astoreth, whom the Phoenicians called Astarte, queen of heaven, with crescent horns.

To whose bright image, nightly by the moon, Sidonian virgins paid their vows and songs. She was not unsung in Sion also, where her temple stood on the offensive mountain, built by that uxorious king — Solomon — whose heart, though large, was beguiled by fair idolatresses and fell to foul idols. Thammuz came next behind, whose annual wound in Lebanon drew the Syrian damsels to lament his fate in amorous songs all a summer's day, while smooth Adonis, from his native rock, ran purple to the sea, supposed to be stained with the blood of Thammuz yearly wounded. The love-tale infected Sion's daughters with similar heat, whose wanton passions in the sacred porch Ezekiel saw when, led by vision, his eye surveyed the dark idolatries of alienated Judah. Next came one who mourned in earnest, when the captive ark maimed his brute image — head and hands lopped off, in his own temple, on the threshold — where he fell flat and shamed his worshippers:

Dagon was his name, a sea-monster, a man from the waist up and a fish below. Yet he had his temple built high in Azotus, dreaded throughout the coast of Palestine — in Gath and Ascalon, and Accaron, and Gaza's frontier bounds.

After him followed Rimmon, whose delightful seat was fair Damascus, on the fertile banks of Abbana and Pharphar, lucid streams. He too was bold against the house of God: he once lost a leper and gained a king — Ahaz, his sottish conqueror, whom he drew to disparage and displace God's altar for one of Syrian fashion, on which to burn his odious offerings, and to adore the gods whom he had vanquished. After these appeared a crew who, under ancient names of renown — Osiris, Isis, Orus, and their train — with monstrous shapes and sorceries deluded fanatical Egypt and her priests to seek their wandering gods disguised in brutish forms rather than human. Nor did Israel escape that infection, when their borrowed gold formed the calf in Oreb; and the rebel king doubled that sin in Bethel and in Dan, likening his Maker to a grass-fed ox — Jehovah, who in one night, as he passed out of Egypt marching, equalled with a single stroke both her firstborn and all her bleating gods.

Belial came last — than whom no Spirit more lewd fell from Heaven, nor any more grossly in love with vice for its own sake. No temple stood to him, nor did any altar smoke for him; yet who was more often than he in temples and at altars, when the priest turns atheist, as did Eli's sons, who filled the house of God with lust and violence?

He also reigns in courts and palaces, and in luxurious cities where the noise of riot ascends above their loftiest towers, and with it injury and outrage; and when night darkens the streets, then forth wander the sons of Belial, swollen with insolence and wine.
Witness the streets of Sodom, and that night in Gibeah, when the hospitable door exposed a matron to avoid a worse rape.

These were the foremost in order and in might. The rest would take long to tell — though highly renowned were the Ionian gods, held to be gods by Javan's offspring, yet confessed to be later than Heaven and Earth, their boasted parents: Titan, Heaven's firstborn, with his enormous brood, whose birthright was seized by younger Saturn; Saturn, in turn, found the same measure from mightier Jove, his own son by Rhea.

So Jove reigned, a usurper. These, known first in Crete and Ida, thence on the snowy top of cold Olympus ruled the middle air, which they called their highest heaven; or they dwelt on the Delphian cliff, in Dodona, and through all the bounds of Doric land; or there were those who, with old Saturn, fled over the Adriatic to the Hesperian fields and roamed over the Celtic to the utmost Isles.

All these and more came flocking, but with downcast and dampened looks — yet looks in which appeared obscurely some glimpse of joy, to have found their Chief not in despair, to have found themselves not wholly lost in their loss. This cast a doubtful hue on his countenance. But he, quickly recollecting his accustomed pride, with high words that bore the semblance of worth without its substance, gently raised their fainting courage and dispelled their fears.

Then he straightaway commanded that, at the warlike sound of loud trumpets and clarions, his mighty standard be raised up. That proud honour Azazel, a tall Cherub, claimed as his right: he at once unfurled the imperial ensign from its glittering staff. Raised high, it shone like a meteor streaming in the wind, rich and emblazoned with gems and golden lustre, Seraphic arms and trophies — all the while, sonorous metal blew martial sounds.

At this the universal host let out a shout that tore Hell's concave and, beyond it, frightened the reign of Chaos and old Night. In a moment, through the gloom, ten thousand banners were seen rising into the air, waving with eastern colours. With them rose a huge forest of spears, and thronging helms appeared, and serried shields in thick array of immeasurable depth. Then they moved in perfect phalanx to the Dorian mood of flutes and soft recorders — such music as once raised heroes of old to the highest temper as they armed for battle, and which breathed, instead of rage, deliberate valour, firm and unmoved by the dread of death into flight or foul retreat;

music not lacking the power to mitigate and assuage troubled thoughts with solemn touches, and to chase anguish, doubt, fear, sorrow, and pain from mortal or immortal minds. Thus, breathing united force with fixed thought, they moved on in silence to soft pipes that charmed their painful steps over the burnt soil. And now, advanced in view, they stand — a horrid front of dreadful length and dazzling arms, in the guise of warriors of old, with ordered spear and shield, awaiting what command their mighty Chief might lay upon them. He darts his experienced eye through the armed files, and soon crosses the whole battalion in review, observing their proper order, their faces and statures like those of gods.

Their number he sums up at last. And now his heart swells with pride, and, hardening in his strength, he glories — for never, since the creation of Man, had there met so embodied a force as this, which, when compared with these, would reckon the best mortal army only as that small infantry warred upon by cranes, even if all the giant brood of Phlegra were joined with the heroic race that fought at Thebes and Ilium, aided on each side by auxiliary gods, or with what resounds in fable or romance of Uther's son — King Arthur — girt with British and Armoric knights;

and all those who since, whether baptized or infidel, jousted at Aspramont, or Montalban, Damascus, Morocco, or Trebisond, or those whom Biserta sent from the African shore when Charlemagne with all his peerage fell at Fontarabbia. Far beyond comparison with mortal prowess, yet they observed their dreaded Commander. He, above the rest in shape and gesture proudly eminent, stood like a tower. His form had not yet lost all its original brightness, nor did he appear less than an Archangel in ruin, and his excess of glory obscured — as when the newly-risen sun looks through the horizontal misty air, shorn of his beams, or when, from behind the moon, he sheds a disastrous twilight of dim eclipse upon half the nations and perplexes monarchs with fear of change. So darkened, yet shone above them all the Archangel. But deep scars of thunder had scored his face, and care sat on his faded cheek. Yet beneath brows of dauntless courage, and considerate pride waiting revenge — cruel his eye, but it also showed signs of remorse and passion, as he beheld his fellow criminals, or rather his followers (far otherwise once beheld in bliss), condemned forever now to have their lot in pain — millions of Spirits amerced of Heaven for his fault, and from eternal splendours flung for his revolt. Yet, faithfully, how they stood, their glory withered — as when heaven's fire has scathed the forest oaks or mountain pines, and with singed tops, though bare, their stately growth stands on the blasted heath. He now prepared to speak: at which their doubled ranks bend from wing to wing, and half enclose him round with all his peers. Attention held them mute.

Three times he tried, and three times, in spite of scorn, tears — such as Angels weep — burst forth. At last words, interwoven with sighs, found their way out: "O myriads of immortal Spirits! O Powers matchless — except by the Almighty! — and that strife was not inglorious, though the outcome was dire, as this place testifies, and this dire change hateful to speak of. But what power of mind, foreseeing or presaging from the depth of past or present knowledge, could have feared how such a united force of gods, how such as stood like these, could ever know defeat?

For who can yet believe, though after loss, that all these puissant legions, whose exile has emptied Heaven, shall fail to reascend, self-raised, and repossess their native seat? For my part — let all the host of Heaven bear witness — if different counsels, or danger shunned by me, have lost us our hopes! But he who reigns Monarch in Heaven had sat on his throne, until then, as one secure, upheld by old reputation, consent, or custom, and though his regal state was put forth to the full, his strength was still concealed — which tempted our attempt and brought about our fall.

Henceforth we know his might, and know our own, so as neither to provoke, nor to dread, a newly provoked war. Our better part remains: to work by close design, by fraud or guile, what force could not accomplish — so that he may also learn at length from us that he who overcomes by force has overcome but half his foe.

Space may yet produce new Worlds. There was a rumour rife in Heaven that he intended, before long, to create one and to plant there a generation whom his choice regard should favour equal to the Sons of Heaven.

Thither, if only to pry, may be our first incursion — thither, or elsewhere. For this infernal pit shall never hold Celestial Spirits in bondage, nor shall the Abyss long cover us under darkness. But these thoughts full counsel must mature. Peace is despaired; for who can think of submission? War, then — war, open or understood — must be resolved."

He spoke; and to confirm his words, millions of flaming swords flew out, drawn from the thighs of mighty Cherubim. The sudden blaze illumined Hell far around. Highly they raged against the Highest, and, fierce with weapons grasped, clashed on their sounding shields the din of war, hurling defiance toward the vault of Heaven.

There stood a hill not far off, whose grisly top belched fire and rolling smoke. The rest of it shone with a glossy crust — undoubted sign that in its womb was hidden metallic ore, the work of sulphur. There, winged with speed, a numerous brigade hastened: as when bands of pioneers with spade and pickaxe go before the royal camp to trench a field or raise a rampart. Mammon led them on — Mammon, the least erect of the Spirits that fell from Heaven. For even in Heaven his looks and thoughts were always bent downward, admiring more the riches of heaven's pavement, the trodden gold, than anything divine or holy otherwise enjoyed in the beatific vision. By him first, men also, taught by his suggestion, ransacked the centre of the earth, and with impious hands rifled the bowels of their mother Earth for treasures better hidden. Soon his crew had opened a spacious wound in the hill, and dug out ribs of gold. Let none wonder that riches grow in Hell — that soil may best deserve the precious bane. And here let those who boast in mortal things, and tell wondering tales of Babel, and the works of Memphian kings, learn how their greatest monuments of fame and strength and art are easily outdone by reprobate Spirits — and in a single hour, what in an age they, with incessant toil and innumerable hands, scarcely accomplish.

Near on the plain, in many prepared cells that underneath had veins of liquid fire sluiced from the lake, a second multitude with wondrous art founded the massive ore, separating each kind, and skimmed off the bullion-dross.

A third had as soon formed within the ground a various mould, and by strange conveyance filled each hollow nook from the boiling cells — as in an organ, from one blast of wind, the sound-board breathes to many rows of pipes.

Presently, out of the earth a huge fabric rose like an exhalation, to the sound of sweet symphonies and voices — built like a temple, where pilasters stood round, and Doric pillars overlaid with golden architrave; nor was there lacking cornice or frieze, with bossy sculptures graven.

The roof was fretted gold. Neither Babylon nor great Alcairo equalled such magnificence in all their glories, when they enshrined Belus or Serapis their gods, or seated their kings — when Egypt with Assyria strove in wealth and luxury. The ascending pile stood fixed at its stately height; and straightway the doors, opening their brazen folds, revealed, wide within, her ample spaces over the smooth and level pavement. From the arched roof, pendent by subtle magic, many rows of starry lamps and blazing cressets, fed with naphtha and asphalt, gave light as from a sky. The hasty multitude entered admiring; and some praise the work, and some the architect. His hand was known in Heaven by many a towered structure high, where sceptred Angels held their residence and sat as Princes, whom the supreme King had exalted to such power and given to rule, each in his Hierarchy, the bright Orders.

Nor was his name unheard or unadored in ancient Greece; and in the Ausonian land men called him Mulciber. They fabled how he fell from Heaven, thrown by angry Jove sheer over the crystal battlements — from morning to noon he fell, from noon to dewy eve, a summer's day; and with the setting sun he dropped from the zenith like a falling star on Lemnos, the Aegaean isle. Thus they relate, erring; for he had fallen long before with this rebellious rout. Nor did it avail him now to have built high towers in Heaven; nor did he escape by all his engines, but was sent headlong, with his industrious crew, to build in Hell.

Meanwhile the winged Heralds, by command of sovereign power, with awful ceremony and the sound of trumpets proclaim throughout the host that a solemn council is forthwith to be held at Pandemonium, the high capital of Satan and his peers. Their summons called, from every band and squared regiment, the worthiest by place or choice. These presently came trooping by hundreds and thousands, attended. All the ways were thronged — the gates and porches wide, but chiefly the spacious hall (though like a covered field where bold champions were wont to ride in armed, and at the Sultan's chair defied the best of Paynim chivalry to mortal combat, or to charge with lance) — swarmed thickly both on the ground and in the air, brushed with the hiss of rustling wings. As bees, in spring-time, when the Sun rides with Taurus,

pour forth their populous youth about the hive in clusters, and fly to and fro among fresh dews and flowers, or on the smoothed plank — the suburb of their straw-built citadel, newly rubbed with balm — expatiate and confer their state affairs: so thick the airy crowd swarmed and were straitened; until, at the signal given, behold a wonder! Those who only moments before had seemed in bigness to surpass Earth's giant sons were now less than the smallest dwarfs, thronging numberless in a narrow room — like that Pygmaean race beyond the Indian mount, or faery elves whose midnight revels, by a forest-side or fountain, some belated peasant sees (or dreams he sees), while overhead the Moon sits as arbitress, and, nearer to the Earth, wheels her pale course. They, intent on their mirth and dance, charm his ear with jocund music —

and at once his heart rebounds with joy and fear. Thus incorporeal Spirits reduced their immense shapes to the smallest forms, and were still at large, though still without number, amid the hall of that infernal court. But far within, and in their own dimensions like themselves, the great Seraphic Lords and Cherubim sat in close recess and secret conclave — a thousand demi-gods on golden seats, crowded and full. Then, after short silence and the reading of the summons, the great council began.

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: High on a royal throne that far outshone the wealth of Ormus and of India, or that place where the gorgeous East with richest hand showers upon her kings barbaric pearl and gold, Satan sat exalted — raised by merit to that bad eminence. From despair thus lifted high beyond hope, he aspires still higher, insatiate to pursue his vain war with Heaven; and, untaught by success, displays his proud imaginations thus: "Powers and Dominions, Deities of Heaven! — since no deep within its gulf can hold immortal vigour, though oppressed and fallen, I do not give up Heaven for lost. From this descent celestial virtues will rise more glorious and more dreaded than if they had never fallen, and will trust themselves to fear no second defeat. As for me, though just right and the fixed laws of Heaven first created me your leader, and next, free choice together with whatever merit I have achieved in council or in battle; yet this loss, thus far recovered, has far more firmly established me on a safe, unenvied throne, yielded with full consent. The happier state in Heaven, which follows dignity, might draw envy from every inferior. But who here will envy one whom the highest place exposes foremost as your bulwark against the Thunderer's aim, and condemns to the greatest share of endless pain? Where there is, then, no good for which to strive, no strife can grow from faction there. For surely no one will claim precedence in Hell; no one whose portion of present pain is so small that he would with ambitious mind covet more. With this advantage, then — toward union, firm faith, and firm accord, more than can exist in Heaven — we now return to claim our ancient just inheritance, more sure of prospering than prosperity could ever have assured us. By what best way, whether of open war or covert guile, we now debate. Whoever can advise, let him speak."

He ceased; and next to him rose Moloch, sceptred king — the strongest and the fiercest Spirit that fought in Heaven, now fiercer by despair. His trust had been to be reckoned by the Eternal as equal in strength, and rather than be less, he cared not to be at all. With that care lost went all his fear: of God, of Hell, or of anything worse, he took no account; and he spoke these words: "My vote is for open war. Of wiles I make no boast, being less expert; let those who need such things contrive them, or contrive them when they need them — not now.

For, while they sit contriving, shall the rest of us — millions who stand in arms and longingly await the signal to ascend — sit lingering here as Heaven's fugitives, and accept for our dwelling-place this dark and shameful den, the prison of his tyranny who reigns by our delay? No! Let us rather choose, armed with Hell-flames and fury, to force an irresistible way all at once over Heaven's high towers, turning our tortures into horrid arms against our Torturer. Then, to meet the noise of his almighty engine, he shall hear infernal thunder, and, for lightning, see black fire and horror shot with equal rage among his Angels, and his throne itself mixed with Tartarean sulphur and strange fire — his own invented torments. But perhaps the way seems difficult and steep to scale with upright wing against a higher foe.

Let those who think so remember — if the sleepy drench of that forgetful lake does not still benumb them — that it is our proper motion to ascend upward to our native seat; descent and fall are what are adverse to us. Who did not feel just lately, when the fierce foe hung on our broken rear insulting us, and pursued us through the Deep, with what compulsion and laborious flight we sank thus low? The ascent is easy, then.

It is the outcome that is feared. Should we again provoke our stronger enemy, his wrath may find some worse way to destroy us — if there is in Hell any fear of being worse destroyed. What can be worse than to dwell here, driven out from bliss, condemned in this abhorred deep to utter woe?

Here the pain of unextinguishable fire must exercise us without hope of end, as the vassals of his anger, when the scourge inexorably and the torturing hour call us to penance. More destroyed than thus, we should be quite abolished and expire.

What, then, do we fear? What do we doubt — to provoke his utmost ire? — which, enraged to the utmost, will either quite consume us, and reduce this essential being of ours to nothing (happier far than to have eternal being in misery), or, if our substance is truly divine and cannot cease to be, then we are at worst just on this side of nothing; and by experience we feel that our power is sufficient to disturb his Heaven, and with perpetual inroads to alarm — though we cannot breach it — his fatal throne. Which, if not victory, is still revenge."

He ended frowning, and his look proclaimed desperate revenge and a battle dangerous to all less than gods. On the other side rose up Belial, more graceful and humane in his manner. A fairer person lost not Heaven; he seemed composed for dignity and high exploit.

But all was false and hollow. Though his tongue dropped manna, and could make the worse reason seem the better, to perplex and dash the most mature counsels, his thoughts were low — industrious for vice, but timorous and slothful for nobler deeds. Yet he pleased the ear, and with persuasive accent thus began: "I should be very much for open war, O Peers, as being not behind anyone in hate, if the very argument most urged as reason to persuade immediate war did not most dissuade me, and seem to cast ominous conjecture on the whole outcome.

When he who most excels in feats of arms — mistrustful in what he counsels and in what he excels at — grounds his courage on despair and utter dissolution, as the scope of all his aim, after some dire revenge,

first, I ask: what revenge? The towers of Heaven are filled with armed watches that render all access impregnable. Often on the bordering Deep their legions encamp, or with obscure wing scout far and wide into the realm of Night, scorning surprise. Or, if we could force our way by violence, and all Hell should rise at our heels in blackest insurrection to confound Heaven's purest light — yet our great Enemy, all incorruptible, would sit unpolluted on his throne, and the ethereal mould, incapable of stain, would soon expel our mischief and purge off our baser fire, victorious. Thus repulsed, our final hope is flat despair: we must exasperate the Almighty Victor to spend all his rage.

And that must end us; that must be our cure — to be no more. A sad cure! For who would willingly lose, though full of pain, this intellectual being, those thoughts that wander through eternity, to perish instead, swallowed up and lost in the wide womb of uncreated Night, devoid of sense and motion? And who knows, even granting this to be good, whether our angry Foe can give it, or ever will? That he can is doubtful; that he never will is certain.

Will he, so wise, let loose his ire all at once, likely through impotence or inadvertence, to give his enemies their wish and end in his anger those whom his anger preserves for endless punishment? "Why, then, do we cease?" say those who counsel war. "We are decreed, reserved, and destined to eternal woe.

Whatever we do, what can we suffer more? What can we suffer worse?" Is this, then, worst — sitting thus, consulting thus, armed thus? What about when we fled amain, pursued and struck with Heaven's afflicting thunder, and begged the Deep to shelter us? This Hell then seemed a refuge from those wounds. Or when we lay chained on the burning lake? That was surely worse.

What if the breath that kindled those grim fires, if once awakened, should blow them into sevenfold rage, and plunge us in the flames? Or what if from above his intermitted vengeance should again arm his red right hand to plague us? What if all her stores were opened, and this firmament of Hell should spout her cataracts of fire — impending horrors, threatening a hideous fall one day on our heads — while we, perhaps, designing or exhorting glorious war, caught in a fiery tempest, shall be hurled, each transfixed on his rock, the sport and prey of racking whirlwinds, or forever sunk under that boiling ocean, wrapped in chains, there to converse with everlasting groans, without respite, without pity, without reprieve, through ages of hopeless end? This would be worse.

War, therefore, whether open or concealed, my voice alike dissuades. For what can force or guile do against him? Who can deceive his mind, whose eye views all things at a single view? From Heaven's height he sees all these vain motions of ours and derides them — not more almighty to resist our might than wise to frustrate all our plots and wiles.

Shall we, then, live thus vile — the race of Heaven thus trampled, thus expelled, to suffer chains and these torments here? By my advice, better these than worse. Since inevitable fate subdues us, and omnipotent decree, the Victor's will — to suffer is equal in strength to doing, nor is the law unjust that so ordains. This was first resolved, if we were wise, when contending against so great a foe, and so doubtful of what might befall.

I laugh when those who are bold and venturous with the spear, if that fails them, shrink and fear what they yet know must follow — to endure exile, or ignominy, or bonds, or pain, the sentence of their Conqueror. This is now our doom. If we can sustain and bear it, our Supreme Foe may in time much remit his anger; and perhaps, so far removed, he will not mind us if we do not offend, satisfied with what is already punished. Then these raging fires will slacken, if his breath does not stir their flames.

Our purer essence will then overcome their noxious vapour; or, inured, we shall not feel them; or, changed at length, and conformed in temper and nature to the place, we shall receive the fierce heat as familiar, and, void of pain, this horror will grow mild and this darkness light.

Besides all this, there is hope of what the never-ending flight of future days may bring — what chance, what change might be worth waiting for — since our present lot appears, if not happy but still only ill, at least not the worst of ills, so long as we do not procure more woe for ourselves."

Thus Belial, with words clothed in the garb of reason, counselled ignoble ease and peaceful sloth — not true peace. And after him Mammon thus spoke: "Either we make war to unseat the King of Heaven, if war be best, or we war to regain our own lost right. To unthrone him we may hope only when everlasting Fate shall yield to fickle Chance, and Chaos shall judge the strife.

The former being vain to hope, it argues the latter equally vain. For what place can there be for us within Heaven's bound, unless we overpower Heaven's supreme Lord? Suppose he should relent and publish grace to all, on promise of renewed subjection: with what eyes could we stand humble in his presence, receive the strict laws imposed on us, to celebrate his throne with warbled hymns, and sing forced hallelujahs to his Godhead, while he sits lordly, our envied sovereign, and his altar breathes ambrosial odours and ambrosial flowers — our servile offerings? This must be our task in Heaven, this our delight. How wearisome — an eternity so spent in worship paid to one we hate! Let us, then, not pursue by impossible force, nor by leave obtained that would be unacceptable — even in Heaven — our state of splendid vassalage. Let us rather seek our own good from ourselves, and, from our own resources, live to ourselves, though in this vast recess, free and accountable to none, preferring hard liberty to the easy yoke of servile pomp. Our greatness will then appear most conspicuous, when we can create great things out of small, useful things out of hurtful, prosperous out of adverse, and thrive under evil in whatever place, working ease out of pain by labour and endurance. Do we dread this deep world of darkness? How often amid thick clouds and dark does Heaven's all-ruling Sire choose to reside, his glory unobscured, and with the majesty of darkness around him cover his throne, from whence deep thunders roar,

mustering their rage, so that Heaven resembles Hell! As he imitates our darkness, cannot we imitate his light when we please? This desert soil does not lack its hidden lustre, gems, and gold. Nor do we lack skill or art from which to raise magnificence. And what more can Heaven show?

Our torments also may, in length of time, become our natural elements: these piercing fires may grow as soft as they are now severe, our temper being changed to match their temper, which must of necessity remove the feeling of pain. All things invite us to peaceful counsels, and the settled state of order — how we may in safety best compose our present evils, with regard to what we are and where, dismissing quite all thoughts of war. You have what I advise."

He had scarcely finished, when such a murmur filled the assembly as when hollow rocks retain the sound of blustering winds, which had all night roused the sea, now with hoarse cadence lulling seafaring men over-watched, whose bark or pinnace, by chance, anchors in a craggy bay after the tempest. Such applause was heard as Mammon ended, and his judgement pleased, counselling peace. For they dreaded another such battlefield worse than Hell itself: so much did the fear of thunder and the sword of Michael still work within them, and no less the desire to found this nether empire, which might rise by policy and long process of time into a rival opposite to Heaven.

When Beelzebub perceived this — than whom, except for Satan, none higher sat — with grave aspect he rose, and in his rising seemed a pillar of state. Deliberation sat engraved deeply on his brow, and public care.

Princely counsel yet shone in his face, majestic though in ruin. Like a sage he stood, with Atlantean shoulders fit to bear the weight of mightiest monarchies. His look drew audience and attention, still as night or summer's noontide air, while thus he spoke: "Thrones and Imperial Powers, Offspring of Heaven, Ethereal Virtues! — or must we now renounce these titles, and, changing our style, be called Princes of Hell? For so the popular vote inclines — to continue here and build up a growing empire — doubtless! — while we dream, and do not know that the King of Heaven has doomed this place to be our dungeon, not our safe retreat beyond his potent arm; has doomed us not to live exempt from Heaven's high jurisdiction, banded in new league against his throne, but to remain in the strictest bondage, though thus far removed, under the inevitable curb, reserved as his captive multitude. For he, most certainly, in height or depth, still first and last will reign sole king, and will lose no part of his kingdom by our revolt, but will extend his empire over Hell, and with an iron sceptre rule us here, as with his golden one he rules those in Heaven.

Why, then, do we sit projecting peace and war? War has determined us and foiled us with irreparable loss. No terms of peace have yet been vouchsafed or sought. For what peace will be given to us, enslaved, but severe custody, stripes, and arbitrary punishment inflicted on us? And what peace can we return, but, as far as in our power lies, hostility and hate, untamed reluctance, and revenge — though slow, yet ever plotting how the Conqueror may least reap his conquest, and least rejoice in doing what we most in suffering feel?

Nor will occasion be lacking, nor shall we need to invade Heaven by a dangerous expedition — Heaven whose high walls fear no assault or siege, no ambush from the Deep. What if we find some easier enterprise? There is a place — if ancient and prophetic fame in Heaven does not err — another World, the happy seat of some new race called Man, who is about this time to be created like us, though less in power and excellence, but more favoured by him who rules above. So was his will pronounced among the Gods, and confirmed by an oath that shook Heaven's whole circumference.

Thither let us bend all our thoughts, to learn what creatures inhabit it, of what mould or substance, how endowed, what their power is, and where their weakness lies — how they may best be attacked, by force or by subtlety. Though Heaven be shut, and Heaven's high Arbitrator sits secure in his own strength, this place may lie exposed, the utmost border of his kingdom, left to the defence of those who hold it. Here, perhaps, some advantageous act may be achieved by sudden onset — either to waste his whole creation with Hell-fire, or to possess it all as our own, and drive the puny inhabitants out as we were driven; or, if not drive them, to seduce them to our party, so that their God may prove their foe, and, with repenting hand, abolish his own works. This would surpass common revenge, interrupt his joy in our confusion, and raise our joy by his disturbance, when his darling sons, hurled headlong to share our lot, shall curse their frail origin and their faded bliss — faded so soon! Advise whether this is worth attempting, or whether we should sit here in darkness hatching vain empires." Thus Beelzebub pleaded his devilish counsel — first devised by Satan, and in part proposed by him. For from where, but from the author of all ill, could spring so deep a malice — to confound the race of mankind in its one root, and to mingle and involve Earth with Hell, all to spite the great Creator? But their spite still serves to augment his glory. The bold design highly pleased those infernal States, and joy sparkled in all their eyes. With full assent they voted. Whereupon he renewed his speech: "Well have you judged, well ended the long debate, Synod of Gods. Like what you are, you have resolved great things, which from the lowest deep will once more lift us up, in spite of fate, nearer our ancient seat — perhaps within view of those bright confines, from which, with neighbouring arms and opportune excursion, we may chance to re-enter Heaven; or else to dwell in some mild zone, not unvisited of Heaven's fair light, secure, and at the brightening orient beam purge off this gloom; and the soft, delicious air, to heal the scars of these corrosive fires, shall breathe her balm. But first, whom shall we send in search of this new World? Whom shall we find sufficient? Who shall tempt with wandering feet the dark, unbottomed, infinite Abyss, and through the palpable obscure find out his strange way, or spread his airy flight, borne up with indefatigable wings over the vast chasm, before he arrives at the happy Isle? What strength, what art, will then suffice? What evasion can bear him safely through the strict sentries and thick stations of watching Angels? Here he will need all circumspection; and we now need no less care in our choice — for on the one we send, the weight of all, and our last hope, relies."

This said, he sat down. Expectation held his look in suspense, as he awaited who would appear to second, to oppose, or to undertake the perilous attempt. But all sat mute, pondering the danger with deep thoughts; and each read in another's countenance his own dismay, astonished. None among the choice and prime of those Heaven-warring champions could be found so bold as to offer or accept, alone, the dreadful voyage. Until at last Satan, whom now transcendent glory raised above his fellows, with monarchal pride conscious of highest worth, unmoved, thus spoke: "O Progeny of Heaven! Empyreal Thrones!

With reason has deep silence and hesitation seized us, though we are undismayed. Long is the way and hard, that leads out of Hell up to the light. Our prison is strong — this huge convex of fire, outrageous to devour, immures us round ninefold, and gates of burning adamant, barred above us, prohibit all egress.

These once passed, if any may pass them, the void abyss of unessential Night receives him next, wide-gaping, and with utter loss of being threatens him, plunged in that abortive gulf. If from there he escapes into whatever world, or unknown region, what remains for him but unknown dangers, and escape equally hard?

But I would ill become this throne, O Peers, and this imperial sovereignty, adorned with splendour and armed with power, if any matter proposed and judged of public moment could deter me from attempting it, in the shape of difficulty or danger. Why do I assume these royalties and not refuse to reign, if I refuse to accept as great a share of hazard as of honour — both due alike to him who reigns, and more hazard is due to him by as much as he is high-honoured above the rest? Go, therefore, mighty Powers, Terror of Heaven, though fallen; at home — while this shall be our home — attend to what may best ease our present misery and render Hell more tolerable, if there is any cure or charm to respite, deceive, or slacken the pain of this ill mansion. Do not interrupt your watch against a wakeful foe, while I abroad through all the coasts of dark destruction seek deliverance for us all. This enterprise none shall share with me." So saying, the Monarch rose, and prevented any reply;

prudent, lest, emboldened by his resolution, others among the chief might now offer what they had before feared — certain to be refused — and, so refused, might stand in opinion as his rivals, winning cheap the high repute that he must earn through huge hazard. But they dreaded the adventure no more than they dreaded his voice forbidding it, and at once rose with him.

Their rising all at once was like the sound of thunder heard remote. Toward him they bend with awful reverence prone, and as a God extol him equal to the Highest in Heaven. Nor did they fail to express how much they praised him for despising his own safety for the general good. For not even the damned Spirits lose all their virtue — lest wicked men should boast of their specious deeds on earth, which glory excites, or of close ambition varnished over with zeal.

Thus they ended their doubtful, dark consultations, rejoicing in their matchless Chief — as when from mountaintops the dusky clouds, ascending while the north wind sleeps, overspread Heaven's cheerful face, and the lowering element scowls over the darkened landscape with snow or shower; yet if by chance the radiant sun, with a sweet farewell, extends his evening beam, the fields revive, the birds renew their notes, and the bleating herds attest their joy, so that hill and valley ring.

O shame to men! Devil with devil damned holds firm concord; men only, among all rational creatures, disagree — though they are under the hope of heavenly grace, and though God proclaims peace, yet they live in hatred, enmity, and strife among themselves, and levy cruel wars wasting the earth, each seeking to destroy the other;
as if — which might well induce us to accord — Man had not hellish foes enough besides, who day and night lie waiting for his destruction!

The Stygian council being thus dissolved, the grand infernal Peers came forth in order. In their midst came their mighty Paramount, and seemed alone the antagonist of Heaven, no less than Hell's dread Emperor, with supreme pomp and god-like imitated state. A globe of fiery Seraphim encircled him, with bright emblazonry and bristling arms.

Then, their session being ended, they commanded a proclamation of the great result with the sound of regal trumpets. Toward the four winds four speedy Cherubim put the sounding alchemy trumpets to their mouths; and, explained by a herald's voice, the hollow Abyss heard far and wide, and all the host of Hell returned the acclamation with a deafening shout.

From this their minds were somewhat at greater ease, and somewhat raised by false presumptuous hope. The ranked Powers disband; and, wandering, each pursues his own way, as inclination or sad choice leads him perplexed, where he may most likely find truce to his restless thoughts and entertain the irksome hours until his great Chief's return.

Some on the plain, or in the air sublime, contend upon the wing or in swift race, as at the Olympian games or Pythian fields. Others curb their fiery steeds, or shun the goal with rapid wheels, or form fronting brigades —

as when, to warn proud cities, war appears waged in the troubled sky, and armies rush to battle in the clouds; before each vanguard the airy knights prick forth and couch their spears, until the thickest legions close; with feats of arms from either end of heaven the sky burns.

Others, with vast Typhoean rage, more fell, rend up both rocks and hills, and ride the air in a whirlwind; Hell scarcely holds the wild uproar — as when Alcides (Hercules), from Oechalia crowned with conquest, felt the envenomed robe, and in his pain tore Thessalian pines up by the roots, and hurled Lichas from the top of Oeta into the Euboic sea. Others, more mild, retreated to a silent valley, and there, to many a harp, sang with angelic notes their own heroic deeds and their unhappy fall by the doom of battle, and complained that Fate should enthral free Virtue to Force or Chance.

Their song was biased; but the harmony — what less could it be when immortal Spirits sing? — suspended Hell, and took the thronging audience with ravishment. In discourse more sweet (for Eloquence charms the Soul, Song charms the Sense) others apart sat on a retired hill, in thoughts more elevated, and reasoned high of Providence, Foreknowledge, Will, and Fate — fixed fate, free will, foreknowledge absolute — and found no end, lost in wandering mazes.

Of good and evil they argued much at that time, of happiness and final misery, of passion and apathy, of glory and shame — all vain wisdom and false philosophy! Yet, with a pleasing sorcery, it could charm pain for a while, or anguish, and excite fallacious hope, or arm the obdurate breast with stubborn patience, as with triple steel.

Another part, in squadrons and gross bands, on bold adventure to discover wide that dismal world — if any clime perhaps might yield them easier habitation — bend their flying march four ways, along the banks of four infernal rivers that disgorge their baleful streams into the burning lake: abhorred Styx, the flood of deadly hate;

sad Acheron of sorrow, black and deep; Cocytus, named from the loud lamentation heard on the rueful stream; fierce Phlegeton, whose waves of torrent fire inflame with rage. Far off from these, a slow and silent stream — Lethe, the river of oblivion — rolls her watery labyrinth, and whoever drinks of her forthwith forgets his former state and being — forgets both joy and grief, pleasure and pain.

Beyond this flood lies a frozen continent, dark and wild, beaten with perpetual storms of whirlwind and dire hail, which on firm land does not thaw but gathers in heaps and seems the ruin of some ancient edifice. All else is deep snow and ice, a gulf as profound as that Serbonian bog between Damiata and old Mount Casius, where whole armies have sunk. The parching air burns frore, and cold performs the effect of fire.

Thither, hauled by harpy-footed Furies, at certain revolutions all the damned are brought; and feel by turns the bitter change of fierce extremes — extremes made fiercer by the change — from beds of raging fire to starve in ice their soft ethereal warmth, and there to pine, immovable, fixed, and frozen round for long periods of time, then hurried back to fire.

They ferry over this Lethean sound both to and fro, their sorrow to augment, and wish and struggle as they pass to reach the tempting stream — to lose, with one small drop, in sweet forgetfulness all pain and woe in a single moment — and so near the brink.

But Fate withstands, and, to oppose their attempt, Medusa with Gorgonian terror guards the ford; and the water of itself flies from all taste of any living being, as once it fled the lip of Tantalus. Thus roving on in confused, forlorn march, the adventurous bands, pale with shuddering horror and with eyes aghast, first viewed their lamentable lot, and found no rest. Through many a dark and dreary vale they passed, and many a dolorous region, over many a frozen and many a fiery alp, rocks, caves, lakes, fens, bogs, dens, and shades of death — a universe of death, which God by curse created evil, for evil only good;

where all life dies, death lives, and Nature, perverse, breeds all monstrous, all prodigious things — abominable, unutterable, and worse than fables have yet feigned or fear conceived — Gorgons, and Hydras, and dire Chimeras.

Meanwhile the Adversary of God and Man, Satan, with thoughts inflamed with highest design, puts on swift wings and toward the gates of Hell explores his solitary flight. Sometimes he scours the right-hand coast, sometimes the left;

now he shaves with level wing the deep, then soars up to the fiery concave towering high. As when, far off at sea, a fleet is descried hanging in the clouds, close-sailing from Bengala by equinoctial winds, or from the isles of Ternate and Tidore — from where merchants bring their spicy drugs; and on the trading flood, through the wide Ethiopian sea to the Cape, they ply stemming nightly toward the pole: so seemed the flying Fiend far off. At last appear Hell's bounds, high reaching to the horrid roof, and gates thrice threefold; three folds were brass, three were iron, three of adamantine rock, impenetrable, impaled with circling fire, yet unconsumed. Before the gates there sat, on either side, a formidable Shape.

The one seemed woman to the waist, and fair, but ended foul in many a scaly fold — voluminous and vast — a serpent armed with mortal sting. About her middle round a cry of Hell-hounds, never ceasing, barked with wide Cerberean mouths full loud, and rang out a hideous peal. Yet, when they wished, they would creep, if anything disturbed their noise, into her womb, and kennel there; yet there still barked and howled within unseen. Far less abhorred than these were those that vexed Scylla, bathing in the sea that parts Calabria from the hoarse Trinacrian shore;

nor uglier those that follow the night-hag, when, called in secret, she rides through the air, lured by the smell of infant blood, to dance with Lapland witches, while the labouring moon eclipses at their charms. The other Shape — if shape it might be called, that shape had none distinguishable in member, joint, or limb;

or substance might be called, what shadow seemed — for each seemed either: it stood black as Night, fierce as ten Furies, terrible as Hell, and shook a dreadful dart. What seemed his head bore the likeness of a kingly crown.

Satan was now at hand, and from his seat the monster moved forward as fast with horrid strides. Hell trembled as he strode. The undaunted Fiend wondered what this might be — wondered, not feared (except God and his Son, no created thing did he value or shun) — and with disdainful look thus began: "From whence and what are you, execrable Shape, that dare, though grim and terrible, to advance your miscreated front across my way to those gates yonder? I mean to pass through them — be assured — without leave asked of you. Retire; or taste your folly and learn by proof, Hell-born thing, not to contend with Spirits of Heaven."

To whom the Goblin, full of wrath, replied: "Are you that traitor Angel? Are you he who first broke peace in Heaven and faith, till then unbroken, and in proud rebellious arms drew after him the third part of Heaven's sons, conspired against the Highest — for which both you and they, outcast from God, are condemned here to waste eternal days in woe and pain?

And do you reckon yourself among Spirits of Heaven, Hell-doomed as you are, and breathe defiance and scorn here, where I reign king — and, to enrage you more, your king and lord? Back to your punishment, false fugitive; and to your speed add wings, lest with a whip of scorpions I pursue your lingering, or with one stroke of this dart seize you with strange horror and with pangs unfelt before."

So spoke the grisly Terror, and in shape, speaking and threatening so, grew tenfold more dreadful and deformed. On the other side, incensed with indignation, Satan stood unterrified, and burned like a comet that fires the length of huge Ophiuchus in the arctic sky, and from his horrid hair shakes pestilence and war. Each levelled his deadly aim at the head; their fatal hands intend no second stroke. And each cast such a frown at the other as when two black clouds, fraught with heaven's artillery, came rattling on over the Caspian — then stand front to front hovering for a space, until winds give the signal to join their dark encounter in mid-air.

So frowned the mighty combatants that Hell grew darker at their frown. So matched they stood; for never but once more was there to be such a matching of so great a foe. And now great deeds would have been done, of which all Hell would have rung, had not the snaky Sorceress who sat close by Hell-gate and kept the fatal key risen, and with hideous outcry rushed between them.

"O father, what does your hand intend," she cried, "against your only son? What fury, O son, possesses you, to bend that mortal dart against your father's head? And do you know for whom? For him who sits above, and laughs the while at you, ordained his drudge to execute whatever his wrath — which he calls justice — bids; his wrath, which one day will destroy you both!"

She spoke, and at her words the hellish Pest forbore. Then Satan returned these words to her: "So strange is your outcry, and so strange are the words you interpose, that my sudden hand, prevented, forbears to tell you yet by deeds what it intends, until I first know from you what thing you are, thus double-formed, and why, first met in this infernal vale, you call me father, and call that phantasm my son. I do not know you, nor have I ever seen till now a sight more detestable than him and you."

To whom thus the Portress of Hell-gate replied: "Have you then forgotten me? Do I seem now to your eye so foul — I who was once deemed so fair in Heaven, when at the assembly, and in sight of all the Seraphim combined with you in bold conspiracy against Heaven's King, all on a sudden miserable pain surprised you, your eyes grew dim and dizzy with darkness, while your head threw forth thick and fast flames, until on your left side, opening wide, I sprang out of your head — most like you in shape and bright countenance, then shining heavenly fair, a goddess armed? Amazement seized all the host of Heaven. At first they recoiled back afraid, and called me Sin, and held me for a portentous sign. But, growing familiar, I pleased, and with attractive graces won the most averse — you chiefly, who, often viewing in me your own perfect image, became enamoured; and took such joy with me in secret that my womb conceived a growing burden. Meanwhile war arose, and fields were fought in Heaven, wherein there remained — for what else could? — clear victory to our Almighty Foe, and loss and rout to our part, throughout all the Empyrean. Down they fell, driven headlong from the pitch of Heaven, down into this Deep; and in the general fall I fell also. At that time this powerful key was given into my hands, with charge to keep these gates forever shut, which none can pass without my opening. Pensive here I sat alone; but I did not sit long, until my womb, pregnant by you and now excessively grown, felt prodigious motion and rueful throes.

At last this odious offspring whom you see, your own begotten, breaking violently on his way, tore through my entrails, so that my whole nether shape, distorted with fear and pain, grew thus transformed. But he, my inbred enemy, issued forth, brandishing his fatal dart, made to destroy. I fled, and cried out "Death!"

Hell trembled at the hideous name, and sighed from all her caves, and resounded back "Death!" I fled; but he pursued — though more inflamed, it seems, with lust than rage — and, far swifter, overtook me, his mother, all dismayed; and in forcible and foul embraces engendering with me, begot from that rape these yelling monsters that with ceaseless cry surround me, as you saw — hourly conceived and hourly born, with infinite sorrow to me. For, when they wish, they return into the womb that bore them, and howl, and gnaw my bowels, their repast; then, bursting forth afresh, with conscious terrors vex me round, so that I find no rest or intermission.

Before my eyes, in opposition, sits grim Death, my son and foe, who set them on; and he would soon devour me, his parent, for want of other prey, but that he knows his end is involved with mine, and knows that I should prove a bitter morsel, and his bane, whenever that shall be — so Fate has pronounced.

But you, O father, I forewarn you — shun his deadly arrow; nor vainly hope to be invulnerable in those bright arms, though tempered in heaven. For that mortal stroke, except him who reigns above, none can resist."

She finished; and the subtle Fiend soon learned his lesson, now milder, and answered smoothly: "Dear daughter — since you claim me for your sire, and here show me my fair son, the dear pledge of dalliance had with you in Heaven, and joys then sweet, now sad to mention through the dire change befallen us, unforeseen and unthought of — know, I come no enemy, but to set free from this dark and dismal house of pain both him and you, and all the heavenly host of Spirits who, armed in our just claims, fell with us from on high. From them I go on this strange errand alone, and one for all myself expose, with lonely steps to tread the unfounded Deep, and through the void immense to search out, with wandering quest, a place foretold should be — and, by concurring signs, must already have been created vast and round — a place of bliss in the neighbourhood of Heaven; and therein placed a race of upstart creatures, to supply perhaps our vacant room, though more removed, lest Heaven, surcharged with a potent multitude, might happen to move new broils. Be this, or whatever more secret matter is now designed, I hasten to know. And, once this is known, I shall soon return, and bring you both to the place where you and Death shall dwell at ease, and up and down unseen wing silently the buxom air, embalmed with odours. There you shall be fed and filled immeasurably; all things shall be your prey."

He ceased; for both seemed highly pleased, and Death grinned horribly a ghastly smile, to hear that his famine should be filled, and blessed his maw destined for that good hour. No less rejoiced his wicked mother, and thus addressed her sire: "The key of this infernal Pit, by due right and by command of Heaven's all-powerful King, I keep, forbidden by him to unlock these adamantine gates. Against all force, Death stands ready to interpose his dart, fearless of being overmatched by any living might.

But what do I owe to his commands above, who hates me, and has thrust me down here into this gloom of profound Tartarus, to sit in hateful office here confined — I, an inhabitant of Heaven and heavenly born — here in perpetual agony and pain, compassed round with terrors and clamours from my own brood, who feed on my bowels?

You are my father; you are my author; you gave me my being. Whom should I obey but you? Whom should I follow? You will bring me soon to that new world of light and bliss, among the gods who live at ease, where I shall reign at your right hand voluptuous, as befits your daughter and your darling, without end."

So saying, from her side she took the fatal key — sad instrument of all our woe. Rolling her bestial train toward the gate, she forthwith drew up high the huge portcullis, which none of all the Stygian Powers but she could have moved. Then in the keyhole she turns the intricate wards, and unfastens with ease every bolt and bar of massive iron or solid rock. On a sudden, the infernal doors fly open with impetuous recoil and jarring sound, and on their hinges grate harsh thunder, which shook the lowest bottom of Erebus. She opened; but to shut was beyond her power. The gates stood wide open, so that with extended wings a bannered host, marching under spread ensigns, might pass through with horse and chariots ranked in loose array:

so wide they stood. Like a furnace-mouth, they cast forth redounding smoke and ruddy flame. Before their eyes in sudden view appear the secrets of the hoary Deep — a dark, illimitable ocean, without bound, without dimension — where length, breadth, and height, and time, and place, are lost; where eldest Night and Chaos, ancestors of Nature, hold eternal anarchy, amid the noise of endless wars, and by confusion stand.

For Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry — four fierce champions — strive here for mastery, and bring their embryo atoms to battle. Around the flag of each faction, in their several clans, light-armed or heavy, sharp, smooth, swift, or slow, they swarm populous, unnumbered as the sands of Barca or Cyrene's torrid soil, levied to side with warring winds, and poise their lighter wings. Whoever they most adhere to rules for a moment. Chaos sits as umpire; and by his decision only further embroils the fray, by which he reigns. Next to him, as high arbiter, Chance governs all. Into this wild Abyss — the womb of Nature, and perhaps her grave — of neither sea, nor shore, nor air, nor fire, but all these mixed confusedly in their pregnant causes, and which must thus ever fight, unless the Almighty Maker ordain them his dark materials to create more worlds — into this wild Abyss the wary Fiend stood on the brink of Hell and looked a while, pondering his voyage; for it was no narrow firth he had to cross. Nor was his ear less pealed with loud and ruinous noises (to compare great things with small) than when Bellona storms with all her battering engines, bent to raze some capital city; or less than if this frame of Heaven were falling, and these elements, in mutiny, had torn the steadfast Earth from her axle. At last he spread his sail-broad vans for flight, and, uplifted in the surging smoke, spurns the ground; thence for many a league, as in a cloudy chair, ascending rides audacious. But that seat soon failing, he meets a vast vacuity. All unawares, fluttering his pennons vain, plumb-down he drops ten thousand fathoms deep — and to this hour would still have been falling, had not, by ill chance, the strong rebuff of some tumultuous cloud, instinct with fire and nitre, hurried him as many miles aloft. That fury stayed — quenched in a boggy Syrtis, neither sea nor good dry land — nigh foundered, on he fares, treading the crude consistence, half on foot, half flying; he needs now both oar and sail.

As when a gryphon through the wilderness with winged course, over hill or moory dale, pursues the Arimaspian who by stealth had purloined from his wakeful custody the guarded gold; so eagerly the Fiend over bog or steep, through strait, rough, dense, or rare, with head, hands, wings, or feet, pursues his way, and swims, or sinks, or wades, or creeps, or flies.

At length a universal wild hubbub of stunning sounds, and voices all confused, borne through the hollow dark, assaults his ear with loudest vehemence. Thither he plies undaunted, to meet whatever Power or Spirit of the nethermost Abyss might reside in that noise, of whom to ask which way the nearest coast of darkness lies bordering on light. When straightway, behold, the throne of Chaos, and his dark pavilion spread wide on the wasteful Deep!
