With him enthroned sat sable-vested Night, eldest of things, the consort of his reign; and by them stood Orcus and Ades, and the dreaded name of Demogorgon; Rumour next, and Chance, and Tumult, and Confusion, all embroiled, and Discord with a thousand various mouths.

To whom Satan, turning boldly, thus spoke: "You Powers and Spirits of this nethermost Abyss, Chaos and ancient Night, I come no spy with purpose to explore or to disturb the secrets of your realm. But, by constraint wandering this darksome desert, since my way lies through your spacious empire up to light, alone and without guide, half lost, I seek what readiest path leads to where your gloomy bounds border on Heaven; or, if some other place, won from your dominion, the Ethereal King has lately possessed, I travel this profound to arrive there. Direct my course.

And, once directed, no mean recompense it brings to your behoof, if I shall reduce that lost region (now that all usurpation is expelled from there) to her original darkness and to your sway — which is my present journey — and once more erect there the standard of ancient Night. Yours be all the advantage, mine the revenge!"

Thus Satan. And to him thus the Anarch old, with faltering speech and uncomposed visage, answered: "I know you, stranger, who you are — that mighty leading Angel, who lately made a stand against Heaven's King, though overthrown.

I saw and heard; for such a numerous host did not flee in silence through the frightened Deep, with ruin upon ruin, rout on rout, confusion worse confounded; and Heaven-gates poured out her victorious bands by millions, in pursuit. I on my frontiers here keep residence; if all I can do will serve so to defend that little which is left, still encroached upon through our intestine broils weakening the sceptre of old Night. First, Hell — your dungeon — stretches far and wide beneath;

and now lately Heaven and Earth, another World hung over my realm, linked in a golden chain to that side of Heaven from whence your legions fell. If that way is your walk, you have not far; so much the nearer is the danger. Go, and speed; havoc, and spoil, and ruin are my gain."

He ceased; and Satan did not stay to reply, but, glad that his sea should now find a shore, with fresh alacrity and renewed force sprang upward, like a pyramid of fire, into the wild expanse. And through the shock of fighting elements, encircled on all sides, he won his way — harder beset and more endangered than when the Argo passed through the Bosporus between the jostling rocks, or when Ulysses on the larboard shunned Charybdis and steered by the other whirlpool.

So with difficulty and labour hard he moved on — with difficulty and labour, he. But once he had passed, soon after, when Man fell, strange alteration: Sin and Death amain, following his track (such was the will of Heaven), paved after him a broad and beaten way over the dark Abyss, whose boiling gulf tamely endured a bridge of wondrous length, continued from Hell and reaching to the utmost orb of this frail World — by which the perverse Spirits with easy intercourse pass to and fro to tempt or punish mortals, except those whom God and good Angels guard by special grace.

But now at last the sacred influence of light appears; and from the walls of Heaven it shoots a glimmering dawn far into the bosom of dim Night. Here Nature first begins her farthest verge, and Chaos retires, as from her outmost works, a broken foe, with less tumult and with less hostile din,

so that Satan, with less toil and now with ease, wafts on the calmer wave by dubious light, and, like a weather-beaten vessel, gladly holds port, though shrouds and tackle are torn; or in the emptier waste, resembling air, weighs his spread wings, at leisure to behold far off the empyreal Heaven, extended wide in circuit, undetermined whether square or round, adorned with opal towers and battlements of living sapphire — once his native seat;

and, close by, hanging in a golden chain, this pendent World, in size like a star of smallest magnitude close by the moon. Thither, full fraught with mischievous revenge, accursed, and in a cursed hour, he hastens.

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: Hail, holy Light, firstborn offspring of Heaven! Or may I, unblamed, express you as a beam coeternal with the Eternal? Since God is light, and never, except in unapproached light, dwelt from eternity — dwelt then in you, bright effluence of bright uncreated essence.

Or do you prefer to be called a pure ethereal stream, whose fountain who shall tell? You were before the sun, before the Heavens; and at the voice of God, as with a mantle, you invested the rising world of waters dark and deep, won from the void and formless infinite.

You I revisit now with bolder wing, having escaped the Stygian pool, though long detained in that obscure sojourn, while in my flight I was borne through utter and through middle darkness, with other notes than to the Orphean lyre I sang of Chaos and eternal Night —

taught by the heavenly Muse to venture down the dark descent and to re-ascend, though that is hard and rare. You I revisit safe, and feel your sovereign vital lamp. But you do not revisit these eyes of mine, that roll in vain to find your piercing ray, and find no dawn.

So thick a drop serene has quenched their orbs, or dim suffusion has veiled them. Yet no less do I continue to wander where the Muses haunt — clear spring, or shady grove, or sunny hill — smitten with the love of sacred song. But chiefly you, Sion, and the flowery brooks beneath that wash your hallowed feet, and flow warbling — you nightly I visit. Nor do I sometimes forget those other two who equalled me in fate, so that I might be equalled with them in renown — remembering your sovereign command, that Man should find grace;

blind Thamyris and blind Maeonides, and Tiresias, and Phineus, prophets of old. Then I feed on thoughts that voluntarily move harmonious numbers — as the wakeful bird sings in darkness, and hidden in the shadiest covert tunes her nocturnal note. Thus with the year the seasons return; but to me there returns no day, nor the sweet approach of evening or morning, nor the sight of vernal bloom, or summer's rose, or flocks, or herds, or the divine human face.

But cloud instead, and ever-lasting dark, surrounds me. I am cut off from the cheerful ways of men, and the fair book of knowledge is presented to me with a universal blank, the works of nature being expunged and erased for me, and wisdom at one entrance quite shut out.

So much the rather do you, celestial Light, shine inward, and through all her powers irradiate the mind. There plant eyes, and purge and disperse all mist from them, that I may see and tell of things invisible to mortal sight.

Now had the Almighty Father from above — from the pure empyrean, where he sits high enthroned above all height — bent down his eye to view at once his own works and the works of his creatures. About him all the Sanctities of Heaven stood thick as stars, and from his sight received beatitude beyond utterance. On his right sat the radiant image of his glory, his only Son. On earth he first beheld our two first parents, still the only two of mankind, placed in the happy garden, reaping immortal fruits of joy and love — uninterrupted joy, unrivalled love, in blissful solitude. Then he surveyed Hell and the gulf between, and Satan there, coasting the wall of Heaven on this side of Night, sublime in the dusky air, and ready now to stoop with wearied wings and willing feet on the bare outside of this world — which seemed firm land embosomed without firmament, uncertain whether it was in ocean or in air.

God, beholding him from his high vantage-point, in which he beholds past, present, and future, thus spoke, foreseeing, to his only Son: "Only begotten Son, do you see what rage transports our Adversary? Whom no prescribed bounds, no bars of Hell, nor all the chains heaped on him there, nor yet the wide intervening main abyss, can hold. So bent he seems on desperate revenge, which shall redound upon his own rebellious head. And now, broken loose through all restraint, he wings his way not far from Heaven, in the precincts of light, directly toward the newly created world and Man placed there, with purpose to try whether he can destroy Man by force, or — worse — pervert him by some false guile; and he shall pervert him.

For Man will hearken to his flattering lies, and easily transgress the sole command, the sole pledge of his obedience. So shall he fall, he and his faithless progeny. Whose fault? Whose but his own? Ingrate, he had of me all that he could have. I made him just and right, sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.

Such I created all the ethereal Powers and Spirits, both those who stood and those who failed. Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell. Had they not been free, what sincere proof could they have given of true allegiance, constant faith, or love, where only what they necessarily must do appeared, and not what they would? What praise could they receive?

What pleasure could I take from such obedience paid, when will and reason (reason also being choice) were useless and vain, both despoiled of freedom, both made passive, serving necessity and not me? They, therefore — as was right — were so created; nor can they justly accuse their Maker, or their making, or their fate, as if predestination had overruled their will, disposed by absolute decree or high foreknowledge. They themselves decreed their own revolt, not I. If I foreknew, foreknowledge had no influence on their fault, which would no less have proved certain if unforeknown.

So without the least impulse or shadow of fate, or anything immutably foreseen by me, they trespass, authors to themselves in all, both in what they judge and in what they choose. For so I formed them free; and free they must remain, until they enthrall themselves — otherwise I would have to change their nature, and revoke the high unchangeable, eternal decree which ordained their freedom. They themselves ordained their fall.

The first sort fell by their own suggestion, self-tempted, self-depraved. Man falls, deceived by the other first. Therefore Man shall find grace; the other shall find none. In mercy and justice both, throughout Heaven and Earth, so shall my glory excel;

but Mercy, first and last, shall shine brightest." Thus while God spoke, ambrosial fragrance filled all Heaven, and in the blessed elect Spirits a sense of new, ineffable joy was diffused. Beyond compare the Son of God was seen most glorious; in him all his Father shone substantially expressed. In his face divine compassion visibly appeared, love without end and grace without measure; which uttering, he thus spoke to his Father:

"O Father, gracious was that word which closed your sovereign command — that Man should find grace. For which both Heaven and earth shall highly extol your praises, with the innumerable sound of hymns and sacred songs, by which your throne, encompassed, shall ever resound you blest.

For should Man finally be lost — should Man, your creature late so loved, your youngest son, fall circumvented thus by fraud, though joined with his own folly? Be that far from you, far be that from you, Father, who are judge of all things made, and who judge only in right.

Or shall the Adversary thus obtain his end, and frustrate yours? Shall he fulfil his malice, and bring your goodness to nought; or return proud — though to his heavier doom, yet with revenge accomplished — and draw after him to Hell the whole race of mankind, by him corrupted? Or will you yourself abolish your creation, and unmake for him what you have made for your glory?

So should your goodness and your greatness both be questioned and blasphemed without defence." To whom the great Creator thus replied: "O Son, in whom my soul has chief delight — Son of my bosom, Son who are alone

my word, my wisdom, and effectual might — all you have spoken is as my thoughts are, all as my eternal purpose has decreed. Man shall not wholly be lost, but such shall be saved as will; yet not by any will in him, but by grace in me freely vouchsafed. Once more I will renew his lapsed powers, though forfeit, and enthralled by sin to foul exorbitant desires.
Upheld by me, he shall once more stand on even ground against his mortal foe; upheld by me, that he may know how frail his fallen condition is, and owe to me all his deliverance, and to none but me.

Some I have chosen of peculiar grace, elect above the rest — so is my will. The rest shall hear me call, and oft be warned of their sinful state, and urged in time to appease the incensed Deity while offered grace invites them. For I will clear their dark senses — as much as may suffice — and soften stony hearts to pray, repent, and render due obedience.

To prayer, repentance, and due obedience — though but endeavoured with sincere intent — my ear shall not be slow, my eye not shut. And I will place within them as a guide my umpire Conscience; whom if they will hear, they shall attain, light after light well used, and, persisting to the end, arrive safely.

This my long sufferance and my day of grace — they who neglect and scorn these shall never taste them. But hard shall be hardened, blind be blinded more, that they may stumble on and fall the deeper. And none but such do I exclude from mercy.

But yet all is not done. Man, disobeying, disloyal, breaks his fealty and sins against the high supremacy of Heaven, aspiring to Godhead. And, so losing all, he has nothing left to expiate his treason but — being devoted and consecrated to destruction — to die, he with his whole posterity. Either he must die, or justice must die — unless for him some other, able and willing, pay the rigid satisfaction, death for death.

Say, heavenly Powers, where shall we find such love? Which of you will be mortal, to redeem Man's mortal crime, and, being just, save the unjust? Dwells such dear charity in all Heaven?" He asked, but all the heavenly choir stood mute, and silence was in Heaven. On Man's behalf no patron or intercessor appeared — much less one who dared draw upon his own head the deadly forfeiture, and set the ransom.

And now, without redemption, all mankind would have been lost, adjudged by severe doom to Death and Hell, had not the Son of God, in whom the fulness dwells of love divine, thus renewed his dearest mediation:

"Father, your word is given: Man shall find grace. And shall not grace find means — grace that finds her way the speediest of your winged messengers, visits all your creatures, and comes to all unprevented, unimplored, unsought?

Happy for Man that grace should come so; he himself, once dead in sins and lost, can never seek her aid. He has no atonement for himself, no fit offering, being indebted and undone. Behold me, then: I for him, life for life, offer myself. On me let your anger fall.

Account me Man; I for his sake will leave your bosom, and put off freely this glory next to you, and at last die for him, well pleased. On me let Death wreak all his rage. Under his gloomy power I shall not long lie vanquished. You have given me to possess life in myself forever; by you I live.

Though now I yield to Death, and am his due for all of me that can die — yet, that debt paid, you will not leave me in the loathsome grave as his prey, nor suffer my unspotted soul to dwell there forever with corruption;

but I shall rise victorious, and subdue my vanquisher, spoiled of his vaunted spoil. Death shall then receive his death's wound, and stoop inglorious, disarmed of his mortal sting. I, through the ample air in high triumph, shall lead Hell captive in spite of Hell, and show the powers of darkness bound. You, pleased at the sight, shall from Heaven look down and smile, while, raised by you, I ruin all my foes.

Death last; and with his carcass I shall glut the grave. Then, with the multitude of my redeemed, I shall enter Heaven, long absent, and return, Father, to see your face, wherein no cloud of anger shall remain, but assured peace and reconcilement. Wrath shall be no more thenceforth, but in your presence joy entire."

His words here ended; but his meek aspect, though silent, still spoke, and breathed immortal love to mortal men. Above that, only filial obedience shone. Like a sacrifice glad to be offered, he awaits the will of his great Father. Admiration seized all Heaven — what this might mean, and whither it would tend, they wondered. But soon the Almighty thus replied:

"O you, in Heaven and Earth the only peace found out for mankind under wrath — O you, my sole delight! Well you know how dear to me are all my works; nor Man the least, though last created, since for him I spare you from my bosom and right hand, to save, by losing you for a while, the whole race that was lost.

You, therefore, whom you alone can redeem, join their nature also to your nature. Be yourself Man among men on Earth, made flesh, when time shall be, of virgin seed, by wondrous birth. Be in Adam's room the head of all mankind, though Adam's son.

As all men perish in him, so in you — as from a second root — shall be restored as many as are restored; without you, none. His crime makes all his sons guilty; your merit, imputed, shall absolve those who renounce their own deeds, both righteous and unrighteous, and live in you transplanted, and from you receive new life. So Man — as is most just — shall satisfy for Man, be judged and die, and dying rise, and rising with him raise his brethren, ransomed with his own dear life.

So heavenly love shall outdo hellish hate — giving itself to death, and dying to redeem. So dearly shall it redeem what hellish hate so easily destroyed, and still destroys in those who, when they may, do not accept grace.

Nor shall you, by descending to assume Man's nature, lessen or degrade your own. Because you have — though enthroned in highest bliss, equal to God, and equally enjoying godlike fruition — quitted all, to save a world from utter loss, and have been found to be Son of God by merit more than by birthright; found worthiest to be so by being good, far more than by being great or high; because in you love has abounded more than glory abounds:

therefore your humiliation shall exalt with you your manhood also to this throne. Here shall you sit incarnate, here shall you reign both God and Man, Son of both God and Man, anointed universal King. All power I give you; reign forever, and take up your merits. Under you, as supreme head, I reduce Thrones, Princedoms, Powers, Dominions.

All knees shall bow to you, of those who live in Heaven, or on Earth, or under Earth in Hell. When you, attended gloriously from Heaven, shall appear in the sky, and shall send from yourself the summoning Arch-Angels to proclaim your dread tribunal — forthwith from all the winds the living, and forthwith the cited dead of all past ages, shall hasten to the general doom; such a peal shall rouse their sleep.

Then, with all your saints assembled, you shall judge bad Men and Angels; they, arraigned, shall sink beneath your sentence. Hell, her numbers full, shall thenceforth be forever shut. Meanwhile the world shall burn, and from her ashes shall spring a new Heaven and Earth, wherein the just shall dwell, and, after all their long tribulations, shall see golden days, fruitful of golden deeds, triumphing with joy and peace, and fair truth.

Then shall you lay aside your regal sceptre, for regal sceptre then shall no more be needed: God shall be all in all. But, all you Gods, adore him who dies to compass all this; adore the Son, and honour him as me."

No sooner had the Almighty ceased, than all the multitude of Angels, with a shout loud as from numbers without number, sweet as from blessed voices uttering joy — Heaven rang with jubilee, and loud Hosannas filled the eternal regions. Lowly reverent toward either throne they bow, and down to the ground with solemn adoration they cast their crowns interwoven with amaranth and gold —

immortal amaranth, a flower which once began to bloom in Paradise, fast by the tree of life; but soon, for man's offence, it was removed to Heaven, where it first grew; there it now grows, and flowers aloft shading the fount of life, and where the river of bliss rolls her amber stream over Elysian flowers through the midst of Heaven.

With these flowers that never fade, the elect Spirits bind their resplendent locks interwreathed with beams. Now, in loose garlands thickly thrown off, the bright pavement, that shone like a sea of jasper, was impurpled, and smiled with celestial roses.

Then, crowned again, they took their golden harps — harps ever tuned, that hung glittering by their side like quivers — and with a sweet preamble of charming symphony they introduce their sacred song, and waken high raptures.

No voice was exempt; no voice but could well join in melodious part — such concord is in Heaven. You, Father, they first sang: Omnipotent, Immutable, Immortal, Infinite, Eternal King; the Author of all being; Fountain of light; yourself invisible amid the glorious brightness where you sit enthroned inaccessible. But when you shade the full blaze of your beams, and, through a cloud drawn round about you like a radiant shrine, your skirts appear dark with excessive bright, they yet dazzle Heaven, so that the brightest Seraphim do not approach, but veil their eyes with both wings.

Next they sang you, the firstborn of all creation, Begotten Son, Divine Similitude, in whose conspicuous countenance — made visible without cloud — the Almighty Father shines, whom else no creature can behold. On you the effulgence of his glory abides impressed; his ample Spirit rests transfused on you.

The Heaven of Heavens and all the Powers therein he created by you; and by you he threw down the aspiring Dominations. You, that day, did not spare your Father's dreadful thunder, nor stop your flaming chariot-wheels, that shook Heaven's everlasting frame, while over the necks of warring, disarrayed Angels you drove.

Returning from pursuit, your Powers with loud acclaim extolled you only, Son of your Father's might, to execute fierce vengeance on his foes. But not so on Man: him, fallen through their malice, Father of mercy and grace, you did not doom so strictly, but inclined much more to pity.

No sooner had your dear and only Son perceived that you had purposed not to doom frail Man so strictly, but much more inclined to pity, than he — to appease your wrath and end the strife of mercy and justice discerned in your face — regardless of the bliss wherein he sat second to you, offered himself to die for Man's offence. O unexampled love, love nowhere to be found less than Divine!

Hail, Son of God, Saviour of Men! Your name shall henceforth be the copious matter of my song, and never shall my heart forget your praise, nor disjoin it from your Father's praise." Thus in Heaven, above the starry sphere, they spent their happy hours in joy and hymning.

Meanwhile on the firm opaque globe of this round world — whose first convex divides the luminous inferior orbs, enclosed from Chaos and from the inroad of old Darkness — Satan, alighted, walks. It seemed a globe when seen from far off; now it seems a boundless continent, dark, waste, and wild, under the frown of Night, starless exposed, and ever-threatened by storms of Chaos blustering round — an inclement sky,

except on that side which, from the wall of Heaven, though far distant, gains some small reflection of glimmering air, less vexed with loud tempest. Here walked the Fiend at large in a spacious field. As when a vulture bred on Imaus, whose snowy ridge bounds the roving Tartar, dislodging from a region scarce of prey, to gorge himself on the flesh of lambs or yeanling kids, on hills where flocks are fed, flies toward the springs of Ganges or Hydaspes, Indian streams —

but on his way lights on the barren plains of Sericana, where the Chinese drive their light cany wagons with sails and wind: so, on this windy sea of land, the Fiend walked up and down alone, bent on his prey.

Alone — for no other creature was to be found in this place, living or lifeless. None yet; but hereafter a store flew up here from the earth, like aerial vapours, of all things transitory and vain, when sin with vanity had filled the works of men —

both all things vain, and all who in vain things built their fond hopes of glory or lasting fame, or of happiness in this life or the next. All who have their reward on earth — the fruits of painful superstition and blind zeal, seeking nothing but the praise of men — here find fit retribution, empty as their deeds.

All the unaccomplished works of Nature's hand — abortive, monstrous, or unkindly mixed — dissolved on earth, float up here, and in vain wander here until final dissolution. Not in the neighbouring moon, as some have dreamed.

Those silver fields more likely hold as inhabitants translated Saints, or middle Spirits between the angelic and the human kind. Hither came first, of ill-joined sons and daughters born from the ancient world, the giants, with many a vain exploit, though then renowned.

Next came the builders of Babel on the plain of Sennaar; and still, with vain design, new Babels they would build if they had wherewithal. Others came singly — he who, to be deemed a God, foolishly leaped into Aetna's flames, Empedocles; and he who, to enjoy Plato's Elysium, leaped into the sea, Cleombrotus; and many more too long to tell — embryos, and idiots, hermits, and friars, white, black, and gray, with all their trumpery.

Here pilgrims roam, who strayed so far to seek in Golgotha him dead, who lives in Heaven; and those who, to be sure of Paradise, dying, put on the habits of Dominick, or thought to pass disguised in Franciscan robes.

They pass the seven planets, and pass the fixed stars, and that crystalline sphere whose balance weighs the trepidation spoken of, and the primum mobile. Now Saint Peter at Heaven's wicket seems to wait for them with his keys; now at the foot of Heaven's ascent they lift their feet — when lo, a violent cross-wind from either coast blows them transverse, ten thousand leagues awry into the devious air. Then you might see cowls, hoods, and habits, with their wearers, tossed and fluttered into rags; then relics, beads, indulgences, dispenses, pardons, bulls — all the sport of winds: all these, whirled aloft, fly over the backside of the world far off into a large and broad Limbo, since called the Paradise of Fools, long after unknown to few; now unpeopled and untrod.

All this dark globe the Fiend found as he passed, and long he wandered, until at last a gleam of dawning light turned his travelled steps thither in haste. Far distant he descries, ascending by magnificent degrees up to the wall of Heaven, a high structure;

at the top of which appeared, but far more rich, the work as of a kingly palace-gate, embellished with a frontispiece of diamond and gold. Thick with sparkling orient gems the portal shone — inimitable on earth, not to be drawn by model or by shading pencil.

These stairs were such as those on which Jacob saw Angels ascending and descending — bright bands of guardians, when, fleeing from Esau to Padan-Aram, in the field of Luz he dreamed by night under the open sky, and waking cried: "This is the gate of Heaven."

Each stair had a mystical meaning; nor did they always stand there, but were sometimes drawn up to Heaven invisible. Underneath flowed a bright sea of jasper, or of liquid pearl, over which those who afterward came from earth, failing, arrived, wafted by Angels, or flew across the lake rapt in a chariot drawn by fiery steeds.

The stairs were then let down — whether to dare the Fiend by an easy ascent, or to aggravate his sad exclusion from the doors of bliss. Directly opposite to these, opened from beneath, just over the blissful seat of Paradise, a passage down to the Earth — a wide passage, far wider than that of after-times over mount Sion, and, though that was large, over the Promised Land, so dear to God,

by which, to visit often those happy tribes, his angels to and fro passed frequent on high behests; and his eye with choice regard ranged from Paneas, the fount of Jordan's flood, to Beersaba, where the Holy Land borders on Egypt and the Arabian shore —

so wide the opening seemed, where bounds were set to darkness, such as bound the ocean wave. From here Satan, now on the lower stair that scaled by steps of gold to Heaven-gate, looks down with wonder at the sudden view of all this world at once. As when a scout, having gone all night through dark and desert ways with peril, at last by break of cheerful dawn obtains the brow of some high-climbing hill, which to his eye unexpectedly discovers the goodly prospect of some foreign land first seen, or of some renowned metropolis with glistening spires and pinnacles adorned, which now the rising sun gilds with his beams:

such wonder seized the malign Spirit, though after Heaven beheld — but much more envy seized him at the sight of all this world, beheld so fair. Round he surveys (and well he might, where he stood so high above the circling canopy of night's extended shade) from the eastern point of Libra to the fleecy star that bears Andromeda, far off in the Atlantic seas beyond the horizon; then from pole to pole he views in breadth; and without longer pause throws his flight directly downward into the world's first region, and with ease winds his oblique way through the pure marble air, among innumerable stars that shone distant as stars, but close at hand seemed other worlds —

or other worlds they seemed, or happy isles, like those Hesperian gardens famed of old, fortunate fields, and groves, and flowery vales, thrice happy isles. But who dwelt happy there he did not stay to inquire. Above them all the golden sun, in splendour most like Heaven, allured his eye; thither his course he bends through the calm firmament (but whether up or down, by centre or eccentric, is hard to tell, or longitude), where the great luminary, aloof from the vulgar constellations thick — which keep their due distance from his lordly eye — dispenses light from far. They, as they move their starry dance in numbers that compute days, months, and years, swiftly turn their various motions toward his all-cheering lamp, or are turned by his magnetic beam, that gently warms the universe, and, though unseen, shoots invisible virtue with gentle penetration to each inward part, even to the deep.

So wondrously was his bright station set. There lands the Fiend — a spot such as perhaps no astronomer yet has ever seen in the sun's lucent orb through his glazed optic tube. The place he found to be bright beyond expression, compared with anything on earth, whether metal or stone;

not all parts alike, but all alike informed with radiant light, like glowing iron with fire. If metal, part seemed gold, part clear silver; if stone, carbuncle most, or chrysolite, ruby or topaz — like the twelve that shone in Aaron's breastplate — and besides, a stone more often imagined than elsewhere seen, that stone, or one like that, which here below philosophers have so long sought in vain; in vain, though by their powerful art they bind volatile Hermes (mercury), and call up unbound old Proteus in various shapes from the sea, drained through a limbeck to his native form.

What wonder, then, if fields and regions here breathe forth pure Elixir, and rivers run potable gold, when with one virtuous touch the arch-chemick sun, so far remote from us, produces here in the dark — mixed with terrestrial humour — so many precious things, of glorious colour and of effect so rare?

Here new matter met the Devil's gaze undazzled. Far and wide his eye commands; for here sight found no obstacle, nor shade, but all sunshine — as when his beams culminate at noon from the equator, as they now shot still directly upward, so that no way round could shadow from opaque body fall. And the air, nowhere so clear, sharpened his visual ray to objects far distant; whereby he soon saw within ken a glorious Angel standing, the same whom John also saw in the sun.

His back was turned, but his brightness not hidden. A golden tiara of beaming sunny rays circled his head; nor less did his locks, illustrious behind on his shoulders, fledged with wings, lie waving round. He seemed employed on some great charge, or fixed in deep cogitation.

Glad was the impure Spirit, now in hope to find one who might direct his wandering flight to Paradise, the happy seat of Man — his journey's end, and our beginning of woe. But first he decides to change his proper shape, which otherwise might bring him danger or delay.

And now he appears as a stripling Cherub, not of the prime, yet one in whose face celestial youth smiled, and to every limb suitable grace was diffused — so well did he feign. Under a coronet his flowing hair played in curls on either cheek; he wore wings of many a coloured plume, sprinkled with gold;

his habit was fit for speed, girt short; and before his decent steps he held a silver wand. He did not draw near unheard. The bright Angel, before he drew near, turned his radiant visage, admonished by his ear, and straightway was known to be the Arch-Angel Uriel — one of the seven who in God's presence, nearest to his throne, stand ready at command, and are his eyes that run through all the Heavens, or down to the Earth bear his swift errands over moist and dry, over sea and land. Him Satan thus accosts:

"Uriel — for you, of those seven Spirits that stand in sight of God's high throne, gloriously bright, are accustomed to be the first interpreter to bring his great authentic will through highest Heaven, where all his sons attend your embassy,

and here, by supreme decree, are likeliest to obtain like honour, and as his eye to visit often this new creation round — unspeakable desire to see and to know all these his wondrous works, but chiefly Man, his chief delight and favour, him for whom he ordained all these his works so wondrous, has brought me from the choirs of Cherubim, thus alone wandering. Brightest Seraph, tell me in which of all these shining orbs has Man his fixed seat; or has he no fixed seat, but all these shining orbs for his choice to dwell in —

that I may find him, and, with secret gaze or open admiration, behold him, on whom the great Creator has bestowed worlds, and on whom he has poured all these graces; that both in him and in all things, as is fitting, we may praise the universal Maker,

who has justly driven out his rebel foes to deepest Hell, and, to repair that loss, created this new happy race of Men to serve him better. Wise are all his ways." So spoke the false dissembler, unperceived —

for neither Man nor Angel can discern hypocrisy, the only evil that walks invisible, except to God alone, by his permissive will, through Heaven and Earth. And often, though wisdom is awake, suspicion sleeps at wisdom's gate, and resigns her charge to simplicity, while goodness thinks no ill where no ill seems. Which now for once beguiled Uriel — though regent of the sun, and held the sharpest-sighted Spirit of all in Heaven —

who to the foul, fraudulent impostor, in his uprightness, thus returned answer: "Fair Angel, your desire, which tends to know the works of God, thereby to glorify the great Work-master, leads to no excess that reaches blame, but rather merits praise the more it seems excess, since it led you hither from your empyreal mansion thus alone, to witness with your eyes what some perhaps, content with report, hear only of in Heaven.

For wondrous indeed are all his works, pleasant to know, and most worthy to be always held in remembrance with delight. But what created mind can comprehend their number, or the infinite wisdom that brought them forth, but hid their causes deep?

I saw when at his word the formless mass, this world's material mould, came to a heap: Confusion heard his voice, and wild uproar stood ruled; stood vast infinitude confined; till at his second bidding Darkness fled, Light shone, and order sprang from disorder.

Then swiftly to their several quarters hastened the cumbrous elements — earth, flood, air, fire; and this ethereal quintessence of Heaven flew upward, animated with various forms, that rolled orbicular and turned into stars numberless, as you see, and how they move.

Each had his place appointed, each his course; the rest walls this universe in a circuit. Look downward on that globe, whose nearer side shines with light from hence, though only reflected. That place is Earth, the seat of Man; that light is his day — which else, as in the other hemisphere, Night would invade. But there the neighbouring moon (so call that opposite fair star), with her timely aid, interposes; and her monthly round, still ending, still renewing, through mid-Heaven, with her borrowed light her triform countenance hence fills and empties, to enlighten the Earth, and in her pale dominion checks the night.

That spot, to which I point, is Paradise, Adam's abode; those lofty shades, his bower. Your way you cannot miss; mine requires me." So saying, he turned; and Satan, bowing low, as is customary in Heaven to superior Spirits, where due honour and reverence no one neglects, took leave, and toward the coast of earth beneath, down from the ecliptic, sped with hoped success, throws his steep flight in many an airy wheel; nor stayed, until he lights on Niphates' top.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: O, for that warning voice which he, who saw the Apocalypse, heard crying aloud in Heaven, when the Dragon, put to his second rout, came furious down to be revenged on men — "Woe to the inhabitants on earth!" — that now, while there was time, our first parents had been warned of the coming of their secret foe, and had escaped, perhaps, his mortal snare! For now Satan, inflamed for the first time with this fresh rage, came down — the tempter before being the accuser of mankind — to wreak on innocent, frail Man his loss of that first battle, and his flight to Hell.

Yet he begins his dire attempt not rejoicing in his speed, though bold far off and fearless, nor with cause to boast. The attempt, now near its birth, rolls and boils in his tumultuous breast, and, like a devilish engine, recoils back upon himself. Horror and doubt distract his troubled thoughts, and stir the Hell within him from the bottom. For within himself he brings Hell, and round about him; nor can he by any change of place fly one step from Hell, any more than he can fly from himself. Now conscience wakes the despair that had slumbered — wakes the bitter memory of what he was, of what he is, and of what he must be, worse; worse sufferings must follow from worse deeds.

Sometimes toward Eden, which now lay pleasant in his view, he fixes his grieved, sad look; sometimes toward Heaven, and the full-blazing sun, which now sat high in its meridian tower. Then, much revolving in thought, he thus began, in sighs:

"O you, that, crowned with surpassing glory, look from your sole dominion like the God of this new world; at whose sight all the stars hide their diminished heads; to you I call — but with no friendly voice; and I add your name of Sun, to tell you how I hate your beams, which bring to my remembrance from what state I fell — how glorious once above your sphere —

till pride and worse ambition threw me down, warring in Heaven against Heaven's matchless King. Ah, why! He deserved no such return from me, whom he created what I was in that bright eminence, and with his good upbraided none; nor was his service hard.

What could be less than to afford him praise, the easiest recompense, and pay him thanks — how due! Yet all his good proved ill in me, and wrought only malice. Lifted up so high, I disdained subjection, and thought one step higher would set me highest, and in a moment quit the immense debt of endless gratitude, so burdensome — still to be paying, still to owe — forgetful of what I still received from him, and not understanding that a grateful mind by owing owes not, but still pays, at once indebted and discharged. What burden, then? O, had his powerful destiny ordained me to be some inferior Angel, I would have stood happy then; no unbounded hope would have raised ambition. Yet why might not some other Power as great have aspired, and drawn me, though mean, to his part? But other Powers as great did not fall; they stand unshaken, armed from within or from without against all temptations.

Had you the same free will and power to stand? You had. Whom, then, have you to accuse, or what, but Heaven's free love dealt equally to all? Be then his love accursed, since love or hate to me alike deals eternal woe.

Nay, cursed be you; since against his will your will chose freely what it now so justly rues. Miserable me! Which way shall I fly infinite wrath, and infinite despair? Which way I fly is Hell; I myself am Hell;

and, in the lowest deep, a lower deep still threatening to devour me opens wide, compared with which the Hell I suffer seems a Heaven. O, then, at last relent: is there no place left for repentance? Is none left for pardon?

None left — but by submission. And that word disdain forbids me, along with my dread of shame among the Spirits beneath, whom I seduced with other promises and other vauntings than of submitting — boasting I could subdue the Omnipotent. Ah me! They little know how dearly I abide that boast so vain, under what torments I inwardly groan, while they adore me on the throne of Hell.

With diadem and sceptre high advanced, the lower still I fall — supreme only in misery. Such joy ambition finds! But, suppose I could repent, and could obtain by act of grace my former state: how soon would height recall high thoughts, how soon would it unsay what feigned submission had sworn! Ease would recant vows made in pain, as violent and void.

For true reconcilement can never grow where wounds of deadly hate have pierced so deep. This would only lead me to a worse relapse, and a heavier fall: so I should dearly purchase a short intermission, bought with double pain.

This my Punisher knows: therefore he is as far from granting peace as I am from begging it. All hope thus excluded, behold, instead of us — the outcast and exiled — his new delight, Mankind created, and for him this world.

So, farewell, hope; and with hope, farewell, fear; farewell, remorse! All good to me is lost. Evil, be you my good. By you, at least, I hold divided empire with Heaven's King; by you, and more than half perhaps, I shall reign —

as Man ere long, and this new world, shall know." Thus while he spoke, each passion dimmed his face, which thrice changed — with pale, with ire, with envy, and with despair — and marred his borrowed visage, and betrayed him as a counterfeit, if any eye beheld it.

For heavenly minds are ever clear of such foul distempers. Soon aware of this, he smoothed each perturbation with outward calm — an artificer of fraud; and he was the first who practised falsehood under a saintly show, to conceal deep malice, couched with revenge.

Yet he had not practised enough to deceive Uriel once warned. Uriel's eye pursued him down the way he went, and on the Assyrian mount saw him disfigured more than could befall a Spirit of the happy sort. He noted his fierce gestures and mad demeanour, as he then stood alone, all unobserved (as he supposed), unseen.

So on he fares, and comes to the border of Eden, where delicious Paradise, now nearer, crowns with her green enclosure — as with a rural mound — the champaign head of a steep wilderness, whose hairy sides, overgrown with thicket, grotesque and wild, denied access; and overhead grew up insuperable heights of loftiest shade — cedar, and pine, and fir, and branching palm, a sylvan scene; and, as the ranks ascend, shade above shade, a woody theatre of stateliest view. Yet higher than their tops sprang up the verdurous wall of Paradise,

which gave our general sire a large prospect into his neighbouring nether empire. Higher than that wall appeared a circling row of goodliest trees, laden with fairest fruit — blossoms and fruits at once, of golden hue, mixed with gay enamelled colours.

On these the sun impressed his beams more gladly than in the fair evening cloud, or in the humid rainbow when God has showered the earth — so lovely seemed that landscape. And now purer air than pure meets his approach, and inspires to the heart a vernal delight and joy, able to drive off all sadness but despair. Now gentle gales, fanning their odoriferous wings, dispense native perfumes, and whisper where they stole those balmy spoils. As when, to those who sail beyond the Cape of Hope, and are now past Mozambique, far off at sea northeast winds blow Sabean odours from the spicy shore of Araby the blest; with such delay, well pleased they slacken their course, and for many a league old Ocean smiles, cheered with the grateful smell —

so those odorous sweets entertained the Fiend, who came as their bane — though he was better pleased with them than Asmodeus with the fishy fume that drove him, though enamoured, from the spouse of Tobit's son, and sent him with a vengeance post-haste from Media to Egypt, there bound fast.

Now Satan had journeyed, pensive and slow, up toward the ascent of that steep, savage hill; but he found no further way, so thickly entwined, as one continued brake, the undergrowth of shrubs and tangling bushes had perplexed all path of man or beast that passed that way.

There was only one gate, and it looked east on the other side. When the arch-felon saw it, he disdained due entrance; and, in contempt, at one flight bound high leaped over all boundary of hill or highest wall, and sheer within lights on his feet. As when a prowling wolf, driven by hunger to seek a new haunt for prey, watching where shepherds pen their flocks at evening in hurdled cotes amid the field, leaps with ease over the fence into the fold;

or as a thief, bent to unhoard the cash of some rich burgher, whose substantial doors — cross-barred and bolted fast — fear no assault, climbs in at the window, or over the tiles: so climbed this first grand thief into God's fold;

so since into his church lewd hirelings climb. Thence he flew up, and on the tree of life — the middle tree and highest there that grew — he sat like a cormorant. Yet not true life did he thereby regain, but sat devising death to those who lived. Nor did he consider the virtue of that life-giving plant, but used it only for prospect — what, if well used, would have been the pledge of immortality. So little does anyone, but God alone, know how to value rightly the good before him — but perverts best things to worst abuse, or to their meanest use.

Beneath him, with new wonder, he now views, exposed to all delight of human sense, in narrow room, Nature's whole wealth — yea, more — a Heaven on Earth. For blissful Paradise was the garden of God, planted by him in the east of Eden. Eden stretched her line from Auran eastward to the royal towers of great Seleucia, built by Grecian kings, or where the sons of Eden long before dwelt in Telassar. In this pleasant soil God ordained his far more pleasant garden.

Out of the fertile ground he caused to grow all trees of noblest kind for sight, smell, and taste; and amid them all stood the tree of life, high eminent, blooming ambrosial fruit of vegetable gold. And next to life, our death, the tree of knowledge, grew fast by — knowledge of good bought dearly by knowing ill.

Southward through Eden flowed a large river, which did not change its course, but passed underneath, engulfed through the shaggy hill — for God had thrown that mountain as his garden-mould, raised high upon the rapid current; which, drawn up through veins of porous earth by kindly thirst, rose as a fresh fountain, and with many a rill watered the garden. Thence, united, it fell down the steep glade, and met the nether flood, which now appears from its darksome passage, and, now divided into four main streams, runs diverse, wandering through many a famous realm and country — of which no account is needed here.

But rather let me tell, if Art could tell, how from that sapphire fount the crisped brooks, rolling on oriental pearl and sands of gold, with mazy error under pendant shades, ran nectar, visiting each plant, and fed flowers worthy of Paradise — which not nice Art in beds and curious knots, but bounteous Nature, poured forth profusely on hill, and dale, and plain, both where the morning sun first warmly smote the open field, and where the unpierced shade imbrowned the noontide bowers. Thus was this place a happy rural seat of various view:

groves whose rich trees wept odorous gums and balm; others whose fruit, burnished with golden rind, hung amiable — Hesperian fables true, if true here only — and of delicious taste. Between them, lawns or level downs, and flocks grazing the tender herb, were interposed; or palmy hillock; or the flowery lap of some well-watered valley spread her store, flowers of all hue, and without thorn the rose.

On another side, shadowy grots and caves of cool recess, over which the mantling vine lays forth her purple grape, and gently creeps luxuriant. Meanwhile murmuring waters fall down the slope hills, dispersed, or unite their streams in a lake, which holds her crystal mirror to the fringed bank crowned with myrtle.

The birds apply their choir; airs, vernal airs, breathing the smell of field and grove, attune the trembling leaves, while universal Pan, knit with the Graces and the Hours in dance, led on the eternal Spring. Not that fair field of Enna, where Proserpine was gathered by gloomy Dis — herself a fairer flower while gathering flowers — which cost Ceres all that pain to seek her through the world; nor that sweet grove of Daphne by Orontes, and the inspired Castalian spring; might strive with this Paradise of Eden. Nor that Nyseian isle, girt with the river Triton, where old Cham — whom Gentiles call Ammon and Libyan Jove — hid Amalthea, and her florid son young Bacchus, from his stepdame Rhea's eye;

nor where Abassin kings guard their issue — Mount Amara, though some have supposed it to be the true Paradise under the Ethiop line, by the Nile's head, enclosed with shining rock, a whole day's journey high — though widely remote from this Assyrian garden, where the Fiend saw, undelighted, all delight, all kinds of living creatures, new to sight, and strange. Two of far nobler shape, erect and tall, godlike erect, clad with native honour in naked majesty, seemed lords of all;

and worthy seemed: for in their divine looks the image of their glorious Maker shone — truth, wisdom, sanctitude severe and pure (severe, but placed in true filial freedom), whence true authority in men. Though both were not equal, as their sex not equal seemed:

for contemplation he, and valour, formed; for softness she, and sweet attractive grace; he for God only, she for God in him. His fair, large front and eye sublime declared absolute rule; and his hyacinthine locks, clustering, hung manly around from his parted forelock, but not below his broad shoulders.

She, as a veil, wore her unadorned golden tresses down to her slender waist, dishevelled, but waved in wanton ringlets, as the vine curls her tendrils — which implied subjection, but required with gentle sway, and by her yielded, by him best received, yielded with coy submission, modest pride, and sweet, reluctant, amorous delay.

Nor were those mysterious parts then concealed. Then there was no guilty shame — that dishonest shame of nature's works, honour dishonourable, sin-bred. How have you — that shame — troubled all mankind with mere shows instead, shows of seeming pure, and banished from man's life his happiest life, simplicity and spotless innocence!

So naked they passed on, nor shunned the sight of God or Angel; for they thought no ill. So hand in hand they passed, the loveliest pair that ever since in love's embraces met — Adam the goodliest of the men since born his sons; Eve the fairest of her daughters.

Under a tuft of shade that stood whispering soft on a green, by a fresh fountain's side, they sat themselves down. And, after no more toil of their sweet gardening labour than sufficed to recommend cool Zephyr, and made ease more easy, and wholesome thirst and appetite more grateful, they fell to their supper-fruits — nectarine fruits which the compliant boughs yielded them, as they sat reclined side-long on the soft, downy bank damasked with flowers.

The savoury pulp they chew, and in the rind, as they thirsted, scoop the brimming stream. Nor did gentle purpose, nor endearing smiles, nor youthful dalliance, as befits a fair couple linked in happy nuptial league, alone as they were, want. About them frisking played all the beasts of the earth, since grown wild, and all those that are the object of chase in wood or wilderness, forest or den:

the lion, sporting, ramped, and in his paw dandled the kid; bears, tigers, ounces, leopards gambolled before them; the unwieldy elephant, to make them mirth, used all his might, and wreathed his lithe proboscis. Close by, the sly serpent, insinuating, wove with Gordian twine his braided train, and gave unheeded proof of his fatal guile. Others couched on the grass, and now, filled with pasture, sat gazing, or ruminating toward bedtime. For the sun, declined, was hasting now with prone career to the ocean isles; and in the ascending scale of Heaven the stars that usher evening rose.

Satan, still gazing, as he stood at first, at length with difficulty recovered sad speech thus: "O Hell! what do my eyes with grief behold! Advanced into our room of bliss, thus high, are creatures of another mould — earth-born, perhaps, not Spirits, yet little inferior to the bright heavenly Spirits. My thoughts pursue them with wonder, and I could love them, so lively shines in them divine resemblance, and such grace the hand that formed them has poured upon their shape.

Ah, gentle pair, you little think how nigh your change approaches, when all these delights will vanish, and deliver you to woe — more woe, the more your taste is now of joy. Happy — but ill-secured, being so happy, to continue long; and this high seat, your Heaven, ill-fenced for Heaven, to keep out such a foe as has now entered. Yet I am no purposed foe to you, whom I could pity thus forlorn, though I am myself unpitied. League with you I seek, and mutual amity, so strait, so close, that I with you must dwell, or you with me henceforth. My dwelling perhaps may not please your sense like this fair Paradise; yet such, accept — it is your Maker's work; he gave it me, which I as freely give. Hell shall unfold her widest gates to entertain you two, and send forth all her kings; there will be room, not like these narrow limits, to receive your numerous offspring. If no better place is to be had, thank him who makes me, against my will, take this revenge on you who do not wrong me, for him who wronged me.

And though I should melt at your harmless innocence, as I do, yet just public reason, honour, and empire enlarged by revenge through conquering this new world, compels me now to do what else, though damned, I would abhor."

So spoke the Fiend, and with necessity — the tyrant's plea — excused his devilish deeds. Then from his lofty stand on that high tree he alights down among the sportive herd of those four-footed kinds, himself now one and now another, as their shape best served his end — to view his prey more closely, and, unespied, to mark what more of their state he might learn, by word or action marked. About them round he now stalks as a lion with fiery glare;

then as a tiger, who by chance has spied in some purlieu two gentle fawns at play, straight couches close; then, rising, changes his crouching watch often, like one who has chosen his ground, from which, rushing, he might most surely seize them both, gripped in each paw. When Adam, first of men, to Eve, first of women, thus began to speak, he turned, all ear, to hear the new utterance flow.

"Sole partner, and sole part, of all these joys — yourself dearer than all — necessarily the Power that made us, and for us this ample world, must be infinitely good, and of his good as liberal and free as he is infinite;

who raised us from the dust, and placed us here in all this happiness — we who at his hand have merited nothing, nor can perform anything of which he has need. He requires from us no other service than to keep this one, this easy charge — of all the trees in Paradise that bear delicious fruit so various, not to taste that one tree of knowledge, planted by the tree of life.

So near grows death to life, whatever death is — some dreadful thing, no doubt; for well you know God has pronounced it death to taste that tree — the only sign of our obedience left, among so many signs of power and rule conferred upon us, and dominion given over all other creatures that possess earth, air, and sea. Then let us not think one easy prohibition hard, we who enjoy free leave so large to all things else, and unlimited choice of manifold delights.

But let us ever praise him, and extol his bounty, following our delightful task — to prune these growing plants, and tend these flowers; which, were it toilsome, yet with you would be sweet." To whom Eve thus replied: "O you for whom and from whom I was formed — flesh of your flesh, and without whom I am to no end — my guide and head! What you have said is just and right.
For to him indeed we owe all praises, and daily thanks; I chiefly, who enjoy so far the happier lot, in enjoying you pre-eminent by so much odds, while you can nowhere find a consort like yourself.

I often remember that day when from sleep I first awoke, and found myself reposed under a shade on flowers, much wondering where and what I was, whence thither brought, and how. Not far distant from there a murmuring sound of waters issued from a cave, and spread into a liquid plain, then stood unmoved, pure as the expanse of Heaven. I went thither with unexperienced thought, and laid me down on the green bank, to look into the clear smooth lake, that to me seemed another sky.

As I bent down to look, just opposite a shape within the watery gleam appeared, bending to look on me. I started back; it started back; but pleased, I soon returned, and, pleased, it returned as soon, with answering looks of sympathy and love. There I had fixed my eyes till now, and pined with vain desire, had not a voice thus warned me: "What you see, what there you see, fair Creature, is yourself;

with you it came and it goes. But follow me, and I will bring you where no shadow stays your coming, and your soft embraces; he whose image you are; him you shall enjoy inseparably yours; to him you shall bear multitudes like yourself, and thence be called Mother of the human race." What could I do but follow straight, invisibly thus led —

until I espied you, fair indeed and tall, under a plane tree; yet I thought you less fair, less winning soft, less amiably mild, than that smooth watery image. I turned back; you, following, cried aloud: "Return, fair Eve;

whom do you flee? Whom you flee, of him you are — his flesh, his bone. To give you being, I lent out of my side to you — nearest my heart — substantial life, to have you by my side henceforth, an individual solace dear.

Part of my soul I seek in you, and I claim you as my other half." With that your gentle hand seized mine; I yielded; and from that time I see how beauty is excelled by manly grace, and wisdom, which alone is truly fair."

So spoke our general mother, and with eyes of unreproved conjugal attraction, and meek surrender, half-embracing leaned on our first father. Half her swelling breast, naked, met his, hidden under the flowing gold of her loose tresses. He, in delight both of her beauty and submissive charms, smiled with superior love — as Jupiter on Juno smiles, when he impregnates the clouds that shed May-flowers — and pressed her matron lip with pure kisses. Aside the Devil turned for envy; yet with a jealous, malign leer eyed them askance, and to himself thus lamented:

"Hateful sight! Tormenting sight! Thus these two, imparadised in one another's arms, the happier Eden, shall enjoy their fill of bliss upon bliss; while I to Hell am thrust, where neither joy nor love, but fierce desire — among our other torments not the least — still pines unfulfilled with the pain of longing.

Yet let me not forget what I have gained from their own mouths: all is not theirs, it seems. There stands one fatal tree, called the tree of knowledge, forbidden them to taste. Knowledge forbidden? Suspicious; reasonless. Why should their Lord envy them that? Can it be sin to know?

Can it be death? And do they only stand by ignorance? Is that their happy state, the proof of their obedience and their faith? O fair foundation laid, on which to build their ruin! Hence I will excite their minds with more desire to know, and to reject envious commands invented with design to keep them low, whom knowledge might exalt equal with Gods. Aspiring to be such, they taste and die. What likelier result can ensue? But first with narrow search I must walk round this garden, and leave no corner unspied.

A chance — but chance — may lead where I may meet some wandering Spirit of Heaven by a fountain's side, or retired in thick shade, from whom to draw what further may be learned. Live while you may, yet happy pair; enjoy, till I return, short pleasures — for long woes are to succeed!"

So saying, he scornfully turned his proud step, but with sly circumspection, and began his roam through wood, through waste, over hill, over dale. Meanwhile in utmost longitude, where Heaven meets earth and ocean, the setting sun slowly descended, and with straight aspect levelled his evening rays against the eastern gate of Paradise. It was a rock of alabaster, piled up to the clouds, conspicuous far, winding with one ascent accessible from earth, one entrance high;

the rest was craggy cliff, that overhung ever as it rose, impossible to climb. Between these rocky pillars Gabriel sat, chief of the angelic guards, awaiting night. About him the unarmed youth of Heaven exercised heroic games; but near at hand was celestial armoury — shields, helms, and spears, hung high, flaming with diamond and with gold.

Thither came Uriel, gliding through the evening on a sunbeam, swift as a shooting star in autumn thwarts the night, when fired vapours impress the air and show the mariner from what point of his compass to beware impetuous winds. He thus began in haste:

"Gabriel, to you your course has by lot given charge and strict watch, that no evil thing approach or enter into this happy place. This day at the height of noon came to my sphere a Spirit, zealous, as he seemed, to know more of the Almighty's works, and chiefly Man, God's latest image. I described his way bent all on speed, and marked his airy gait.

But in the mount that lies from Eden northward, where he first lighted, I soon discerned his looks alien from Heaven, obscured with foul passions. My eye pursued him still, but under shade I lost sight of him. One of the banished crew, I fear, has ventured from the deep to raise new troubles; to find him must be your care."

To whom the winged warrior thus returned: "Uriel, no wonder if your perfect sight, amid the sun's bright circle where you sit, sees far and wide. In at this gate none pass the vigilance here placed, but such as come well known from Heaven; and since the meridian hour no creature has come thence. If a Spirit of other sort, so minded, has overleaped these earthly bounds on purpose, you well know how hard it is to exclude spiritual substance with a corporeal bar.

But if, within the circuit of these walks, in whatever shape he lurks, of whom you tell, by morrow's dawning I shall know." So he promised; and Uriel returned to his charge on that bright beam, whose point, now raised, bore him slope downward to the sun, now fallen beneath the Azores — whether the prime orb, incredible how swift, had rolled thither diurnal, or whether this less voluble earth, by shorter flight to the east, had left him there arraying with reflected purple and gold the clouds that attend on his western throne.

Now came still Evening on, and Twilight gray had clad all things in her sober livery. Silence accompanied; for beast and bird — they to their grassy couch, these to their nests — were slunk, all but the wakeful nightingale.

She all night long sang her amorous descant; Silence was pleased. Now glowed the firmament with living sapphires. Hesperus, that led the starry host, rode brightest, until the moon, rising in clouded majesty, at length, apparent queen, unveiled her peerless light, and over the dark threw her silver mantle.

Then Adam thus to Eve: "Fair Consort, the hour of night, and all things now retired to rest, remind us of like repose; since God has set labour and rest, as day and night, for men successive. And the timely dew of sleep, now falling with soft slumbrous weight, inclines our eyelids. Other creatures all day long rove idle, unemployed, and less need rest.
Man has his daily work of body or mind appointed, which declares his dignity, and the regard of Heaven on all his ways; while other animals range unactive, and of their doings God takes no account.

Tomorrow, before fresh morning streaks the east with first approach of light, we must be risen, and at our pleasant labour, to reform yon flowery arbours, yonder alleys green — our walk at noon — with branches overgrown, that mock our scant tending, and require more hands than ours to lop their wanton growth.

Those blossoms also, and those dropping gums that lie bestrown, unsightly and unsmooth, ask riddance, if we mean to tread with ease. Meanwhile, as Nature wills, night bids us rest." To whom thus Eve, with perfect beauty adorned: "My Author and Disposer, what you bid, unargued I obey; so God ordains.

God is your law; you are mine. To know no more is woman's happiest knowledge, and her praise. Conversing with you, I forget all time; all seasons and their change all please alike. Sweet is the breath of Morn, her rising sweet, with charm of earliest birds; pleasant the sun, when first on this delightful land he spreads his orient beams, on herb, tree, fruit, and flower, glistening with dew; fragrant is the fertile earth after soft showers; and sweet the coming on of grateful, mild Evening; then silent Night, with this her solemn bird, and this fair moon, and these the gems of Heaven, her starry train —

but neither breath of Morn, when she ascends with charm of earliest birds; nor rising sun on this delightful land; nor herb, fruit, flower, glistening with dew; nor fragrance after showers; nor grateful, mild Evening; nor silent Night, with this her solemn bird; nor walk by moon, or by glittering starlight, is sweet without you.

But why do these shine all night long? For whom this glorious sight, when sleep has shut all eyes?" To whom our general ancestor replied: "Daughter of God and Man, accomplished Eve, these have their course to finish around the earth by tomorrow evening, and from land to land in order — though it is to nations yet unborn — they set and rise, ministering light prepared;

lest total Darkness should by night regain her old possession, and extinguish life in Nature and all things. These soft fires not only enlighten, but with kindly heat of various influence foment and warm, temper or nourish, or in part shed down their stellar virtue on all kinds that grow on earth, thereby made apter to receive perfection from the sun's more potent ray.

These, then, though unbeheld in the deep of night, shine not in vain. Nor think, though there were no men, that Heaven would want spectators, God want praise: millions of spiritual creatures walk the earth unseen, both when we wake and when we sleep.

All these with ceaseless praise behold his works both day and night. How often from the steep of echoing hill or thicket have we heard celestial voices to the midnight air — sole, or responsive each to others' note — singing their great Creator? Often in bands, while they keep watch, or nightly walk their rounds, with heavenly touch of instrumental sounds joined in full harmonic number, their songs divide the night, and lift our thoughts to Heaven."

Thus talking, hand in hand alone they passed on to their blissful bower. It was a place chosen by the sovereign Planter, when he framed all things to Man's delightful use. The roof of thickest covert was inwoven shade — laurel and myrtle, and whatever higher grew of firm and fragrant leaf. On either side, acanthus and each odorous bushy shrub fenced up the verdant wall. Every beauteous flower — iris of all hues, roses, and jasmine — reared high their flourished heads between, and wrought a mosaic. Underfoot the violet, crocus, and hyacinth, with rich inlay, broidered the ground, more coloured than with stones of costliest emblem. No other creature here — bird, beast, insect, or worm — dared to enter, such was their awe of Man. In no shadier bower, more sacred and sequestered, though but feigned, did Pan or Sylvanus ever sleep, nor was it haunted by Nymph or Faunus. Here, in close recess, with flowers, garlands, and sweet-smelling herbs, espoused Eve first decked her nuptial bed;

and heavenly choirs sang the hymenaean, on that day when the genial Angel brought her to our sire in naked beauty, more adorned and more lovely than Pandora, whom the Gods endowed with all their gifts, and O! too like her in sad event — when, brought by Hermes to the unwiser son of Japhet, she ensnared mankind with her fair looks, to be avenged on him who had stolen Jove's authentic fire.

Thus arrived at their shady lodge, both stood, both turned, and under open sky adored the God that made both sky, air, earth, and heaven which they beheld — the moon's resplendent globe and starry pole. "You also made the night, Maker Omnipotent, and you the day, which we, employed in our appointed work, have finished — happy in our mutual help and mutual love, the crown of all our bliss, ordained by you. And this delicious place for us is too large, where your abundance wants partakers, and uncropped falls to the ground.

But you have promised from us two a race to fill the earth, who shall with us extol your infinite goodness, both when we wake, and when we seek, as now, your gift of sleep." This said, unanimously — and observing no other rites, but pure adoration, which God likes best — hand in hand they went into their inmost bower; and, having eased off those troublesome disguises which we wear, straight side by side they were laid. Nor, I suppose, did Adam turn from his fair spouse, nor did Eve refuse the mysterious rites of connubial love,

whatever hypocrites austerely talk of purity, and place, and innocence, defaming as impure what God declares pure, and commands to some, leaves free to all. Our Maker bids increase; who bids abstain but our Destroyer, foe to God and Man?

Hail, wedded Love, mysterious law, true source of human offspring, sole propriety in Paradise of all things otherwise common! By you adulterous Lust was driven from men among the bestial herds to range; by you, founded in reason, loyal, just, and pure, dear relations, and all the charities of father, son, and brother, were first known.

Far be it from me to write you as sin or blame, or to think you unbefitting holiest place, perpetual fountain of domestic sweets, whose bed is undefiled, and is pronounced chaste, both present and past, as saints and patriarchs used.

Here Love employs his golden shafts; here lights his constant lamp, and waves his purple wings; reigns here and revels — not in the bought smile of harlots, loveless, joyless, unendeared, casual fruition; nor in court-amours, mixed dance, or wanton mask, or midnight ball, or serenade, which the starved lover sings to his proud fair — best quitted with disdain.

These, lulled by nightingales, embracing, slept; and on their naked limbs the flowery roof showered roses, which the morning repaired. Sleep on, blest pair; and O! yet happiest, if you seek no happier state, and know to know no more.

Now had night measured with her shadowy cone halfway up hill this vast sublunar vault, and from their ivory gate the Cherubim, issuing forth at the accustomed hour, stood armed to their night watches in warlike parade.

When Gabriel thus spoke to his next in power: "Uzziel, draw half of these off, and coast the south with strictest watch; let these others wheel to the north; our circuit meets full west." Like flame they part, half wheeling to the shield, half to the spear.

From these, he called two strong and subtle Spirits that stood near him, and gave them thus in charge: "Ithuriel and Zephon, with winged speed search through this garden, leave no nook unsearched; but chiefly where those two fair creatures lodge, now perhaps laid asleep, secure of harm.

This evening, arriving from the sun's decline, someone told of an infernal Spirit seen hither bent (who could have thought?), having escaped the bars of Hell, on bad errand no doubt. Such, where you find him, seize fast, and bring hither."

So saying, he led on his radiant files, dazzling the moon. These directed to the bower in search of whom they sought. There they found him, squat like a toad, close at the ear of Eve, attempting by his devilish art to reach the organs of her fancy, and with them forge illusions, as he pleased, phantasms and dreams —

or, if, inspiring venom, he might taint the animal spirits that from pure blood arise like gentle breaths from rivers pure, from there raise at least distempered, discontented thoughts, vain hopes, vain aims, inordinate desires, blown up with high conceits engendering pride.

Him, thus intent, Ithuriel with his spear touched lightly; for no falsehood can endure the touch of celestial temper, but returns by force to its own likeness. Up he starts, discovered and surprised. As when a spark lights on a heap of nitrous powder, laid, fit for the tun, to store some magazine against a rumoured war, the smutty grain, diffused with sudden blaze, inflames the air —

so started up in his own shape the Fiend. Back stepped those two fair Angels, half amazed to behold so suddenly the grisly king; yet thus, unmoved with fear, they accost him soon: "Which of those rebel Spirits adjudged to Hell are you, that have escaped your prison? And why, transformed, did you sit like an enemy in wait, here watching at the head of these that sleep?"

"Do you not know me?" said Satan, filled with scorn; "do you not know me? You once knew me to be no mate for you, when you sat there where you dared not soar. Not to know me argues yourselves unknown — the lowest of your throng; or, if you know me, why do you ask, and superfluously begin your message, like to end as much in vain?"

To whom thus Zephon, answering scorn with scorn: "Think not, revolted Spirit, that your shape is the same, or your brightness undiminished, as to be known as when you stood in Heaven upright and pure. That glory, when you were no more good, departed from you; and now you resemble your sin and your place of doom, obscure and foul.

But come, for you, be sure, shall give account to him who sent us, whose charge is to keep this place inviolable, and these from harm." So spoke the Cherub; and his grave rebuke, severe in youthful beauty, added invincible grace. Abashed, the Devil stood, and felt how awful goodness is, and saw virtue in her shape how lovely; he saw, and pined at his loss. But chiefly, to find here observed that his lustre was visibly impaired, he yet seemed undaunted. "If I must contend," said he, "best with the best — the sender, not the sent — or with all at once; more glory will be won, or less be lost." "Your fear," said Zephon bold, "will save us the trial of what the least can do single against you, wicked, and therefore weak."

The Fiend did not reply, overcome with rage; but, like a proud steed reined in, went haughty on, champing his iron curb. To strive or to fly he held it vain; awe from above had quelled his heart, not else dismayed. Now they drew near the western point, where those half-rounding guards had just met, and closing, stood joined in squadron, awaiting next command. To them their Chief, Gabriel, from the front thus called aloud:

"O friends! I hear the tread of nimble feet hasting this way, and now by glimpse discern Ithuriel and Zephon through the shade; and with them comes a third of regal port, but of wan, faded splendour; who by his gait and fierce demeanour seems the Prince of Hell, not likely to part from here without contest.

Stand firm; for in his look defiance lours." He had scarcely ended, when those two approached, and briefly related whom they brought, where he was found, how busied, in what form and posture couched. To whom with stern regard thus Gabriel spoke:

"Why have you, Satan, broken the bounds prescribed to your transgressions, and disturbed the charge of others, who approve not to transgress by your example, but have power and right to question your bold entrance on this place —

employed, it seems, to violate sleep, and those whose dwelling God has planted here in bliss?" To whom thus Satan with contemptuous brow: "Gabriel? You had in Heaven the esteem of being wise, and such I held you; but this question asked puts me in doubt. Is there anyone who loves his pain?

Who would not, finding way, break loose from Hell, though thither doomed? You would yourself, no doubt, and boldly venture to whatever place farthest from pain, where you might hope to change torment for ease, and soonest recompense dole with delight — which in this place I sought.

To you it is no reason, who know only good, and have not tried evil; and you will object the will of him who binds us! Let him more surely bar his iron gates, if he intends our stay in that dark durance. That is as much as was asked.

The rest is true — they found me where they say; but that implies neither violence nor harm." Thus he in scorn. The warlike Angel, moved, disdainfully half smiling, thus replied: "O loss of one in Heaven to judge of what is wise since Satan fell, whom folly overthrew, and who now returns from his escaped prison, gravely in doubt whether to hold them wise or not, who ask what boldness brought him hither unlicensed from the bounds prescribed to him in Hell —

so wise he judges it to fly from pain, however, and to escape his punishment! So judge still, presumptuous, until the wrath which you incur by flying shall meet your flight sevenfold, and scourge that wisdom back to Hell, which taught you yet no better — that no pain can equal infinite anger provoked.

But why you alone? Why did not all Hell come broken loose with you? Is pain less painful to them, less to be fled? Or are you less hardy than they to endure it? Courageous Chief! The first in flight from pain! Had you alleged to your deserted host this cause of flight, you surely would not have come sole fugitive."

To which the Fiend, frowning stern, thus answered: "Not that I endure less, or shrink from pain, insulting Angel! Well you know I stood your fiercest, when in battle the blasting volleyed thunder made all speed to your aid, and seconded your else not dreaded spear.

But still your words, at random, as before, argue your inexperience in what befits a faithful leader — after hard assays and past ill successes — not to hazard all through ways of danger himself untried.
