I, therefore — I alone — first undertook to wing the desolate abyss, and spy this newly created world, of which in Hell fame is not silent, here in the hope of finding a better abode, and to settle my afflicted Powers here on earth, or in mid air;

though for possession I am put to try once more what you and your gay legions dare against us — whose easier business were to serve their Lord high up in Heaven, with songs to hymn his throne, and practised distances to cringe, not fight." To whom the warrior Angel soon replied:

"To say and straight unsay — pretending first to be wise in flying pain, next professing to be the spy — argues no leader but a liar traced, Satan. And could you have added "faithful"? O name, O sacred name of faithfulness profaned!

Faithful to whom? To your rebellious crew? Army of Fiends, fit body to fit head. Was this your discipline and faith engaged, your military obedience — to dissolve allegiance to the acknowledged Power supreme?

And you, sly hypocrite, who now would seem the patron of liberty — who more than you once fawned, and cringed, and servilely adored Heaven's awful Monarch? Why, but in hope to dispossess him, and yourself to reign?

But mark what I now tell you: Avaunt; flee, neither stop where you fled! If from this hour within these hallowed limits you appear, back to the infernal pit I drag you chained, and seal you so as henceforth not to scorn the facile gates of Hell, too slightly barred."

So he threatened; but Satan gave no heed to threats, but, waxing more in rage, replied: "When I am your captive, then talk of chains, proud limitary Cherub! But before then, expect to feel a far heavier load yourself from my prevailing arm — though Heaven's King ride on your wings, and you with your compeers, used to the yoke, draw his triumphant wheels in progress through the road of Heaven star-paved."

While thus he spoke, the bright angelic squadron turned fiery red, sharpening their phalanx in mooned horns, and began to hem him round with ported spears, as thick as when a field of Ceres ripe for harvest waving bends her bearded grove of ears, which way the wind sways them; the careful ploughman doubting stands, lest on the threshing floor his hopeless sheaves should prove chaff. On the other side, Satan, alarmed, collecting all his might, stood dilated, like Teneriffe or Atlas, unremoved:

his stature reached the sky, and on his crest sat Horror plumed. Nor did he lack in his grasp what seemed both spear and shield. Now dreadful deeds might have ensued — not only Paradise in this commotion, but the starry cope of Heaven perhaps, or all the elements at least, might have gone to wrack, disturbed and torn with the violence of this conflict — had not the Eternal, to prevent such horrid fray, soon hung forth in Heaven his golden scales, yet seen between Astrea and the Scorpion sign, in which first he weighed all things created, the pendulous round earth with balanced air in counterpoise; now he ponders all events, battles and realms. In these he put two weights, the sequel each of parting and of fight.

The latter quickly flew up, and kicked the beam. Which Gabriel spying, thus bespoke the Fiend: "Satan, I know your strength, and you know mine; neither is our own, but given. What folly, then, to boast what arms can do? Since yours can do no more than Heaven permits, nor mine, though doubled now to trample you as mire. For proof, look up, and read your lot in yonder celestial sign,
where you are weighed, and shown how light, how weak, if you resist." The Fiend looked up, and knew his mounted scale aloft; no more. But fled, murmuring; and with him fled the shades of night.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: Now Morn, advancing her rosy steps in the eastern clime, sowed the earth with orient pearl, when Adam woke, as was his custom. His sleep was airy-light, bred from pure digestion and bland temperate vapours, which only the sound of leaves and fuming rills — Aurora's fan — lightly dispersed, together with the shrill matin song of birds on every bough. So much the more was his wonder to find Eve unwaked, with tresses disarranged, and glowing cheek, as though from unquiet rest. Leaning on his side, half-raised, with looks of cordial love he hung over her enamoured, and beheld beauty which, whether waking or asleep, shot forth peculiar graces. Then with voice mild — as when Zephyrus breathes upon Flora — softly touching her hand, he whispered thus: "Awake, my fairest, my espoused, my latest found, Heaven's last best gift, my ever new delight!

Awake: the morning shines, and the fresh field calls us. We lose the prime, when we might mark how our tender plants spring, how the citron grove blows, what drops the myrrh, and what the balmy reed; how nature paints her colours; how the bee sits on the bloom extracting liquid sweet."

Such whispering waked her; but with startled eye she looked on Adam, whom embracing, she thus spoke: "O sole one in whom my thoughts find all repose, my glory, my perfection! Glad I see your face, and morn returned. For this night (such a night I never passed till now) I have dreamed — if dreamed — not, as I am often wont, of you, or of works of day past, or of the morrow's next design, but of offence and trouble, such as my mind never knew until this irksome night. I thought, close at my ear, one called me forth to walk, with gentle voice; I thought it yours. It said: "Why are you sleeping, Eve? Now is the pleasant time, the cool, the silent — except where silence yields to the night-warbling bird, that now, awake, tunes sweetest his love-laboured song; now reigns the full-orbed moon, and with more pleasing light, shadowy, sets off the face of things — in vain, if none regards. Heaven wakes with all his eyes; but whom to behold, save you, Nature's desire?

In whose sight all things rejoice, ravished, attracted by your beauty still to gaze." I rose as at your call, but did not find you; to find you I then directed my walk. And on, I thought, alone I passed through ways that brought me all at once to the tree of forbidden knowledge. Fair it seemed, much fairer to my fancy than by day.

And, as I wondering looked, beside it stood one shaped and winged like one of those from Heaven by us often seen; his dewy locks distilled ambrosia. On that tree he also gazed; and "O fair plant," said he, "with fruit surcharged, does none deign to ease your load, and taste your sweet — neither God nor Man? Is knowledge so despised?

Or does envy, or some other reserve, forbid to taste? Forbid who will, none shall from me withhold your offered good any longer. Why else was it set here?" This said, he did not pause, but with venturous arm he plucked, he tasted. Damp horror chilled me at such bold words backed with a deed so bold.

But he, thus overjoyed: "O fruit divine, sweet of yourself, but much more sweet thus cropped, forbidden here, it seems, as only fit for Gods, yet able to make Gods of Men — and why not Gods of Men, since good, the more communicated, grows more abundant, the author not impaired, but honoured more?

Here, happy creature, fair angelic Eve! Partake of it also. Happy though you are, you may be happier; worthier you cannot be. Taste this, and be henceforth among the Gods yourself a Goddess — not to earth confined, but sometimes in the air, as we are; sometimes ascending to Heaven, by merit your own, and seeing what life the Gods live there, and such live you!" So saying, he drew near, and held to me — even to my mouth — some of that same fruit which he had plucked. The pleasant, savoury smell so quickened my appetite that I thought I could not but taste. Forthwith up to the clouds with him I flew, and beneath beheld the earth outstretched immense, a prospect wide and various. Wondering at my flight and change to this high exaltation, suddenly my guide was gone, and I, I thought, sank down, and fell asleep. But O, how glad I woke to find this but a dream!" Thus Eve related her night; and thus Adam answered, sad:

"Best image of myself, and dearer half, the trouble of your thoughts this night in sleep affects me equally. Nor can I like this strange dream, sprung of evil, I fear — yet evil, from whence? In you there can harbour none, created pure. But know that in the soul there are many lesser faculties, that serve Reason as chief. Among these Fancy next holds her office: of all external things which the five watchful senses represent, she forms imaginations, airy shapes, which Reason, joining or disjoining, frames into all that we affirm or deny, and call our knowledge or opinion. Then Reason retires into her private cell, when nature rests.

Often in her absence mimic Fancy wakes to imitate her; but, misjoining shapes, she often produces wild work, and most in dreams — ill-matching words and deeds long past or late. Some such resemblances, I think, I find of our last evening's talk in this dream of yours, but with strange addition. Yet do not be sad.

Evil into the mind of God or Man may come and go, and so unreproved, and leave no spot or blame behind. Which gives me hope that what in sleep you abhorred to dream, waking you will never consent to do.

Do not be disheartened, then, nor cloud those looks that are wont to be more cheerful and serene than when fair morning first smiles on the world. And let us rise to our fresh employments among the groves, the fountains, and the flowers that now open their choicest bosomed smells, reserved from night, and kept for you in store."

So he cheered his fair spouse, and she was cheered. But silently she let a gentle tear fall from either eye, and wiped them with her hair. Two other precious drops that stood ready, each in its crystal sluice, he kissed, before they fell, as the gracious signs of sweet remorse and pious awe that feared to have offended.

So all was cleared, and they haste to the field. But first, from under the shady arboreous roof, as soon as they had come out into open sight of day-spring, and the sun — who, scarcely risen, with wheels yet hovering over the ocean brim, shot his dewy ray parallel to the earth, discovering in wide landscape all the east of Paradise and Eden's happy plains — lowly they bowed adoring, and began their orisons, each morning duly paid in various style. For neither various style nor holy rapture did they lack, to praise their Maker, in fit strains pronounced or sung unmeditated. Such prompt eloquence flowed from their lips, in prose or numerous verse, more tuneable than needed lute or harp to add more sweetness; and they thus began:

"These are your glorious works, Parent of good, Almighty! Yours is this universal frame, thus wondrous fair; yourself how wondrous then! Unspeakable, who sit above these heavens to us invisible, or dimly seen in these your lowest works — yet these declare your goodness beyond thought, and power divine.

Speak, you who best can tell, you sons of light, Angels — for you behold him, and with songs and choral symphonies, day without night, circle his throne rejoicing. You in Heaven, on Earth join all you Creatures to extol him first, him last, him midst, and without end.

Fairest of stars, last in the train of night — if you do not better belong to the dawn, sure pledge of day that crowns the smiling morn with your bright circlet — praise him in your sphere, while day arises, that sweet hour of prime.

You Sun, of this great world both eye and soul, acknowledge him your greater; sound his praise in your eternal course, both when you climb, and when you have gained high noon, and when you fall. Moon, that now meets the orient sun, now flees, with the fixed Stars, fixed in their orb that flies;

and you five other wandering Fires (the planets), that move in mystic dance, not without song, resound his praise who out of darkness called up light. Air, and you Elements — the eldest birth of Nature's womb, that in quaternion run perpetual circle, multiform; and mix and nourish all things — let your ceaseless change vary to our great Maker still new praise.

You Mists and Exhalations, that now rise from hill or steaming lake, dusky or gray, till the sun paints your fleecy skirts with gold, rise in honour to the world's great Author; whether to deck with clouds the uncoloured sky, or wet the thirsty earth with falling showers, rising or falling still advance his praise.

His praise, you Winds, that from four quarters blow, breathe soft or loud; and, wave your tops, you Pines, with every plant, in sign of worship wave. Fountains, and you that warble as you flow melodious murmurs, warbling tune his praise.

Join voices, all you living Souls: you Birds, that singing ascend up to Heaven's gate, bear on your wings and in your notes his praise. You that in waters glide, and you that walk the earth, and stately tread, or lowly creep —

witness if I be silent, morn or even, to hill, or valley, fountain, or fresh shade, made vocal by my song, and taught his praise. Hail, universal Lord! Be bounteous still to give us only good; and if the night has gathered anything of evil, or concealed it, disperse it, as now light dispels the dark!"

So they prayed, innocent. And firm peace soon returned to their thoughts, and wonted calm. On to their morning's rural work they hasten, among sweet dews and flowers, where any row of fruit-trees, over-woody, reached too far its pampered boughs, and needed hands to check fruitless embraces. Or they led the vine to wed her elm: she, espoused, twines her marriageable arms about him, and with him brings her dower, the adopted clusters, to adorn his barren leaves. Heaven's high King beheld them thus employed with pity, and to him called Raphael — the sociable Spirit, who deigned to travel with Tobias, and secured his marriage with the seven-times-wedded maid.

"Raphael," he said, "you hear what stir Satan, escaped from Hell through the darksome gulf, has raised on Earth in Paradise; and how he has disturbed this night the human pair; how he designs in them at once to ruin all mankind.

Go, therefore, and spend half this day as friend with friend conversing with Adam, in whatever bower or shade you find him retired from the heat of noon, to respite his day-labour with repast, or with repose. And bring on such discourse as may advise him of his happy state — a happiness left in his power to will, left to his own free will; his will, though free, yet mutable. Therefore warn him to beware, lest, too secure, he swerve. Tell him also his danger, and from whom — what enemy, lately himself fallen from Heaven, is plotting now the fall of others from the like state of bliss;

by violence? No, for that shall be withstood; but by deceit and lies. Let him know this, lest, wilfully transgressing, he pretend surprise — unadmonished, unforewarned." So spoke the Eternal Father, and fulfilled all justice. Nor did the winged Saint delay, after his charge received. But from among a thousand celestial Ardours, where he stood veiled with his gorgeous wings, springing up light, he flew through the midst of Heaven. The angelic choirs, parting on each hand, gave way to his speed through all the empyreal road; until, arrived at the gate of Heaven, the gate self-opened wide on golden hinges turning, as by work divine the sovereign Architect had framed.

From there no cloud, or star interposed, obstructed his sight, however small he saw it — not unlike to other shining globes; Earth, and the garden of God crowned with cedars above all hills. As when by night the glass of Galileo, less assured, observes imagined lands and regions in the moon;

or as a pilot, amidst the Cyclades, as Delos or Samos first appearing, discerns a cloudy spot — down thither prone in flight he speeds, and through the vast ethereal sky sails between worlds and worlds, with steady wing now on the polar winds, then with quick fan winnows the buxom air. Until, within the soaring range of towering eagles, he seems to all the fowls a phoenix, gazed at by all as that sole bird, when, to enshrine his relics in the Sun's bright temple, to Egyptian Thebes he flies.

At once on the eastern cliff of Paradise he lights, and returns to his proper shape, a winged Seraph. Six wings he wore, to shade his divine lineaments. The pair that clad each broad shoulder came mantling over his breast with regal ornament; the middle pair girt his waist like a starry zone, and round his loins and thighs skirted with downy gold and colours dipped in Heaven; the third pair shadowed his feet from either heel with feathered mail, of sky-tinctured grain. Like Maia's son (Hermes) he stood, and shook his plumes, so that heavenly fragrance filled the wide circuit. All the bands of Angels under watch knew him at once, and rose in honour to his state and to his high message —

for on some high message they guessed him bound. He passed their glittering tents, and is now come into the blissful field, through groves of myrrh, and flowering odours — cassia, nard, and balm; a wilderness of sweets. For here Nature ran wanton, as in her prime, and played at will her virgin fancies, pouring forth more sweet, wild above rule or art, an enormous bliss.

Adam discerned him coming onward through the spicy forest, as he sat in the door of his cool bower, while now the mounted sun shot down directly his fervid rays to warm the earth's inmost womb — more warmth than Adam needed.

And Eve within, due at her hour, prepared for dinner savoury fruits of taste to please true appetite, and not to disrelish thirst for nectarous draughts between, from milky stream, berry, or grape. To her thus Adam called:

"Haste hither, Eve, and behold a sight worth seeing: eastward among those trees, what glorious shape comes this way moving; seems another morn risen on mid-noon. Some great behest from Heaven to us perhaps he brings, and will vouchsafe this day to be our guest. But go with speed, and what your stores contain, bring forth, and pour abundance, fit to honour and receive our heavenly stranger. Well we may afford to give our givers their own gifts, and bestow largely from what is largely bestowed, where Nature multiplies her fertile growth, and by disburdening grows more fruitful — which instructs us not to spare."

To whom thus Eve: "Adam, earth's hallowed mould, of God inspired! A small store will serve, where a store ripe for use hangs on the stalk in all seasons — save what by frugal storing gains firmness to nourish, and consumes superfluous moisture.

But I will hasten, and from each bough and brake, each plant and juiciest gourd, will pluck such choice to entertain our Angel-guest, as he beholding shall confess that here on Earth God has dispensed his bounties as in Heaven."

So saying, with dispatchful looks in haste she turns, on hospitable thoughts intent — what choice to choose for delicacy best; what order, contrived so as not to mix tastes not well joined, inelegant; but bring taste after taste upheld with kindliest change.

Then she bestirs herself, and from each tender stalk whatever Earth, all-bearing mother, yields in India East or West, or middle shore, in Pontus or the Punic coast, or where Alcinous reigned — fruit of all kinds, in coat rough, or smooth rind, or bearded husk, or shell — she gathers, a large tribute, and on the board heaps with unsparing hand. For drink she crushes the grape, inoffensive must, and meaths from many a berry, and from sweet kernels pressed she tempers dulcet creams. Nor does she want fit pure vessels to hold these. Then she strews the ground with rose and unfumed odours from the shrub.

Meanwhile our primitive great sire, to meet his God-like guest, walks forth, without more train attending than his own complete perfections; in himself was all his state, more solemn than the tedious pomp that waits on princes, when their rich retinue long of horses led, and grooms besmeared with gold, dazzles the crowd, and sets them all agape.

Nearer his presence Adam, though not awed, yet with submissive approach and meek reverence, as bowing low to a superior nature, thus said: "Native of Heaven — for no other place than Heaven can contain such a glorious shape;

since, by descending from the thrones above, you have deigned for a while to be without those happy places, and to honour these — vouchsafe to rest with us two only, who yet by sovereign gift possess this spacious ground, in yonder shady bower; and to sit and taste what the garden choicest bears, till this meridian heat be over, and the sun more cool decline."

To whom the angelic Virtue thus answered, mild: "Adam, I came for that reason. Nor are you so created, nor have you such a place to dwell in here, as may not often invite even Spirits of Heaven to visit you. Lead on, then, where your bower overshades. For these mid-hours, till evening rises, I have at will." So to the sylvan lodge they came, which smiled like Pomona's arbour, decked with florets and fragrant smells. But Eve, unadorned save with herself, more lovely fair than Wood-Nymph, or the fairest feigned Goddess of those three that on Mount Ida naked strove, stood to entertain her guest from Heaven. No veil she needed, being virtue-proof; no infirm thought altered her cheek. To her the Angel bestowed "Hail" — the holy salutation long after used to blessed Mary, second Eve:

"Hail, Mother of Mankind, whose fruitful womb shall fill the world more numerous with your sons than with these various fruits the trees of God have heaped this table!" Their table was raised of grassy turf, and had mossy seats round; and on her ample square, from side to side, all autumn was piled — though spring and autumn here danced hand in hand. A while they held discourse,

no fear lest dinner cool. Then thus began our author: "Heavenly stranger, please to taste these bounties, which our Nourisher — from whom all perfect good, unmeasured out, descends — has caused the earth to yield for us for food and for delight. Unsavoury food perhaps to spiritual natures; I know only this, that one celestial Father gives to all."

To whom the Angel: "Therefore what he gives (whose praise be ever sung) to Man in part spiritual, may by the purest Spirits be found no ungrateful food. And food alike those pure intellectual substances require, as does your rational; and both contain within them every lower faculty of sense, whereby they hear, see, smell, touch, taste — tasting they concoct, digest, assimilate, and turn corporeal to incorporeal.

For know, whatever was created needs to be sustained and fed. Of elements, the grosser feeds the purer: earth the sea, earth and the sea feed air, the air those ethereal fires; and the moon first, as lowest.

From this cause there are those unpurged spots in her round face — vapours not yet turned into her substance. Nor does the moon exhale no nourishment from her moist continent to higher orbs. The sun that imparts light to all receives from all his alimental recompense in humid exhalations, and at evening sups with the ocean. Though in Heaven the trees of life bear ambrosial fruitage, and vines yield nectar; though from off the boughs each morn we brush mellifluous dews, and find the ground covered with pearly grain; yet God has here so varied his bounty with new delights, as may compare with Heaven; and do not think I shall be nice to taste." So down they sat, and fell to their food — not seemingly the Angel, nor in mist (that common gloss of Theologians), but with keen dispatch of real hunger, and with concoctive heat to transubstantiate: what redounds transpires through Spirits with ease. Nor wonder — if by fire of sooty coal the empirick alchemist can turn, or holds it possible to turn, metals of drossiest ore to perfect gold, as from the mine. Meanwhile at table Eve ministered naked, and crowned their flowing cups with pleasant liquors. O innocence deserving Paradise! If ever, then — then had the sons of God excuse to have been enamoured at that sight. But in those hearts love unlibidinous reigned, nor was jealousy — the injured lover's hell — understood.

Thus when with meats and drinks they had sufficed, not burdened nature, a sudden thought arose in Adam — not to let the occasion pass given him by this great conference, to know of things above his world, and of the being of those who dwell in Heaven, whose excellence he saw transcend his own so far; whose radiant forms, divine effulgence, whose high power, so far exceeded human. And thus to the empyreal minister he framed his wary speech:

"Inhabitant with God, now I know well your favour, in this honour done to Man, under whose lowly roof you have vouchsafed to enter, and to taste these earthly fruits — food not of Angels, yet so accepted, as that more willingly you could not seem at Heaven's high feasts to have fed. Yet what comparison?" To whom the winged Hierarch replied:

"O Adam, One Almighty is, from whom all things proceed, and up to him return, if not depraved from good — created all such to perfection, one first matter all, endowed with various forms, various degrees of substance, and, in things that live, of life;

but more refined, more spirituous, and pure, as placed nearer to him, or nearer tending, each in their several active spheres assigned, till body up to spirit works, in bounds proportioned to each kind. So from the root springs lighter the green stalk; from thence the leaves more airy; last the bright consummate flower breathes odorous spirits. Flowers and their fruit — Man's nourishment — by gradual scale sublimed, aspire to vital spirits, to animal, to intellectual; give both life and sense, fancy and understanding; whence the soul Reason receives, and reason is her being, whether discursive or intuitive. Discourse is oftenest yours; the latter is most ours — differing but in degree, the same in kind.

Do not wonder, then, if what God saw good for you, I do not refuse, but convert, as you do, to proper substance. Time may come, when Men may participate with Angels, and find no inconvenient diet, nor too light a fare;

and from these corporal nutriments perhaps your bodies may at last all turn to spirit — improved by tract of time — and, winged, ascend ethereal, as we; or may, at choice, dwell here or in heavenly Paradises;
if you be found obedient, and retain unalterably firm his love entire, whose progeny you are. Meanwhile enjoy your fill of whatever happiness this happy state can comprehend, incapable of more."

To whom the patriarch of mankind replied: "O favourable Spirit, propitious guest, well have you taught the way that might direct our knowledge, and the scale of nature set from centre to circumference, on which, in contemplation of created things, by steps we may ascend to God. But say, what meant that caution joined — "If you be found obedient"? Can we want obedience then to him, or possibly desert his love, who formed us from the dust and placed us here full to the utmost measure of what bliss human desires can seek or apprehend?"

To whom the Angel: "Son of Heaven and Earth, attend! That you are happy, you owe to God; that you continue such, you owe to yourself — that is, to your obedience; therein stand. This was that caution given to you; be advised.
God made you perfect, not immutable; and he made you good, but to persevere he left it in your power. He ordained your will by nature free, not overruled by inextricable fate, or by strict necessity.

He requires our voluntary service, not our necessitated; such finds no acceptance with him, nor can it find any. For how can hearts, not free, be tried whether they serve willingly or not, who will but what they must by destiny, and can choose no other?

Myself, and all the angelic host that stand in sight of God, enthroned, hold our happy state, as you hold yours, while our obedience holds — on no other surety. Freely we serve, because we freely love, as it is in our will to love or not. In this we stand or fall;

and some are fallen — fallen to disobedience — and so from Heaven to deepest Hell. O fall from what high state of bliss, into what woe!" To whom our great progenitor: "Attentive, and with more delighted ear, divine instructor, I have heard your words, than when cherubic songs by night from neighbouring hills send aerial music. Nor did I not know myself to be created free both in will and in deed.

Yet my constant thoughts assured me — and still assure me — that we shall never forget to love our Maker, and obey him whose command, though single, is yet so just. But though what you tell has passed in Heaven, some doubt moves within me; but more desire to hear — if you consent — the full relation, which must needs be strange, worthy of sacred silence to be heard.

And we have yet large day; for scarcely has the sun finished half his journey, and scarcely begins his other half in the great zone of Heaven." Thus Adam made request; and Raphael, after short pause assenting, thus began:

"High matter you enjoin me, O prime of men, sad task and hard. For how shall I relate to human sense the invisible exploits of warring Spirits? How, without remorse, tell the ruin of so many, once glorious and perfect while they stood? How last unfold the secrets of another world, perhaps not lawful to reveal? Yet for your good this is dispensed. And what surmounts the reach of human sense, I shall delineate so, by likening spiritual to corporeal forms, as may express them best — though what if Earth be but a shadow of Heaven, and things therein each to the other like, more than on earth is thought?

As yet this world was not, and Chaos wild reigned where these Heavens now roll, where Earth now rests upon her centre poised; when on a day (for time, though in eternity, applied to motion, measures all things durable by present, past, and future) — on such a day as Heaven's great year brings forth, the empyreal host of Angels, called by imperial summons, appeared innumerable before the Almighty's throne forthwith, from all the ends of Heaven, under their Hierarchs in bright orders.

Ten thousand thousand ensigns high advanced, standards and gonfalons between van and rear, stream in the air, and serve for distinction of hierarchies, of orders, and degrees; or in their glittering tissues bear emblazoned holy memorials — acts of zeal and love recorded eminent. Thus when in orbs of inexpressible circuit they stood, orb within orb, the Father Infinite — by whom, embosomed in bliss, sat the Son — from the midst, as from a flaming mount whose top brightness had made invisible, thus spoke:

"Hear, all you Angels, progeny of light: Thrones, Dominations, Princedoms, Virtues, Powers. Hear my decree, which, unrevoked, shall stand. This day I have begotten whom I declare my only Son, and on this holy hill him I have anointed, whom you now behold at my right hand. Your head I appoint him;

and by myself I have sworn, all knees in Heaven shall bow to him, and shall confess him Lord. Under his great vicegerent reign abide united, as one individual soul, forever happy. He who disobeys him disobeys me, breaks union — and that day, cast out from God and the blessed vision, falls into utter darkness, deep engulfed; his place ordained without redemption, without end."

So spoke the Omnipotent; and with his words all seemed well pleased — all seemed, but were not all. That day, as other solemn days, they spent in song and dance about the sacred hill — mystic dance, which yonder starry sphere of planets and of fixed, in all her wheels, resembles most nearly; intricate mazes, eccentric, intervolved, yet regular then most, when they seem most irregular;

and in their motions their divine harmony so smooths her charming tones, that God's own ear listens delighted. Evening now approached (for we have also our evening and our morning — we have ours for change delectable, not need). Forthwith from dance to sweet repast they turn, desirous. While all stood in circles, tables are set, and on a sudden piled with Angels' food; and rubied nectar flows in pearl, in diamond, and massy gold, the fruit of delicious vines, the growth of Heaven.

Reposed on flowers, and crowned with fresh florets, they eat, they drink, and in sweet communion quaff immortality and joy, secure of surfeit — where full measure only bounds excess — before the all-bounteous King, who showered with copious hand, rejoicing in their joy.

Now when ambrosial night, with clouds exhaled from that high mount of God (whence light and shade both spring), had changed the face of brightest Heaven to grateful twilight (for night does not come there in darker veil), and roseate dews disposed all but the unsleeping eyes of God to rest;

wide over all the plain — and wider far than all this globous earth in plain outspread (such are the courts of God) — the angelic throng, dispersed in bands and files, extend their camp by living streams among the trees of life. Numberless pavilions, suddenly reared celestial tabernacles, where they slept, fanned with cool winds — save those who in their course sang melodious hymns about the sovereign throne, alternating all night long. But not so waked Satan — so call him now; his former name is heard no more in Heaven. He, of the first, if not the first Arch-Angel, great in power, in favour and pre-eminence — yet fraught with envy against the Son of God, that day honoured by his great Father, and proclaimed Messiah King anointed — could not bear through pride that sight, and thought himself impaired.

Deep malice thence conceiving, and disdain, as soon as midnight brought on the dusky hour friendliest to sleep and silence, he resolved with all his legions to dislodge, and leave the throne supreme unworshipped, unobeyed, contemptuous. And awakening his next subordinate, thus to him in secret he spoke:

"Are you sleeping, Companion dear? What sleep can close your eyelids? And do you remember what decree of yesterday so late has passed the lips of Heaven's Almighty? You were wont to impart your thoughts to me; I, mine to you.

Both waking, we were one; how then can now your sleep dissent? You see new laws imposed. New laws from him who reigns may raise new minds in us who serve, new counsels to debate what doubtful may ensue. More in this place to utter is not safe. Assemble those of all those myriads of whom we lead the chief.

Tell them that by command, before dim night withdraws her shadowy cloud, I must hasten — and all who under me wave their banners — homeward, with flying march, where we possess the quarters of the north. There to prepare fit entertainment to receive our King, the great Messiah, and his new commands — who speedily through all the hierarchies intends to pass triumphant, and give laws."

So spoke the false Arch-Angel, and infused bad influence into the unwary breast of his associate. He together calls, or several one by one, the regent Powers under him regent; tells, as he was taught, that the Most High commanding — now, before night, before dim night had disincumbered Heaven — the great hierarchal standard was to move.

He tells the suggested cause, and casts between ambiguous words and jealousies, to sound or taint integrity. But all obeyed the wonted signal and the superior voice of their great Potentate; for great indeed was his name, and high was his degree in Heaven.

His countenance, as the morning-star that guides the starry flock, allured them; and with lies he drew after him the third part of Heaven's host. Meanwhile the Eternal eye, whose sight discerns the most abstruse thoughts, from forth his holy mount, and from within the golden lamps that burn nightly before him, saw (without their light) rebellion rising; saw in whom, and how it spread among the sons of morn; what multitudes were banded to oppose his high decree.

And, smiling, to his only Son thus said: "Son, you in whom I behold my glory in full resplendence, Heir of all my might, nearly it now concerns us to be sure of our Omnipotence, and with what arms we mean to hold what we anciently claim of deity or empire. Such a foe is rising, who intends to erect his throne equal to ours, throughout the spacious north;

nor content with that, he has it in his thought to try in battle what our power is, or our right. Let us advise, and to this hazard draw with speed what force is left, and all employ in our defence, lest unawares we lose this our high place, our sanctuary, our hill."

To whom the Son, with calm aspect and clear — lightning divine, ineffable, serene — made answer: "Mighty Father, you rightly have your foes in derision, and, secure, laugh at their vain designs and vain tumults. A matter to me of glory, whom their hate illustrates, when they see all regal power given to me to quell their pride, and in the event know whether I am dextrous to subdue your rebels, or be found the worst in Heaven."

So spoke the Son. But Satan, with his Powers, was far advanced on winged speed — a host innumerable as the stars of night, or stars of morning, dew-drops, which the sun impearls on every leaf and every flower.

They passed regions, the mighty regencies of Seraphim, and Potentates, and Thrones, in their triple degrees — regions to which all your dominion, Adam, is no more than what this garden is to all the earth, and all the sea, stretched from one entire globe into longitude. Having passed these, at length they came into the limits of the north, and Satan came to his royal seat, high on a hill, far blazing, as a mount raised on a mount, with pyramids and towers hewn from diamond quarries, and rocks of gold —

the palace of great Lucifer (so call that structure, interpreted in the dialect of men). Not long after, he, affecting all equality with God, in imitation of that mount whereon Messiah was declared in sight of Heaven, called it the Mountain of the Congregation.

For thither he assembled all his train, pretending he was so commanded to consult about the great reception of their King, who was to come thither. And with calumnious art of counterfeited truth he thus held their ears:

"Thrones, Dominations, Princedoms, Virtues, Powers! If these magnific titles still remain not merely titular — since by decree another has now engrossed to himself all power, and eclipsed us under the name of King anointed, for whom all this haste of midnight-march and hurried meeting here is only to consult how we may best, with whatever may be devised of new honours, receive him, when he comes to receive from us the yet unpaid knee-tribute — prostration vile!

Too much to one! But how is it doubly to be endured, to one and to his image now proclaimed? But what if better counsels might erect our minds, and teach us to cast off this yoke? Will you submit your necks, and choose to bend the supple knee? You will not, if I trust my knowledge of you rightly, or if you know yourselves — natives and sons of Heaven, possessed before by none; and if not all equal, yet free, equally free; for orders and degrees jar not with liberty, but well consist.

Who can then, in reason or in right, assume monarchy over such as live by right his equals — if less in power and splendour, in freedom equal? Or can introduce law and edict upon us, who without law do not err? Much less, for that, to be our Lord, and look for adoration — abusing those imperial titles, which assert our being ordained to govern, not to serve."

Thus far his bold discourse had audience without control. When among the Seraphim Abdiel — than whom none adored the Deity with more zeal, and obeyed divine commands — stood up, and in a flame of severe zeal thus opposed the current of his fury:

"O argument blasphemous, false, and proud! Words which no ear in Heaven ever expected to hear — least of all from you, Ingrate — in place yourself so high above your peers! Can you with impious obloquy condemn the just decree of God, pronounced and sworn, that to his only Son, by right endowed with regal sceptre, every soul in Heaven shall bend the knee, and in that due honour confess him rightful King? Unjust, you say — flatly unjust — to bind with laws the free, and to let one reign monarch over equals, one over all with unsucceeded power.

Shall you give law to God? Shall you dispute with him the points of liberty, who made you what you are, and formed the Powers of Heaven such as he pleased, and circumscribed their being? Yet, taught by experience, we know how good, and how provident he is of our good and of our dignity; how far from any thought to make us less — bent rather to exalt our happy state, under one head more nearly united. But to grant it you unjust, that equal over equals monarch reign:

yourself, though great and glorious, do you count — or all angelic nature joined in one — equal to him, the Begotten Son? By whom, as by his Word, the Mighty Father made all things, even you; and all the Spirits of Heaven were created by him in their bright degrees — crowned them with glory, and to their glory named Thrones, Dominations, Princedoms, Virtues, Powers, essential Powers — nor are they obscured by his reign, but made more illustrious. For he, the head, becoming one of our number thus reduced:

his laws our laws; all honour done to him returns our own. Cease, then, this impious rage, and tempt not these; but hasten to appease the incensed Father, and the incensed Son, while pardon may yet be found if sought in time."

So spoke the fervent Angel. But his zeal none seconded — as being out of season judged, or as singular and rash. Whereat the Apostate rejoiced, and more haughty, thus replied: "Do you say, then, that we were formed — and are the work of secondary hands, by task transferred from Father to his Son? A strange point, and new!

A doctrine we would know whence learned. Who saw when this creation was? Do you remember your making, while the Maker gave you being? We know of no time when we were not as now; know of none before us. Self-begot, self-raised by our own quickening power, when the fatal course had circled his full orb — the birth mature of this our native Heaven, ethereal sons.

Our puissance is our own; our own right hand shall teach us highest deeds, by proof to try who is our equal. Then you shall behold whether by supplication we intend to approach, and, beseeching or besieging, to begird the almighty throne. Carry this report, these tidings, to the anointed King;

and fly, before evil intercept your flight." He said; and like the sound of deep waters, hoarse murmur echoed to his words in applause through the infinite host. Nor was the flaming Seraph the less fearless — though alone encompassed round with foes, he thus answered bold:

"O Spirit alienate from God, O Spirit accursed, forsaken of all good! I see your fall determined, and your hapless crew involved in this perfidious fraud — contagion spread both of your crime and of your punishment. Henceforth no more be troubled how to quit the yoke of God's Messiah. Those indulgent laws will not now be vouchsafed; other decrees against you have gone forth without recall.

That golden sceptre, which you did reject, is now an iron rod to bruise and break your disobedience. Well you did advise — yet not for your advice or threats do I flee these wicked tents devoted to destruction; lest the impending wrath, raging into sudden flame, not distinguish. For soon expect to feel his thunder on your head — devouring fire.

Then, lamenting, learn who created you, when you shall know who can uncreate you." So spoke the Seraph Abdiel, faithful found among the faithless — faithful only he; among innumerable false, unmoved, unshaken, unseduced, unterrified, he kept his loyalty, his love, his zeal.

Neither number nor example worked with him to swerve from truth, or change his constant mind, though he was single. From amidst them forth he passed, a long way through hostile scorn, which he sustained superior; nor did he fear anything of violence. And, with retorted scorn, he turned his back on those proud towers, doomed to swift destruction.

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: All night the dreadless Angel, unpursued, held his way through Heaven's wide plain; until Morn, awakened by the circling Hours, with rosy hand unbarred the gates of light. There is a cave within the mount of God, fast by his throne, where light and darkness in perpetual round lodge and dislodge by turns, which makes through Heaven a grateful vicissitude, like day and night.

Light issues forth, and at the other door obsequious darkness enters, till her hour to veil the Heaven — though darkness there might well seem twilight here. And now the Morn went forth, such as in highest Heaven arrayed in gold empyreal. From before her vanished Night, shot through with orient beams; when all the plain, covered with thick embattled squadrons bright, chariots, and flaming arms, and fiery steeds, reflecting blaze on blaze, first met his view.

War he perceived, war on the point of joining; and he found already known what he had thought to report as news. Gladly then he mixed among those friendly Powers, who received him with joy and loud acclamations, that one — that of so many fallen myriads, one — returned not lost. On to the sacred hill they led him, high applauded, and presented before the seat supreme; from which a voice, from the midst of a golden cloud, was thus mildly heard:

"Servant of God, well done! Well have you fought the better fight, who single have maintained against revolted multitudes the cause of truth, in word mightier than they in arms; and for the testimony of truth have borne universal reproach — far worse to bear than violence. For this was all your care: to stand approved in sight of God, though worlds judged you perverse. The easier conquest now remains to you, aided by this host of friends: to return back on your foes more glorious than, scorned, you departed; and to subdue by force those who refuse reason for their law — right reason for their law, and for their King Messiah, who reigns by right of merit.

Go, Michael, prince of celestial armies; and you, Gabriel, next in military prowess, lead forth to battle these my invincible sons. Lead forth my armed Saints, by thousands and by millions, ranged for fight, equal in number to that Godless rebellious crew. With fire and hostile arms fearlessly assault them; and, pursuing to the brow of Heaven, drive them out from God and bliss, into their place of punishment, the gulf of Tartarus, which opens ready wide his fiery Chaos to receive their fall."

So spoke the Sovereign Voice; and clouds began to darken all the hill, and smoke to roll in dusky wreaths — reluctant flames, the sign of wrath awakened. Nor with less dread the loud ethereal trumpet from on high began to blow.

At which command the Powers militant, who stood for Heaven, joined in mighty quadrate of irresistible union, moved on their bright legions in silence, to the sound of instrumental harmony, that breathed heroic ardour to adventurous deeds under their God-like leaders, in the cause of God and his Messiah. On they move, indissolubly firm; nor does hill in the way, nor straitening vale, nor wood, nor stream, divide their perfect ranks; for high above the ground their march was, and the passive air upbore their nimble tread. As when the whole kind of birds, in orderly array on wing, came summoned over Eden to receive their names from you — so over many a tract of Heaven they marched, and over many a wide province, tenfold the length of this terrestrial. At last, far in the horizon to the north appeared from skirt to skirt a fiery region, stretched in battle aspect; and on nearer view, bristled with innumerable upright beams of rigid spears, and helmets thronged, and shields various, portrayed with boastful argument — the banded Powers of Satan hasting on with furious expedition. For they thought that that same day, by fight or by surprise, to win the mount of God, and on his throne to set the Envier of his state, the proud aspirer. But their thoughts proved foolish and vain in the mid way. Though strange it seemed to us at first, that Angel should war with Angel, and meet in fierce hosting, who were wont to meet so often in festivals of joy and love unanimous, as sons of one great Sire, hymning the Eternal Father. But the shout of battle now began, and the rushing sound of onset soon ended each milder thought.

High in the midst, exalted as a God, the Apostate sat in his sun-bright chariot — idol of divine majesty, enclosed with flaming Cherubim and golden shields. Then he lighted from his gorgeous throne, for now between host and host there was left but narrow space, a dreadful interval, and front to front they stood in terrible array of hideous length. Before the cloudy van, on the rough edge of battle before it joined, Satan, with vast and haughty strides, advanced, and came towering, armed in adamant and gold.

Abdiel did not endure that sight, where he stood among the mightiest, bent on highest deeds; and thus his own undaunted heart explores: "O Heaven! that such resemblance of the Highest should yet remain, where faith and reality remain not! Why should not strength and might there fail where virtue fails, or prove weakest where boldest — though to fight unconquerable?

His puissance, trusting in the Almighty's aid, I mean to try — whose reason I have tried and found unsound and false. Nor is it anything but just that he who in debate of truth has won should win in arms; victor alike in both disputes. Though brutish and foul is that contest, when reason has to deal with force; yet it is most reasonable that such unreason be overcome."

So pondering, and stepping forth from his armed peers opposite, half-way he met his daring foe — the more incensed at this interception — and thus securely defied him: "Proud one, are you met? Your hope was to have reached the height of your aspiring unopposed, the throne of God unguarded, and his side abandoned, at the terror of your power or potent tongue. Fool! not to think how vain it is to rise in arms against the Omnipotent,

who out of smallest things could, without end, have raised incessant armies to defeat your folly; or with solitary hand reaching beyond all limit, at one blow, unaided, could have finished you, and overwhelmed your legions under darkness. But you see all are not of your train; there are those who prefer faith and piety to God — though to you then not visible, when I alone seemed in your world erroneous, to dissent from all. My sect you see; now learn, too late, how few sometimes may know, when thousands err."

To whom the grand foe, with scornful eye askance, thus answered: "Ill for you — but in a wished hour of my revenge, first sought for — you return from flight, seditious Angel, to receive your merited reward, the first taste of this provoked right hand; since first that tongue, inspired with contradiction, dared oppose a third part of the Gods, met in synod to assert their deities; who, while they feel divine vigour within them, can allow omnipotence to none. But well you come before your fellows, ambitious to win from me some plume, so that your success may show destruction to the rest. This pause between (lest unanswered you boast), let me tell you: at first I thought that Liberty and Heaven were to heavenly souls all one. But now I see that most through sloth would rather serve — ministering Spirits, trained up in feast and song!

Such you have armed — the minstrelsy of Heaven — to contend servility with freedom, as the comparison of both their deeds this day shall prove." To whom in brief thus Abdiel sternly replied: "Apostate! You still err, nor will find an end of erring, since you are remote from the path of truth.

Unjustly you deprave it with the name of servitude — to serve whom God ordains, or Nature. God and Nature bid the same, when he who rules is worthiest, and excels those whom he governs. This is servitude: to serve the unwise, or him who has rebelled against his worthier — as yours now serve you, yourself not free, but to yourself enthralled.

Yet lewdly you dare upbraid our ministering. Reign in Hell, your kingdom; let me serve in Heaven ever-blessed God, and obey his divine behests, worthiest to be obeyed. Yet expect chains in Hell, not realms. Meanwhile, from me returned, as you just said, from flight, receive on your impious crest this greeting."

So saying, he lifted high a noble stroke, which hung not, but with tempest-swiftness fell on Satan's proud crest, so that no sight nor motion of swift thought — much less his shield — could intercept such ruin. Ten paces huge he recoiled backward; on the tenth, bended on his knee, his massy spear upheld him — as if on earth, winds underground or waters forcing their way had sidelong pushed a mountain from its seat, half sunk with all its pines. Amazement seized the rebel Thrones, but greater rage, to see their mightiest thus foiled. Our side was filled with joy, and shouted — presage of victory, and fierce desire of battle. Whereat Michael bid sound the Arch-Angel trumpet; through the vast of Heaven it sounded, and the faithful armies rang "Hosanna to the Highest!" Nor stood at gaze the adverse legions; no less hideously they joined the horrid shock. Now storming fury rose, and such clamour as was never heard in Heaven till then. Arms on armour clashing brayed horrible discord, and the maddening wheels of brazen chariots raged. Dire was the noise of conflict; overhead the dismal hiss of fiery darts in flaming volleys flew, and, flying, vaulted either host with fire.

So under fiery canopy both main battles rushed together, with ruinous assault and inextinguishable rage. All Heaven resounded; and had Earth been then, all Earth would have shaken to her centre. What wonder? when millions of fierce encountering Angels fought on either side, the least of whom could wield these elements and arm himself with the force of all their regions. How much more power an army raised against a numberless army to raise dreadful combustion warring, and disturb (though not destroy) their happy native seat —

had not the Eternal King Omnipotent, from his stronghold of Heaven, high over-ruled and limited their might. Though numbered such that each divided legion might have seemed a numerous host; each armed hand in strength a legion; yet each warrior seemed a leader in fight, as if in chief — expert when to advance, or stand, or turn the sway of battle, when to open, and when to close the ridges of grim war. No thought of flight, none of retreat, no unbecoming deed that argued fear: each relied on himself, as if the moment of victory lay in his arm alone. Deeds of eternal fame were done, but infinite; for wide was spread that war, and various. Sometimes on firm ground a standing fight; then, soaring on main wing, they tormented all the air; all air then seemed conflicting fire. Long time in even scale the battle hung; until Satan, who that day had shown prodigious power, and met in arms no equal, ranging through the dire attack of confused, fighting Seraphim, at length saw where the sword of Michael smote, and felled squadrons at once; with huge two-handed sway brandished aloft, the horrid edge came down wide-wasting. Such destruction to withstand he hastened, and opposed the rocky orb of tenfold adamant — his ample shield, of vast circumference. At his approach the great Arch-Angel ceased from his warlike toil, glad, as hoping here to end the intestine war in Heaven with the arch-foe subdued or dragged captive in chains. With hostile frown and visage all inflamed, he first thus began:

"Author of evil — unknown till your revolt, unnamed in Heaven — now plenteous as you see are these acts of hateful strife, hateful to all, though heaviest by just measure on yourself and your adherents. How have you disturbed Heaven's blessed peace, and brought into nature misery, uncreated till the crime of your rebellion! How have you instilled your malice into thousands, once upright and faithful, now proved false! But do not think to trouble holy rest here; Heaven casts you out from all her confines. Heaven, the seat of bliss, brooks not the works of violence and war.

Hence, then — and let evil go along with you, your offspring, to the place of evil, Hell; you and your wicked crew! There mingle your broils, before this avenging sword begins your doom, or some more sudden vengeance, winged from God, precipitates you with augmented pain."

So spoke the Prince of Angels; to whom thus the Adversary: "Do not think by wind of airy threats to awe one whom yet by deeds you cannot awe. Have you turned the least of these to flight? Or, if to fall, they rise unvanquished — easier to transact with me than that you should hope, imperious, and with threats to chase me hence. Do not err: that will not end the strife which you call evil, but we style the strife of glory; which we mean to win, or turn this Heaven itself into the Hell you fable. Here, however, we will dwell free, if not to reign. Meanwhile, bring your utmost force, and join to your aid him named Almighty: I flee not, but have sought you far and near."

They ended parley, and both addressed themselves for fight unspeakable — for who, though with the tongue of Angels, can relate, or to what things on earth conspicuous liken them, that may lift human imagination to such height of Godlike power? For most like Gods they seemed, whether they stood or moved — in stature, motion, and arms fit to decide the empire of great Heaven.

Now they waved their fiery swords, and in the air made horrid circles. Two broad suns — their shields — blazed opposite, while Expectation stood in horror. From each hand the angelic throng retired with speed from where had been the thickest fight, and left a large field, unsafe within the wind of such commotion — such as, to set forth great things by small, if, nature's concord broken, war were sprung among the constellations, two planets, rushing from malign aspect of fiercest opposition, should combat in mid sky, and confound their jarring spheres.

Together both, with next to almighty arm uplifted imminent, aimed one stroke that might determine, and not need to be repeated — as of power not appearing twice at once. Nor did odds appear in might or swift prevention. But the sword of Michael, given to him from the armoury of God, was so tempered that neither keen nor solid object could resist that edge. It met the sword of Satan, descending with steep force to smite, and cut it sheer in half; nor stayed, but with swift wheel reverse, deep entering, shared all his right side. Then Satan first knew pain, and writhed himself to and fro convolved; so sorely the griding sword with discontinuous wound passed through him. But the ethereal substance closed, not long divisible; and from the gash a stream of nectarous humour issued, flowing sanguine — such as celestial Spirits may bleed — and stained all his armour, erewhile so bright.

Forthwith on all sides to his aid ran many strong Angels, who interposed defence, while others bore him on their shields back to his chariot, where it stood retired off from the files of war. There they laid him, gnashing with anguish, and spite, and shame, to find himself not matchless, and his pride humbled by such a rebuke — so far beneath his confidence to equal God in power.

Yet soon he healed; for Spirits that live throughout, vital in every part, not like frail man in entrails, heart, or head, liver, or reins — cannot but by annihilation die; nor in their liquid texture can receive a mortal wound any more than can the fluid air.

All heart they live, all head, all eye, all ear, all intellect, all sense; and, as they please, they limb themselves, and assume colour, shape, or size, condense or rare, as likes them best. Meanwhile in other parts like deeds deserved memorial, where the might of Gabriel fought, and with fierce ensigns pierced the deep array of Moloch, furious king; who defied him, and threatened to drag him bound at his chariot wheels; nor did he refrain his blasphemous tongue from the Holy One of Heaven. But anon, cloven down to the waist, with shattered arms and uncouth pain, he fled bellowing. On each wing Uriel, and Raphael, their vaunting foe — though huge, and armed in a rock of diamond — vanquished Adramelech and Asmadai, two potent Thrones that disdained to be less than Gods, but learned meaner thoughts in their flight, mangled with ghastly wounds through plate and mail.

Nor stood Abdiel unmindful to annoy the atheist crew, but with redoubled blow scorched and blasted and overthrew Ariel, and Arioch, and the violence of Ramiel. I might relate of thousands, and eternize their names here on earth; but those elect Angels, content with their fame in Heaven, seek not the praise of men. The other sort — though wondrous in might and in acts of war, and no less eager of renown — yet by doom are cancelled from Heaven and sacred memory. Nameless in dark oblivion let them dwell.

For strength divided from truth and justice is unpraiseworthy, deserves nothing but dispraise and ignominy; yet it aspires to glory, vainglorious, and through infamy seeks fame. Therefore eternal silence be their doom.

And now, their mightiest quelled, the battle swerved, gored with many an inroad. Deformed rout entered, and foul disorder. All the ground was strewn with shivered armour; and in a heap chariot and charioteer lay overturned, and fiery-foaming steeds. What still stood recoiled over-wearied; and through the faint Satanic host, scarcely defensive, or surprised with pale fear, then first surprised with fear, and with the sense of pain, they fled ignominious, brought to such evil by sin of disobedience — till that hour not liable to fear, or flight, or pain.

Far otherwise the inviolable Saints, in cubic phalanx firm, advanced entire, invulnerable, impenetrably armed. Such high advantages their innocence gave them over their foes: not to have sinned, not to have disobeyed. In fight they stood unwearied, not exposed to pain by wound, though moved from their place by violence. Now Night began her course, and, inducing darkness over Heaven, imposed grateful truce, and silence on the odious din of war.

Under her cloudy covert both retired, victor and vanquished. On the field of battle Michael and his Angels, prevalent, encamping, placed their watches in guard round about — waving Cherubic fires. On the other side, Satan with his rebellious host disappeared, dislodged far in the dark; and, void of rest, he called his potentates to council by night.

And in the midst, thus undismayed, he began: "O companions dear, now tried in danger, now known in arms not to be overpowered — found worthy not of liberty alone (too mean a pretence), but of what we more affect, honour, dominion, glory, and renown;

who have sustained, for one day in doubtful fight (and if one day, why not eternal days?), what Heaven's Lord had most powerful to send against us from about his throne, and judged sufficient to subdue us to his will — but it proves not so. Then fallible, it seems, of the future we may deem him, though till now we thought him omniscient. True it is, less firmly armed, we endured some disadvantage and pain, till now unknown; but, known, as soon scorned.

For now we find this our empyreal form incapable of mortal injury — imperishable; and, though pierced with wound, soon closing, and healed by native vigour. Then think the remedy of an evil so small as easy. Perhaps more valid arms, more violent weapons, when next we meet, may serve to better us and worse our foes, or equal what made the odds between us — since in nature there is none. If some other hidden cause left them superior, while we can preserve unhurt our minds and sound understanding, due search and consultation will disclose it."

He sat; and next stood up in the assembly Nisroch, chief of the Principalities. As one who had escaped from cruel fight, sore toiled, his riven arms hacked to havoc, cloudy in aspect, he thus answering spoke:

"Deliverer from new Lords, leader to free enjoyment of our right as Gods — yet hard even for Gods, and too unequal work we find, to fight in pain against those who are unpained, impassive. From this evil ruin must needs ensue; for what avails valour or strength, though matchless, quelled with pain which all subdues, and makes slack the hands even of the mightiest? The sense of pleasure we might well spare out of life perhaps, and not repine, but live content — which is the calmest life;

but pain is perfect misery, the worst of evils, and, excessive, overturns all patience. He, therefore, who can invent with what more forcible we may offend our yet unwounded enemies, or arm ourselves with like defence — to me deserves no less than what we owe for our deliverance."

Whereto with composed look Satan replied: "Not uninvented is that which you rightly believe so vital to our success — I bring it. Which of us, who beholds the bright surface of this ethereous mould whereon we stand, this continent of spacious Heaven, adorned with plant, ambrosial fruit, flower, gems, and gold,

is so superficial as not to consider whence they grow? Deep underground, materials dark and crude, of spirituous and fiery foam, until, touched by Heaven's ray and tempered, they shoot forth so beauteous, opening to the ambient light.

These, in their dark nativity, the deep shall yield to us, pregnant with infernal flame; which, thickly rammed into hollow engines, long and round, shall, at the other bore with touch of fire, dilated and infuriate, send forth from far, with thundering noise, among our foes such implements of mischief as shall dash to pieces and overwhelm whatever stands adverse — so that they shall fear we have disarmed the Thunderer of his only dreaded bolt.

Nor long shall our labour be; and before dawn, effect shall end our wish. Meanwhile revive; abandon fear. Joined to strength and counsel, think nothing hard — much less to be despaired of." He ended, and his words enlightened their drooping cheer, and revived their languished hope.

All admired the invention; and each wondered how he had missed being the inventor — so easy it seemed once found, which yet, unfound, most would have thought impossible. Yet, perhaps, of your race in future days, if malice should abound, someone intent on mischief, or inspired with devilish machination, might devise a like instrument to plague the sons of men for sin, bent on war and mutual slaughter.

Forthwith from council they flew to the work. None stood arguing; innumerable hands were ready. In a moment they turned up wide the celestial soil, and saw beneath the originals of nature in their crude conception. Sulphurous and nitrous foam they found; they mingled them, and, with subtle art, concocted and adusted, they reduced them to blackest grain, and conveyed it into store.

Part dug up hidden veins (nor does this earth have unlike entrails) of mineral and stone, with which to found their engines and their balls of missive ruin. Part provide incentive reed, pernicious, to fire with one touch.

So all, before day-spring, under conscious night, they secretly finished, and set in order, with silent circumspection, unespied. Now when fair morn appeared orient in Heaven, up rose the victor-Angels, and the matin trumpet sang to arms. In arms they stood of golden panoply — a refulgent host, soon banded. Others from the dawning hills look round; and scouts light-armed scour each coast, each quarter to descry the distant foe — where lodged, or where fled, or if for fight, in motion or in halt. They soon met him, moving nigh under spread ensigns, in slow but firm battalion. Back with speediest sail Zophiel, of Cherubim the swiftest wing, came flying, and in mid air aloud thus cried:

"Arm, Warriors, arm for fight! The foe is at hand, whom we thought fled; he will save us long pursuit this day. Do not fear his flight. So thick a cloud he comes, and in his face I see settled sad resolution, and secure. Let each gird his adamantine coat well, and each fit well his helm, grip fast his orbed shield, borne even or high. For this day, if I conjecture aught, will pour down no drizzling shower, but rattling storm of arrows barbed with fire."

So he warned them. Aware themselves, soon in order, quit of all impediment, instant and without disturb they took alarm, and onward moved embattled. When behold! not distant far, with heavy pace, the foe approaching gross and huge, in hollow cube, training his devilish enginery, impaled on every side with shadowing squadrons deep, to hide the fraud. At first interview both stood a while. But suddenly at the head appeared Satan, and thus was heard commanding loud:

"Vanguard, unfold the front to right and left, that all who hate us may see how we seek peace and composure, and with open breast stand ready to receive them, if they like our overture, and do not turn back perverse.

But this I doubt. However, witness, Heaven! Heaven, you witness anon, while we freely discharge our part. You, who are appointed, stand — do as you have in charge; and briefly touch what we propound, and loud, that all may hear!"

So scoffing in ambiguous words, he had scarce ended, when to right and left the front divided, and to either flank retired — which to our eyes disclosed a new and strange sight: a triple-mounted row of pillars laid on wheels (for like to pillars they mostly seemed, or hollowed bodies made of oak or fir, with branches lopped, felled in wood or mountain), of brass, iron, stony mould — had not their mouths with hideous orifice gaped wide upon us, portending hollow truce. At each, behind, a Seraph stood, and in his hand a reed stood waving, tipped with fire; while we, in suspense, stood collected within our thoughts, puzzled. Not long; for suddenly all at once their reeds came forth and were applied to a narrow vent with nicest touch. Immediately in a flame, but soon obscured with smoke, all Heaven appeared, from those deep-throated engines belched, whose roar disembowelled with outrageous noise the air, and tore all her entrails, foully disgorging their devilish glut — chained thunderbolts and hail of iron globes. These, levelled on the victor host, smote with such impetuous fury that whomever they hit could not stand on their feet — though standing else as rocks; down they fell by thousands, Angel rolled on Arch-Angel —

the sooner for their arms. Unarmed, they might, as Spirits, have easily evaded swift by quick contraction or removal; but now foul dissipation followed, and forced rout; nor did it serve to relax their serried files.

What should they do? If they rushed on, repeated repulse and doubled indecent overthrow would render them yet more despised, and a laughter to their foes. For in view stood ranked another row of Seraphim, in posture to discharge their second tier of thunder. Back, defeated, to return they worse abhorred. Satan beheld their plight, and to his mates in derision thus called:

"O Friends! Why do these proud victors not come on? A little while ago they were fiercely coming; and when we, to entertain them fairly with open front and breast (what more could we do?), propounded terms of composition, straight they changed their minds, flew off, and fell into strange vagaries, as though they would dance. Yet for a dance they seemed somewhat extravagant and wild — perhaps for joy of offered peace. But I suppose, if our proposals were once again heard, we should compel them to a quick result."

To whom Belial thus, in like gamesome mood: "Leader! The terms we sent were terms of weight, of hard contents, and full of force urged home; such as we might perceive amused them all, and stumbled many. Who receives them right had need from head to foot well understand.

If not understood, they have this further gift — they show us when our foes do not walk upright." So among themselves they stood scoffing in pleasant vein, heightened in their thoughts beyond all doubt of victory. Eternal Might they presumed so easy to match with their inventions; and made a scorn of his thunder, and derided all his host, while these stood a while in trouble. But they stood not long.

Rage prompted them at length, and found them arms fit to oppose such hellish mischief. Forthwith (behold the excellence, the power which God has placed in his mighty Angels!) they threw their arms away, and to the hills (for Earth has this variety from Heaven of pleasure situate in hill and dale) they ran, they flew, light as the lightning's glimpse.

Loosening them from their foundations to and fro, they plucked up the seated hills, with all their load — rocks, waters, woods; and, lifting them by their shaggy tops, bore them in their hands. Amazement, be sure, and terror seized the rebel host, when they saw the bottoms of the mountains turned upward, coming so dreadfully toward them.

Until on those cursed engines' triple row they saw them overwhelmed, and all their confidence buried deep under the weight of mountains. Themselves were invaded next; main promontories were flung on their heads, shadowing them as they came through the air, and oppressed whole armed legions.

Their armour helped their harm: crushed in and bruised into their substance pent, it wrought them implacable pain, and many a dolorous groan — long struggling underneath, before they could wind their way out of such prison, though Spirits of purest light, purest at first, now grown gross by sinning.

The rest, in imitation, took to like arms, and uptore the neighbouring hills. So hills amid the air encountered hills, hurled to and fro with dire casting; so that underground they fought in dismal shade.

Infernal noise! War seemed a civil game to this uproar. Horrid confusion heaped upon confusion rose. And now all Heaven would have gone to wrack, overspread with ruin, had not the Almighty Father, where he sits shrined in his sanctuary of Heaven secure, consulting on the sum of things, foreseen this tumult, and permitted all, advised —

that his great purpose he might so fulfil: to honour his anointed Son avenged upon his enemies, and to declare all power transferred upon him. Whence to his Son, the Assessor of his throne, he thus began:

"Effulgence of my glory, Son beloved, Son in whose face invisible is beheld visibly what by Deity I am; and in whose hand is done what by decree I do — Second Omnipotence! — two days are past, two days as we compute the days of Heaven, since Michael and his Powers went forth to tame these disobedient. Sore has their fight been, as was likeliest when two such foes met armed.

For I left them to themselves; and you know, they were formed equal in their creation, save what sin has impaired — which yet has wrought insensibly, for I suspend their doom. Whence in perpetual fight they must needs last endless, and no solution will be found.

War wearied has performed what war can do; and to disordered rage has let loose the reins, armed with mountains, as with weapons — which makes wild work in Heaven, and dangerous to the main. Two days are therefore past; the third is yours.

For you I have ordained it; and thus far have permitted, so that the glory may be yours of ending this great war, since none but you can end it. Into you such immense virtue and grace I have transfused, that all in Heaven and Hell may know your power beyond compare;

and, this perverse commotion thus governed, manifest you worthiest to be Heir of all things — to be Heir, and to be King by sacred unction, your deserved right. Go, then, you Mightiest, in your Father's might;

ascend my chariot; guide the rapid wheels that shake Heaven's basis. Bring forth all my war — my bow and thunder; gird on my almighty arms, and sword upon your puissant thigh. Pursue these sons of darkness; drive them out from all Heaven's bounds into the utter deep.

There let them learn, as likes them, to despise God, and Messiah his anointed King." He said; and on his Son with direct rays shone full. He, the Son, expressed all his Father fully, ineffably received into his face.

And thus the Filial Godhead spoke in answer: "O Father, O Supreme of heavenly Thrones — First, Highest, Holiest, Best — you always seek to glorify your Son, I always you, as is most just. This I account my glory, my exaltation, and my whole delight, that you, well pleased in me, declare your will fulfilled — to fulfil which is all my bliss.

Sceptre and power, by your giving, I assume, and shall more gladly resign, when in the end you shall be all in all, and I in you forever; and in me all whom you love. But whom you hate, I hate; and can put on your terrors, as I put your mildness on — image of you in all things. And shall soon, armed with your might, rid Heaven of these rebelled —

driven down to their prepared ill mansion, to chains of darkness, and the undying worm — those who from your just obedience could revolt, whom to obey is happiness entire. Then shall your Saints unmixed, and separated far from the impure, circling your holy mount, sing unfeigned Hallelujahs to you, hymns of high praise, and I among them Chief."

So saying, he, bowing over his sceptre, rose from the right hand of Glory where he sat. And the third sacred morn began to shine, dawning through Heaven. Forth rushed with whirlwind sound the chariot of Paternal Deity, flashing thick flames, wheel within wheel undrawn, itself instinct with Spirit, but convoyed by four Cherubic shapes. Four wondrous faces each had; as with stars, their bodies all and wings were set with eyes; with eyes the wheels of beryl, and careering fires between;

over their heads a crystal firmament, whereon a sapphire throne, inlaid with pure amber, and colours of the showery rainbow. He, in celestial panoply all armed of radiant Urim, work divinely wrought, ascended. At his right hand Victory sat eagle-winged; beside him hung his bow and quiver with three-bolted thunder stored;

and from about him fierce effusion rolled of smoke, and flickering flame, and dire sparkles. Attended with ten thousand thousand Saints, he came onward; far off his coming shone. And twenty thousand (I heard their number) chariots of God, half on each hand, were seen.

He on the wings of Cherub rode sublime on the crystalline sky, enthroned in sapphire, illustrious far and wide; but by his own first seen. Unexpected joy surprised them, when the great ensign of Messiah blazed aloft, borne by Angels — his sign in Heaven.

Under whose conduct Michael soon reduced his army, circumfused on either wing, under their Head embodied all in one. Before him Power Divine prepared his way. At his command the uprooted hills retired each to its place; they heard his voice, and went obsequious. Heaven renewed her wonted face, and with fresh florets hill and valley smiled.

His hapless foes saw this, but stood hardened, and rallied their Powers to rebellious fight, insensate, conceiving hope from despair. Could such perverseness dwell in heavenly Spirits? But to convince the proud, what signs avail, or what wonders move the obdurate to relent?

They, hardened more by what might most reclaim, grieving to see his glory, at the sight took envy; and, aspiring to his height, stood re-embattled fierce; by force or fraud thinking to prosper, and at length prevail against God and Messiah, or at last to fall in universal ruin. Now they drew to final battle, disdaining flight or faint retreat. When the great Son of God to all his host on either hand thus spoke:

"Stand still in bright array, you Saints; here stand, you Angels armed; this day from battle rest. Faithful has been your warfare, and accepted of God, fearless in his righteous cause; and as you have received, so have you done, invincibly. But of this cursed crew the punishment belongs to other hand.

Vengeance is his, or whose he alone appoints. Number is not ordained for this day's work, nor multitude. Stand only, and behold God's indignation poured by me on these godless.
