Not you, but me, they have despised, yet envied; against me is all their rage, because the Father — to whom in Heaven supreme kingdom, and power, and glory appertain — has honoured me according to his will.

Therefore to me he has assigned their doom, that they may have their wish, to try with me in battle which proves the stronger — they all, or I alone against them — since by strength they measure all, not emulous of other excellence, nor caring who excels them.

Nor will I vouchsafe any other strife with them." So spoke the Son, and changed his countenance into terror too severe to be beheld, and full of wrath bent on his enemies. At once the Four spread out their starry wings with dreadful contiguous shade, and the orbs of his fierce chariot rolled, as with the sound of torrent floods, or of a numerous host.

He drove right onward upon his impious foes, gloomy as night. Under his burning wheels the steadfast empyrean shook throughout — all but the throne itself of God. Full soon he arrived among them; in his right hand grasping ten thousand thunders, which he sent before him, such as fixed plagues in their souls. They, astonished, lost all resistance, all courage; down their idle weapons dropped.

Over shields, and helms, and helmed heads he rode, of Thrones and mighty Seraphim prostrate, who wished the mountains might now again be thrown on them, as a shelter from his ire. Nor less on either side tempestuously fell his arrows — from the fourfold-visaged Four, distinct with eyes, and from the living wheels, distinct alike with multitude of eyes.

One Spirit ruled in them; and every eye glared lightning, and shot forth pernicious fire among the accursed, that withered all their strength, and left them drained of their wonted vigour, exhausted, spiritless, afflicted, fallen.

Yet half his strength he did not put forth, but checked his thunder in mid volley; for he meant not to destroy, but to root them out of Heaven. The overthrown he raised, and as a herd of goats or a timorous flock thronged together, drove them before him thunder-struck, pursued with terrors and with furies, to the bounds and crystal wall of Heaven; which, opening wide, rolled inward, and a spacious gap disclosed into the wasteful deep. The monstrous sight struck them with horror backward, but far worse urged them behind. Headlong they threw themselves down from the verge of Heaven; eternal wrath burnt after them to the bottomless pit.

Hell heard the unsufferable noise, Hell saw Heaven ruining from Heaven, and would have fled affrighted. But strict Fate had cast too deep her dark foundations, and had bound too fast. Nine days they fell. Confounded Chaos roared, and felt tenfold confusion in their fall through his wild anarchy; so huge a rout encumbered him with ruin. Hell at last, yawning, received them whole, and on them closed —

Hell, their fit habitation, fraught with unquenchable fire, the house of woe and pain. Disburdened Heaven rejoiced, and soon repaired her mural breach, returning whence it rolled. Sole victor, from the expulsion of his foes, Messiah turned his triumphal chariot.

All his Saints, who had stood silent as eye-witnesses of his almighty acts, advanced with jubilee to meet him; and, as they went, shaded with branching palm, each bright Order sang triumph, and sang him victorious King, Son, Heir, and Lord — to whom dominion was given, worthiest to reign. He, celebrated, rode triumphant through mid Heaven, into the courts and temple of his Mighty Father, throned on high — who received him into glory, where now he sits at the right hand of bliss.

Thus, measuring things in Heaven by things on Earth, at your request, and that you may beware by what is past, I have revealed to you what might otherwise have been hidden from human race: the discord which befell, and war in Heaven among the angelic Powers, and the deep fall of those who too highly aspired, who rebelled with Satan — he who now envies your state, who now is plotting how he may seduce you also from obedience, that with him, bereaved of happiness, you may partake his punishment, eternal misery —

which would be all his solace and revenge, as a despite done against the Most High, once to gain you as companion of his woe. But do not listen to his temptations; warn your weaker partner. Let it profit you to have heard, by terrible example, the reward of disobedience. Firm they might have stood, yet fell. Remember, and fear to transgress."

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: Descend from Heaven, Urania -- if that name rightly belongs to you, whose divine voice I have followed, soaring above the Olympian heights, above the flight of Pegasus's wing! It is the meaning I invoke, not just the name. For you do not dwell among the nine Muses on old Olympus, but are heavenly-born. Before the hills appeared or any fountain flowed, you conversed with eternal Wisdom, your sister, and played in the presence of the Almighty Father, delighting him with your celestial song. Led upward by you into the Heaven of Heavens, I have dared to enter as an earthly guest and breathe the air of heaven, tempered by you. Now guide me safely back down to my native element.

Otherwise, from this flying steed unreined, like Bellerophon who fell from a lesser height onto the Aleian field to wander lost and forlorn, I too may fall. Half my song remains unsung, though now within a narrower scope -- the visible sphere of daily life.

Standing on earth, not carried above the sky, I sing more safely with my mortal voice, unchanged to hoarse or mute, though fallen on evil days and evil tongues. In darkness, surrounded by dangers and loneliness -- yet not alone, while you visit my sleep nightly or when morning colors the east. Still guide my song, Urania, and find me a fit audience, though few.

But drive far away the savage clamor of Bacchus and his revelers -- the same wild mob that tore the Thracian poet Orpheus apart in Rhodope, where woods and rocks had ears to listen in rapture until the savage noise drowned both harp and voice, and even the Muse could not protect her son. Do not fail me who implore you.

For you are heavenly; the other Muses are empty dreams. Tell me, Goddess, what happened after Raphael, the friendly archangel, had warned Adam by the terrible example of the angels' fall to beware of rebellion. This was to prevent the same fate from befalling Adam or his race in Paradise, charged not to touch the forbidden tree on pain of transgression. That single command was so easy to obey amid the choice of every other pleasure, though temptation might wander near. Adam, with his companion Eve, had listened to the whole story with rapt attention. He was filled with admiration and deep thought at hearing of such high and strange things -- things so unimaginable as hatred in Heaven and war so near the peace of God in bliss, with such terrible confusion. But the evil, soon driven back, had recoiled like a flood upon those who started it, for evil cannot mix with blessedness. Adam soon put aside the doubts in his heart. Now led on, still sinless, with a desire to know more about what concerned him directly -- how this world of Heaven and Earth first began,

when and from what it was created, for what purpose, and what had happened in Eden or beyond before his own memory -- like one whose thirst, still barely quenched, eyes the flowing stream and feels new thirst stirred by its murmuring -- he proceeded to ask his heavenly guest.

"Great things, far different from this world, you have revealed, divine interpreter, wonderfully strange to our ears! Sent down by favor from the heavenly realm to warn us in time of what might otherwise have been our loss, unknown and beyond human knowledge to discover.

For this we owe immortal thanks to the infinitely Good, and we receive his warning with solemn purpose to observe his sovereign will unfailingly, the purpose of our existence. But since you have graciously condescended to share things beyond earthly understanding that nonetheless concerned our knowledge, as highest wisdom saw fit, please descend now to lower matters and tell us what may be equally useful to know. How did this Heaven that we see, adorned with innumerable moving lights, first begin? And how did this surrounding air that fills all space, embracing this flowering Earth? What cause moved the Creator, who had rested through all eternity in holy peace, to build so late in Chaos? And once the work began, how quickly was it finished? We ask not to pry into the secrets of his eternal empire but rather to magnify his works -- for the more we know, the more we can praise them.

The great light of day still has far to travel, though its path is steep. Held by your voice in suspense, the sun itself listens and will gladly delay to hear you tell of the origin of all things and the rising birth of Nature from the invisible Deep.

Or if the evening star and the moon hasten to be your audience, Night will bring silence with her, and Sleep will stay awake to listen. Or we can bid sleep stay away until your song ends and dismiss you before morning dawns."

So Adam earnestly asked his distinguished guest. The godlike angel answered mildly: "Your request, cautiously framed, shall be granted, though to recount the Almighty's works -- what words or tongue of any Seraph could be equal to that task, or what human heart could comprehend it?

Yet what you can grasp, which may best serve to glorify the Maker and bring you greater happiness, shall not be withheld from you. I have received such a commission from above to answer your desire for knowledge within proper bounds. Beyond those bounds, do not ask. Do not let your own inventions fill in what has not been revealed, which the invisible King, alone omniscient, has concealed in night.

These things are not to be shared, on Earth or in Heaven. But enough remains besides to search and discover. Knowledge is like food and needs temperance just as much as appetite -- the discipline to know in proportion what the mind can properly hold.

Otherwise it overwhelms, and wisdom quickly turns to folly, just as excess nourishment turns to gas. Know then that after Lucifer -- so named because he once shone brightest among the heavenly host, brighter than the morning star among the other stars -- fell with his flaming legions through the Deep into his assigned place, and the great Son returned victorious with his saints, the Omnipotent Eternal Father from his throne beheld their diminished numbers and spoke to his Son.

"At least our jealous enemy has failed. He thought all would rebel like himself, and with their help he trusted to seize this impregnable fortress, the seat of supreme Deity, and dispossess us. He drew many into his fraud, who know this place no more.

Yet by far the greater part have kept their station, I see. Heaven, still populous, retains numbers enough to fill its wide realms and to attend this high temple with proper worship, rites, and solemn ceremonies.

But lest he boast in his heart that the harm already done -- Heaven depopulated, which he foolishly thinks damages me -- cannot be repaired, I can repair that loss, if loss it is to lose those who lost themselves. In a moment I will create another world and, from one man, a race of innumerable humans to dwell there -- not here -- until by degrees of earned merit they open the way up to this place, tried through long obedience.

Then Earth shall be changed to Heaven and Heaven to Earth -- one kingdom of joy and union without end. Meanwhile, spread out, you Powers of Heaven, and enjoy this wider space. And you, my Word, my begotten Son -- through you I accomplish this. Speak, and let it be done!

I send my overshadowing Spirit and Might along with you. Ride forth and command the Deep to become, within appointed bounds, both Heaven and Earth. The Deep is boundless because I Am, and I fill Infinity, so no space is empty.

Though I, uncircumscribed, may choose to withdraw and not exert my goodness, which is free to act or not -- Necessity and Chance have no power over me. What I will is Fate." So spoke the Almighty. His Word, the Son in his divine nature, gave his words immediate effect.

God's acts are instantaneous, swifter than time or motion, but they cannot be told to human ears without the process of speech, told as earthly understanding can receive them. Great triumph and rejoicing filled Heaven when this was declared as the Almighty's will.

They sang glory to the Most High, and goodwill to future humanity, and peace in their future dwellings. Glory to him whose just avenging wrath had driven the ungodly from his sight and from the homes of the righteous. Glory and praise to him whose wisdom had ordained good out of evil -- creating, instead of malicious spirits, a better race to fill their vacant place and spread his goodness to worlds and ages without end.

So sang the heavenly hosts. Meanwhile, the Son appeared on his great expedition, girded with Omnipotence, crowned with the radiance of divine Majesty. Wisdom, love, and all his Father shone immensely in him.

Around his chariot poured numberless Cherubim, Seraphim, Potentates, Thrones, Virtues, and winged spirits, along with winged chariots from the armory of God. There myriads of them had stood ready since ancient times between two brazen mountains, harnessed for a solemn day. This celestial fleet came forth spontaneously, for Spirit lived within them. They attended their Lord. Heaven opened wide her everlasting gates, moving harmoniously on golden hinges, to let forth the King of Glory with his powerful Word and Spirit, going out to create new worlds.

They stood on heavenly ground. From the shore they gazed out at the vast, immeasurable abyss -- wild as a sea, dark, wasteful, churning. Furious winds heaved its waves mountain-high, as if to assault Heaven's heights and mix the center with the outermost pole.

"Silence, you troubled waves! And you, Deep, be at peace!" said the Almighty Word. "Let your discord end!" He did not pause but, uplifted on the wings of Cherubim in his Father's glory, rode far into Chaos and the world yet unborn.

For Chaos heard his voice. His entire train followed in bright procession to witness Creation and the wonders of his might. Then the blazing wheels stopped. He took in his hand the golden compasses, prepared in God's eternal storehouse, to mark the boundaries of this universe and all created things.

One foot he placed at the center, and the other he turned round through the vast dark depths, saying: "This far extend, this far your boundaries -- this be your proper circumference, O World!" So God created Heaven and Earth. Matter was unformed and void. Profound darkness covered the abyss. But the Spirit of God spread his brooding wings over the watery calm, infusing vital power and warmth throughout the fluid mass. He purged downward the black, cold, infernal dregs opposed to life. Then he founded and shaped like things with like. The rest he separated into their proper places, spinning out the air between them.

The Earth hung self-balanced on her center. "Let there be Light," said God. And Light, the first of all created things, pure quintessence, sprang from the deep. From the east it began its journey through the dim atmosphere, gathered in a radiant cloud, for the Sun did not yet exist. It dwelt for a time in a cloudy tabernacle. God saw that the light was good.

He divided light from darkness by the hemisphere -- Light he named Day, and Darkness he named Night. So the first day passed, evening and morning. Nor did it go uncelebrated or unsung by the heavenly choirs, who beheld the first light rising from darkness.

It was the birthday of Heaven and Earth. With joy and shouting they filled the hollow sphere of the universe. They struck their golden harps and praised God and his works in hymns, singing of the Creator both at the first evening and the first morning.

Again God said: "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters." And God made the firmament -- an expanse of pure, transparent, elemental air, diffused in a circuit to the outermost edge of this great round world. It was a firm and sure partition dividing the waters below from those above. For he built this world surrounded by calm waters, like a crystalline ocean, with the far-removed chaos kept at a distance, lest its fierce extremes disturb the whole structure.

He named the firmament Heaven. So evening and morning chorus sang the second day. The Earth had been formed but still lay immature in the womb of waters, not yet visible. Over the entire face of the Earth, the main ocean flowed -- not idle, but with warm, life-giving moisture softening the whole globe, preparing the great mother Earth to conceive. Then God said: "Let the waters under Heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear."

Immediately the mountains emerged, enormous, thrusting their broad bare backs up into the clouds, their tops reaching the sky. As high as the swelling hills rose, so low sank a hollow basin, broad and deep, ready to receive the waters. The waters rushed eagerly into it, rolling up like drops of rain converging on dry ground.

Part rose in crystal walls or direct ridges in their haste. Such urgency the great command impressed on the swift floods! Like armies rushing to their standard at the sound of a trumpet, the watery throng rolled wave after wave, finding their way -- if steep, with the force of a torrent; if through flat land, gently ebbing. Neither rock nor hill withstood them.

But they found their way, either underground or in wide, winding circuits, wearing deep channels in the soft, oozy ground. This was easy before God commanded the ground to be dry. The rivers now flow perpetually in these channels, drawing their humid streams.

The dry land he called Earth. The great collection of gathered waters he called Seas. He saw that it was good, and said: "Let the Earth bring forth green grass, herbs yielding seed, and fruit trees yielding fruit according to their kinds, with their seed within them upon the Earth."

He had barely spoken when the bare Earth, until then a desert, unsightly and unadorned, brought forth tender grass whose green carpet covered her entire surface. Then herbs of every leaf sprang up and suddenly flowered, opening their various colors and making her bosom fragrant and beautiful. These had barely bloomed when the clustering vine crept forth, the swelling gourd appeared, the corny reed stood up in the field like a battalion, and humble shrubs with their curly foliage spread out. Last of all, the stately trees rose as if in dance, spreading branches laden with abundant fruit or gemmed with blossoms. The hills were crowned with tall woods.

The valleys were tufted with greenery, and borders of trees lined every river. Earth now looked like Heaven -- a place where gods might dwell, or wander with delight, loving its sacred shades. Though God had not yet sent rain upon the Earth, and there was no man to till the ground, a dewy mist rose up and watered everything. Every plant of the field God had made before it grew on the green stem, and every herb before it sprouted. God saw that it was good.

So evening and morning marked the third day. Again the Almighty spoke: "Let there be lights high in the expanse of Heaven to divide day from night. Let them serve as signs for seasons, days, and circling years.

And let them be lights, as I ordain their duty in the firmament of Heaven, to give light on the Earth." And it was so. God made two great lights -- great for their usefulness to Man: the greater to rule the day, the lesser to rule the night in alternation. He also made the stars and set them in the heavens to illuminate the Earth and to rule in turn by day and night, and to divide light from darkness. God surveyed his great work and saw that it was good.

For among the celestial bodies, he first framed the Sun as a mighty sphere, at first without light, though made of ethereal substance. Then he formed the Moon as a globe, and every size of star, sowing the heavens thickly with stars, like seeds in a field.

He took by far the greater portion of light, transplanted it from its cloudy dwelling, and placed it in the Sun's orb, made porous to receive and drink in the liquid light and firm enough to hold the gathered beams. The Sun became a great palace of light.

To the Sun, as to a fountain, the other stars came to draw light in their golden vessels. From it the morning planet gilded her horns. By reflection or absorption they increased their own small light, though so far from human sight they appeared as mere points of diminished brightness. First the glorious lamp was seen in the east, regent of day, invested with bright rays and joyful to run its course through Heaven's high road. The gray dawn and the Pleiades danced before it, shedding sweet influence. Less bright, the Moon was set opposite in the leveled west, his mirror, borrowing her full-faced light from him. She needed no other light in that position and kept that distance until night. Then in the east she rose in her turn, and her reign with a thousand lesser lights was shared with a thousand thousand stars. Then Heaven was first adorned with these bright luminaries that set and rose. Glad evening and glad morning crowned the fourth day.

And God said: "Let the waters bring forth abundantly creatures with living souls. And let birds fly above the Earth on the open firmament of Heaven." God created the great whales and every living, creeping creature that the waters produced in abundance, each according to its kind.

And every winged bird according to its kind. He saw that it was good and blessed them, saying: "Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, lakes, and running streams. And let the birds multiply on the Earth."

At once the seas, bays, and inlets swarmed with innumerable fish that glided under the green waves with fins and shining scales, some in great schools that filled the mid-ocean. Some swam alone or in pairs, grazing on seaweed pastures through groves of coral, or darting with quick, playful movements to show the sun their golden-spotted coats.

Others attended at ease in their pearly shells to absorb moist nourishment, or watched for food under rocks in their jointed armor. On smooth surfaces seals played and curved dolphins sported. Some creatures, huge in bulk, wallowed ungainly and enormous through the ocean. There Leviathan, the largest of all living creatures, stretched out on the deep like a floating land, sleeping or swimming. At its gills it drew in the sea, and at its spout it sent it out again.

Meanwhile, from tepid caves, marshes, and shores, equally numerous broods hatched from eggs. They soon burst forth, and their young quickly grew feathers and wings. They spread their feathers and soared into the sky, looking down on the earth below like a cloud. There the eagle and the stork built their nests on cliffs and cedar tops.

Some flew loosely through the air. Others, more wisely, flew in formation, arranged in wedge shape, their aerial caravan flying high over seas and lands. With mutual support they eased each other's flight. So the wise crane navigated her yearly voyage on the winds. The air floated as they passed, fanned by countless feathers.

From branch to branch, smaller birds filled the woods with song and spread their painted wings until evening. Even then the solemn nightingale did not stop warbling but tuned her soft songs all night. Others bathed their downy breasts on silver lakes and rivers. The swan, with arched neck between her white wings, proudly rowed along with oar-like feet. Yet often they left the water and, rising on stiff wings, towered into the high aerial sky. Others walked firmly on the ground -- the crested rooster, whose trumpet call marks the silent hours, and the peacock whose splendid train adorns him with the vivid colors of rainbows and starry eyes. Thus the waters were filled with fish and the air with birds. Evening and morning marked the fifth day.

The sixth and last day of creation arose with evening harps and morning music. God said: "Let the Earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds -- cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth, each after its kind." The Earth obeyed. Straightaway, opening her fertile womb, she gave birth to innumerable perfect living creatures, fully formed and grown. Out of the ground they rose, as from their lairs -- wild beasts that dwell in forests, thickets, and dens.

Among the trees they rose in pairs and walked. Cattle appeared in fields and green meadows. Some were rare and solitary; others grazed in flocks or sprang up in broad herds. The grassy earth seemed to calve. Now half-appeared the tawny lion, pawing to free its hind parts, then springing loose as if breaking from bonds, shaking its tawny mane. The leopard, the panther, and the tiger rose like moles, throwing up mounds of earth. The swift stag pushed up its branching head from underground. Behemoth, the largest beast born of the earth, heaved up its enormous bulk. Fleeced flocks and bleating sheep rose like growing plants. Between sea and land appeared the hippopotamus and the scaly crocodile.

At once every creeping thing came forth from the ground -- insects and worms. Some waved their fan-like wings, tiny yet dressed in all the brilliant colors of summer, spotted with gold and purple, azure and green.

Others drew out their long bodies in sinuous tracks along the ground. Not all were small creatures of nature. Some of the serpent kind were enormous in length and thickness, with coiling folds and even wings. First crept the industrious ant, tiny yet great-hearted, a model of frugality and forethought.

Perhaps a pattern of just equality for the future, organized in its communal colonies. Next appeared the female bee, who feeds her husband drone with delicious food and builds her waxen cells stored with honey. The rest of the creatures are too numerous to count, and you already know their natures and have named them. Nor unknown to you was the serpent, subtlest beast of all the field -- sometimes huge, with brazen eyes and a terrifying hairy mane, though to you it was not harmful but came obediently at your call.

Now Heaven in all her glory shone, rolling in the motions the great First Mover's hand had set in course. Earth in her rich garments looked perfect and lovely. Air, water, and earth were filled with bird, fish, and beast flying, swimming, and walking. Yet the sixth day was not finished.

There was still missing the masterpiece, the crowning purpose of everything created so far -- a creature who, unlike the others, would not go on all fours like brutes but would be endowed with sacred reason, able to stand upright and govern the rest, knowing himself. From that self-knowledge he would be noble enough to correspond with Heaven, yet grateful enough to acknowledge the source of all his blessings, directing his heart, voice, and eyes upward in devotion to worship God Supreme, who made him chief of all creation. Therefore the Omnipotent Eternal Father -- for where is he not present? -- spoke audibly to his Son.

"Let us make Man now in our image, in our likeness, and let them rule over the fish and birds of sea and air, over the beasts of the field, over all the Earth, and over every creeping thing that crawls on the ground."

Having said this, he formed you, Adam -- you, O Man -- from the dust of the ground. Into your nostrils he breathed the breath of life. In his own image he created you, in the image of God, an exact expression. And you became a living soul.

Male he created you. But your companion, female, for reproduction. Then he blessed humanity and said: "Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the Earth. Subdue it, and hold dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and every living thing that moves on the Earth."

Wherever this happened -- for no place yet had a distinct name -- from there, as you know, he brought you into this delightful grove, this garden planted with God's own trees, beautiful to behold and delicious to taste.

He freely gave you all their pleasant fruit for food. Every variety is here that the whole Earth yields, an endless selection. But of the tree whose fruit gives knowledge of good and evil, you must not eat. On the day you eat of it, you shall die.

Death is the penalty imposed. Be careful, and govern your appetite well, lest Sin surprise you and her dark companion Death follow. Here he finished, and everything he had made he viewed and declared entirely good.

So evening and morning completed the sixth day. Yet not until the Creator, finished with his work though never wearied, returned upward to the Heaven of Heavens, his high dwelling place. From there he would behold this newly created world -- the addition to his empire -- and see how it appeared from his throne, how good and fair, answering his great design. He rode upward, followed by the acclaim and harmonious sound of ten thousand harps that tuned angelic harmonies. The earth and air resounded. You remember, for you heard it. The heavens and all the constellations rang. The planets in their stations stood still, listening, while the bright procession ascended in jubilation.

"Open, you everlasting gates!" they sang. "Open, you Heavens! Throw wide your living doors and let in the great Creator, returned from his work -- magnificent, his six days' work, a World! Open, and henceforth open often, for God will delight in frequently visiting the dwellings of just people, sending his winged messengers on errands of grace." So sang the glorious ascending train. He rode through Heaven, which opened wide its blazing portals, leading directly to God's eternal house.

A broad and ample road, whose dust is gold and whose pavement is stars -- as the stars appear to you in the Milky Way, that band you see nightly powdered with stars, circling the sky. And now on Earth the seventh evening rose in Eden, for the Sun had set and twilight was coming from the east before night. At the holy mount of Heaven's highest point, the imperial throne of the Godhead, fixed forever firm and sure, the Son arrived and sat down with his great Father. For the Father too had gone -- invisible yet present, such is the privilege of Omnipresence -- and had ordained the work as both Author and End of all things. Now resting from his work, he blessed and made holy the seventh day, resting on that day from all he had done. But not in silence was it kept holy. The harp played without rest. The solemn pipe and dulcimer, all instruments of sweet stops, all sounds produced by string or golden wire, made soft tunings intermixed with choral or solo voice. Clouds of incense from golden censers hid the mount.

They sang of Creation and the six days' works: "Great are your works, Jehovah! Your power is infinite! What thought can measure you, or tongue describe you! You are greater now in your return than when you defeated the giant angels. That day your thunder was magnified. But to create is greater than to destroy what has been created.

Who can harm you, mighty King, or limit your empire? You easily repelled the foolish attempt of the rebel spirits and their worthless plans. They thought to diminish you and reduce the number of your worshipers. But whoever seeks to diminish you only serves to reveal your might more clearly. You use their evil to create even more good.

Witness this newly made world -- another Heaven, not far from Heaven's gate, founded in view on the clear glassy sea. It is almost immeasurably vast, filled with countless stars, each star perhaps a world destined for habitation. But you know their appointed times. Among these, the seat of Man -- Earth, surrounded by her ocean -- is their pleasant dwelling place. Three times happy are humanity and their children, whom God has advanced so far!

Created in his image, to dwell there and worship him, and in reward to rule over his works on earth, in sea, and in air, and to multiply a race of worshipers, holy and just. Three times happy, if they know their happiness and persevere in righteousness!"

So they sang, and Heaven's highest sphere rang with hallelujahs. Thus was the Sabbath observed. And now consider your request fulfilled -- you asked how this world and the face of things first began, and what happened before your memory, from the beginning. This knowledge, passed from you to your descendants, will inform all future generations. If you seek anything else, not exceeding human understanding, ask."

chapters.title: Book VIII
paragraphs: The angel finished speaking, and his voice left such a charm in Adam's ear that for a while Adam thought he was still speaking. He stood fixed, listening. Then, as if newly woken, he gratefully replied: "What sufficient thanks or equal repayment can I offer you, divine historian? You have generously satisfied my thirst for knowledge and condescended to tell me things I could never have discovered on my own. I have heard them with wonder and delight, and I attribute proper glory to the high Creator, as is due. Yet some doubt remains that only you can resolve.

When I look at this magnificent frame of Heaven and Earth and calculate their sizes -- this Earth being just a speck, a grain, an atom compared to the vast firmament with its countless stars that seem to revolve through incomprehensible spaces (their distance and swift daily return prove as much) -- all of it apparently just to shed light on this tiny dark globe, one day and one night, seemingly useless for anything else -- I often wonder how wise and frugal Nature could commit such disproportion. Why create so many nobler bodies, so much greater and more numerous, just for this one purpose? Why impose such restless revolution on their orbits, repeated day by day, while this Earth sits still, served by nobler bodies than herself? Without the slightest motion of her own, she receives as tribute the immense journey of bodiless speed bringing warmth and light.

Such swiftness that no number can describe!" So spoke our forefather. By his expression, he seemed to be entering into deep, abstract thought. Eve, noticing this from where she sat retired but still in sight, rose with majestic grace -- grace that won every onlooker's wish for her to stay -- and went out among her fruits and flowers to visit her nursery and see how they were growing. They sprang up at her approach and grew more gladly at her fair care.

Yet she did not leave because she was uninterested in such conversation or unable to understand it. She preferred to hear Adam explain these high matters to her privately, knowing he would add grateful digressions and solve complex questions with affectionate asides. Not just his words but his manner pleased her. When do such loving couples exist today?

With goddess-like grace she went, not unattended. A retinue of winning Graces waited on her as on a queen, and from her radiance shot darts of desire into every eye, making everyone wish she would stay in sight.

Raphael now answered Adam's question with kind and ready goodwill: "I do not blame you for asking or searching. Heaven is like the book of God set before you, in which to read his wondrous works and learn his seasons, hours, days, months, or years.

Whether Heaven moves or Earth does not matter, if you calculate correctly. The rest the great Architect has wisely concealed from both Man and Angel, not revealing his secrets to be scrutinized by those who ought rather to admire. Or if they wish to try their guesses, he has left the structure of the heavens to their debates -- perhaps to amuse himself with laughter at their quaint, wide-of-the-mark theories. When they try to model Heaven and calculate the stars, they will struggle with how to manage the mighty frame -- how to build and unbuild and contrive to save the appearances, scribbling the sphere over with centers and eccentric circles, cycle upon cycle, orbit within orbit.

Already by your reasoning I can guess that you, who are to lead your offspring, suppose that bright and greater bodies should not serve the lesser and dimmer, nor should Heaven make such journeys while Earth sits still, receiving the benefit. But consider first that great or bright does not necessarily mean excellent. The Earth, though small and not glittering compared to Heaven, may contain more solid good than the Sun, which shines but is barren.

The Sun's power has no effect on itself but only on the fruitful Earth. There its beams, otherwise inactive, find their purpose. Yet the bright celestial bodies exist not just for the Earth but for you, Earth's inhabitant.

As for Heaven's vast circuit, let it speak of the Maker's magnificent generosity, who built so spacious and stretched his design so far that Man may know he does not dwell in his own property. He is lodged in a small portion, and the rest is reserved for uses known best to the Lord.

The swiftness of those celestial circles, though numberless, attribute to God's omnipotence, who could add almost spiritual speed to physical bodies. Remember, I have traveled from Heaven since this morning's hour and arrived in Eden before noon -- an inexpressible distance by any known number. But I mention this only to address the question of motion in the heavens, which was what moved you to doubt -- not because I necessarily affirm it.

God, to keep his ways beyond human comprehension, placed Heaven so far from Earth that earthly sight, if it presumes to judge, might err about things too remote. What if the Sun is the center of the world, and the other stars, drawn by its attractive power and their own, dance around it in various orbits?

Their wandering courses -- now high, now low, now visible, now hidden, moving forward, backward, or standing still -- you see six of them doing this. What if the seventh, planet Earth, though seeming so steady, actually makes three different motions invisibly?

Otherwise you would have to attribute those motions to several different spheres moving in contradictory, oblique directions. Or save the Sun its labor by assuming a swift invisible sphere beyond all stars carries day and night around -- which you need not believe if the industrious Earth, turning eastward, can fetch day by itself, while its far side meets night from the Sun's beam. What if the light Earth sends through the clear air serves the Moon as a star, lighting her by day just as she lights Earth by night? What if there is land on the Moon, with fields and inhabitants? You see her spots -- they might be clouds, and clouds might bring rain that grows crops in her softened soil. There may be other suns, with their own attendant moons, sharing male and female light.

These two great principles animate the world, and each sphere may perhaps contain living beings. For such vast space in Nature, unoccupied by living souls, desert and desolate, existing only to shine, hardly contributing even a glimpse of light conveyed so far down to this habitable world (which returns light back to them) -- this seems an obvious problem to debate.

But whether things are this way or not -- whether the Sun, dominant in the heavens, rises over the Earth, or Earth rises to face the Sun; whether the Sun begins his fiery road from the east, or Earth from the west advances her silent course, spinning so smoothly on her soft axis that she seems to sleep while carrying you along on the smooth air --

do not trouble yourself with hidden matters. Leave them to God above. Serve and fear him! As for other creatures, wherever God places them, let him arrange things as he sees best. Rejoice in what he gives you -- this Paradise and your fair Eve. Heaven is too high for you to know what happens there. Be wise about humble things.

Think only about what concerns you and your existence. Do not dream of other worlds, what creatures live there, in what state or condition. Be content that this much has been revealed to you, not only about Earth but about highest Heaven."

Adam, cleared of his doubt, replied: "How fully you have satisfied me, pure Intelligence of Heaven, serene angel! Freed from complications, you have taught me to live the easiest way -- not to disturb the sweetness of life with perplexing thoughts. God has told anxious worries to dwell far from us. Let us not seek them out with wandering notions and empty speculations.

But the mind and imagination tend to roam unchecked, without end, until warned or taught by experience to learn that knowing a great deal about remote, obscure, and subtle things is not the highest wisdom. Rather, to know what lies before us in daily life -- that is the primary wisdom. Anything beyond that is mere smoke, emptiness, or foolish irrelevance.

It leaves us unpracticed, unprepared, and constantly searching in the matters that truly concern us. Therefore, let us descend from this lofty subject to a lower, more practical one. Perhaps in speaking of things at hand, some topic may arise that is not inappropriate to ask about, with your kind permission.

I have heard you tell what happened before my memory begins. Now hear me tell my story, which perhaps you have not heard. The day is far from spent, and you can see how cleverly I devise reasons to keep you here longer.

I am inviting you to listen while I talk -- foolish, except for the hope of your reply. For while I sit with you, I feel as though I am in Heaven. Your conversation is sweeter to my ears than the most delicious palm fruit is to thirst and hunger after labor at the hour of noon. Such fruits satisfy and soon become enough, pleasant as they are. But your words, filled with divine grace, bring a sweetness that never cloys."

Raphael answered with heavenly gentleness: "Nor are your lips graceless, Father of men, nor your tongue lacking eloquence. God has poured his gifts abundantly on you, both inward and outward, his fair image.

Whether speaking or silent, grace and comeliness attend you. Every word and motion of yours is fitting. We in Heaven think no less of you on Earth than we do of a fellow-servant, and we gladly inquire into God's ways with Man.
For God, we see, has honored you and set his equal love on Man. So please continue, for I was absent that day, as it happened, bound on a distant journey toward the gates of Hell.

We were formed into a full legion -- such was our command -- to watch and make sure no spy or enemy emerged while God was engaged in his work of creation, in case he, angered by such a bold incursion, might have mixed destruction with creation.

Not that the rebels would dare attempt anything without God's permission. But God sends us on such errands as sovereign King, for the sake of proper order and to accustom us to ready obedience. We found Hell's dismal gates shut fast and strongly barricaded.

But long before we arrived, we heard from within a noise quite different from the sound of dance or song -- torment, loud lamentation, and furious rage. We were glad to return to the borders of light before the Sabbath evening. So we had been ordered.

But now your turn to speak. I am listening, as pleased with your words as you are with mine." So spoke the godlike Power, and our forefather began: "For a man to tell how his life began is a strange thing, for who knows his own beginning? A desire to converse with you still longer has led me to try. I found myself, as if newly woken from the deepest sleep, lying softly on a flowery bed in a fragrant sweat, which the Sun's beams soon dried, feeding on the rising moisture.

At once I turned my wondering eyes toward Heaven and gazed for a while at the wide sky. Then, moved by quick instinct, I sprang upward and stood on my feet. Around me I saw hills, valleys, shady woods, sunny plains, and the liquid murmur of flowing streams. I saw creatures that lived and moved, walking or flying.

Birds sang on the branches. Everything smiled. My heart overflowed with fragrance and joy. I examined myself, limb by limb, and sometimes walked, sometimes ran, with supple joints as lively energy directed.

But who I was, where I was, from what cause, I did not know. I tried to speak, and at once my tongue obeyed. I could readily name whatever I saw. 'You, Sun,' I said, 'fair light, and you, bright Earth, so fresh and beautiful, you hills and valleys, rivers, woods, and plains, and you living, moving creatures -- tell me, if you saw, how I came here. How did I get here? Not by myself -- then by some great Maker, preeminent in goodness and power.'

'Tell me how I may know him, how I may worship him, from whom I have the gift of motion and life, and who makes me feel I am happier than I realize.' While I called out this way, wandering I knew not where from the place where I first drew breath and first beheld this happy light, I sat down on a green, shady bank covered with flowers. There gentle sleep first found me. With a soft pressure, it seized my drowsy senses. I felt no disturbance, though I thought I was passing back to my former state of nothingness, about to dissolve.

When suddenly a dream stood at my head. Its inner vision gently stirred my imagination to believe I still existed and lived. One came to me, divine in form, who said: 'Your home awaits you, Adam. Rise, first Man, first Father of men innumerable! Called by you, I come as your guide to the garden of bliss, your prepared dwelling.' So saying, he took me by the hand and raised me. Over fields and waters, gliding smoothly as though through air without taking steps, he led me up a wooded mountain. Its high flat top was broad, enclosed and planted with the finest trees, with walks and bowers. What I saw of the Earth before seemed hardly pleasant in comparison. Every tree was laden with the fairest fruit that tempted the eye. A sudden appetite stirred in me to pluck and eat. At this I woke and found that everything before my eyes was real, as the dream had vividly foreshadowed. Here my wandering would have started again, had not the one who was my guide appeared from among the trees -- a Divine Presence. Rejoicing but with awe, I fell at his feet in worship. He raised me and said mildly: 'Whom you sought, I am. I am the Author of all you see above, around, and beneath you.'

'I give you this Paradise. Count it yours to cultivate and keep. Eat freely and gladly of the fruit of every tree in the garden. Fear no scarcity. But of the tree whose fruit brings knowledge of good and evil, which I have placed as the pledge of your obedience and faith in the middle of the garden beside the Tree of Life -- remember my warning and refuse to taste it. Know the bitter consequence: the day you eat of it, breaking my sole command, you shall inevitably die. From that day you shall be mortal. You shall lose this happy state and be expelled into a world of sorrow and suffering.' He pronounced this stern prohibition, which still echoes dreadfully in my ear, though it is my choice not to incur it. But soon his expression cleared and his gracious purpose renewed.

'Not only these fair boundaries but all the Earth I give to you and to your race as lords. Possess it, and rule over all things that live in it -- beast, fish, and bird. In sign of this, behold every bird and beast approaching you two by two according to its kind, to receive from you their names and pay you homage.' As he spoke, every bird and beast appeared, approaching in pairs. These four-footed ones came with gentle submission. Each bird stooped on its wing.

I named them as they passed and understood their natures. God endowed me with instant knowledge and comprehension. But among them I did not find what I felt I still lacked. I dared to speak to the heavenly Vision.

"O you who surpass all these and all humanity far beyond my ability to name -- how may I worship you, Author of this universe and of all this good given to Man? For whose well-being you have so abundantly and generously provided everything! But I see no one here who shares it with me. What happiness can I enjoy alone? Or, enjoying everything alone, what contentment can I find?"

I spoke boldly, perhaps presumptuously. The bright Vision, seeming to smile more brightly, replied: "What do you call solitude? Is not the Earth filled with various living creatures, and the air full of them, all at your command? Do you not know their language and their ways? They too know and reason in their own fashion. Find your pastime and exercise your rule among them. Your realm is large."

So spoke the Universal Lord, and seemed to settle the matter. But I, with permission to speak and humble respect, replied: "Let my words not offend you, Heavenly Power, my Maker. Be gracious while I speak.

Have you not made me your representative here, with these creatures set far beneath me? What real companionship can exist among such unequals? What harmony or true delight? These must be mutual, given and received in proper proportion. Where one partner is intense and the other still unresponsive, no real fellowship is possible. Both would soon become tedious. The fellowship I speak of must be able to share all the delights of reason. Brute animals cannot be human companions. They rejoice each with their own kind -- lion with lioness.

So fitly you have paired them. Even less can a bird consort with a beast, or a fish with a bird, or an ox with an ape. Worse still can man converse with beast, and least of all among all these." To this the Almighty answered, not displeased.
"You seek a fine and subtle happiness, Adam, particular in your choice of companions. I see you will take no pleasure, even amid pleasure, if you are solitary. What do you think of me and my state?

Do I seem to you sufficiently happy, or not? I am alone from all eternity. I know no one who is my second, my equal, or anything close to my equal. With whom, then, can I hold conversation except with the creatures I made, who are infinitely below me in descent -- far more beneath me than other creatures are beneath you?"

I humbly answered: "To grasp the height and depth of your eternal ways exceeds all human thought, Supreme of things! You are perfect in yourself. In you no deficiency can be found. Not so with Man, who is imperfect by nature. The cause of his desire to help or comfort his deficiencies through conversation with his like is his very incompleteness. You have no need to reproduce, being already infinite,

and though one, complete through all attributes. But Man by his very number must show his single imperfection and beget his like, his image multiplied. In his unity he is defective, requiring the mutual love and dearest friendship that only an equal partner can provide.

You, though alone in your secret being, are best accompanied by yourself and do not seek social communication. Yet being pleased, you can raise your creature to any height of union or communion you wish, even to the point of making them divine.

I, by conversing with these animals, cannot raise them from their lowly state, nor find satisfaction in their ways." So I spoke boldly, using the freedom permitted me, and found acceptance. The gracious Divine Voice replied.

"I was pleased to test you this far, Adam, and I find you knowing -- not only of beasts, which you have rightly named, but of yourself, expressing well the free spirit within you, my image, not shared with brute creatures.

Your good reason for disliking their fellowship, I approve. Be always so minded. Before you even spoke, I knew it was not good for Man to be alone. The company you saw was not intended for you. I brought them only as a test to see how well you could judge what was fit and proper.

What I bring next shall please you, be assured -- your likeness, your fit companion, your other self, exactly matching your heart's desire." He finished, or I heard no more. For now my earthly senses, long strained to the breaking point by this sublime heavenly conversation, gave way. Overwhelmed by what exceeded mortal capacity, dazzled and exhausted, I sank down. Sleep fell on me instantly, called by Nature to my aid, and closed my eyes.

He closed my eyes but left open my inner sight, the faculty of imagination. In a trance-like state, though sleeping, I seemed to see where I lay. I saw the glorious form still standing before me, the same one before whom I had stood awake.

He stooped, opened my left side, and took from it a rib, along with warm, vital blood. Wide was the wound, but it was immediately filled with flesh and healed. From that rib, with his hands he shaped and fashioned a creature.

Under his forming hands, a being grew -- manlike but of different sex, so lovely and fair that everything that had seemed beautiful in all the world now appeared common or was summed up and contained in her and her looks. From that moment, her presence infused a sweetness into my heart I had never felt before, and into all things from her radiance breathed a spirit of love and desire.

She vanished, and I was left in darkness. I woke desperate to find her, or else to mourn her loss forever and give up all other pleasures. When beyond hope I saw her, not far away -- just as I had seen her in my dream, adorned with everything Earth or Heaven could bestow to make her lovely. She came toward me, led by her heavenly Maker, though he was unseen, and guided by his voice. She had been taught the sanctity and rites of marriage.

Grace was in every step. Heaven was in her eyes. Dignity and love were in every gesture. Overjoyed, I could not help crying aloud: 'This makes amends! You have fulfilled your words, bounteous and generous Creator, Giver of all fair things! But fairest of all your gifts is this! I see now bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh, myself standing before me. Woman is her name, taken from Man. For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife,

and they shall be one flesh, one heart, one soul.' She heard me, and though divinely brought, her innocence and virgin modesty -- her virtue and the consciousness of her worth, wanting to be courted and not won without pursuit, not forward or pushy but modest -- or to say it all, Nature herself, though pure of any sinful thought, worked in her so that when she saw me, she turned away.

I followed. She knew what honor required and with graceful dignity accepted my plea. To our wedding bower I led her, blushing like the dawn. All Heaven and its happy constellations shed their finest influence on that hour. The Earth gave signs of celebration, and every hill rejoiced.

The birds sang joyfully. Fresh breezes whispered through the woods, and from their wings flung roses and fragrances from the spice bush, sporting playfully. At last the nightingale sang the bridal song, and the evening star was bid to hasten to light the wedding lamp.

So I have told you my entire story, brought to the summit of earthly happiness that I enjoy. I must confess, in all other things I find delight, but the kind that, used or not, causes no change in the mind and no strong desire. I mean the pleasures of taste, sight, smell, herbs, fruits, flowers, walks, and birdsong. But here the case is utterly different. I am transported when I behold her, transported by her touch. Here I first felt passion, a strange stirring! In all other pleasures I remain superior and unmoved, but here alone I am weak against the power of Beauty's gaze.

Either Nature failed in me and left some part not strong enough to withstand such an effect, or in taking from my side she perhaps took more than enough -- at least she bestowed too much outward beauty on Eve, elaborate in exterior show but less precise in inward faculties.

For I well understand that by nature's plan she is my inferior in mind and inward abilities, which are the highest things. Outwardly too she resembles less than I the image of the one who made us both, and less expresses the character of the dominion given to us over other creatures. Yet when I approach her loveliness, she seems so perfectly complete in herself, so aware of her own worth, that whatever she chooses to do or say seems wisest, most virtuous, most discreet, and best.

All higher knowledge falls degraded in her presence. Wisdom loses confidence when debating with her and resembles Folly. Authority and Reason wait on her as if she, not I, were the primary creation. And to crown it all, an air of greatness and nobility makes its home in her most lovable qualities, creating around her something like an angelic guard of awe."

The angel replied with a contracted brow: "Do not blame Nature. She has done her part. Do yours. Do not doubt Wisdom -- she will not desert you if you do not dismiss her when you need her most, by giving too much value to things less excellent, as you yourself perceive.

For what is it that transports you so? An exterior? Fair, no doubt, worthy of your cherishing, honoring, and loving -- but not your subjection. Weigh yourself against her, then judge your worth. Self-esteem, grounded in what is just and right and well-managed, often profits more than anything else. The more you master that skill, the more she will acknowledge you as her head and yield all her appearances to your realities.

She was made attractive precisely for your delight -- so beautiful that with honor you may love your wife, who sees you least wise only when you see yourself that way. But if the physical sense of touch, by which humanity is propagated, seems so supremely delightful beyond all else -- consider that the same is given to cattle and every beast. It would not have been given commonly to all if anything in that pleasure were so extraordinary as to subdue the soul of Man or stir deep passion in him.

Whatever higher qualities you find in her company -- the attractive, human, rational ones -- love those. You do well to love, but not in passion. True love does not consist of passion. Love refines thoughts, enlarges the heart. Its proper seat is in reason, and it is judicious. Love is the ladder by which you may ascend to heavenly love. Do not sink into mere physical pleasure, which is why no mate was found for you among the beasts."

Adam replied, half embarrassed: "It is not her outward beauty alone, nor what is common to all kinds in reproduction -- though I hold the marriage bed in higher, even reverent, esteem -- that delights me so much. What delights me most are those graceful acts, those thousand daily courtesies that flow from all her words and actions, mixed with love and sweet compliance. These show a genuine union of minds -- or in us both, one soul.

The harmony I see in a married pair is more pleasing than harmonious music to the ear. Yet these things do not enslave me. I share with you what I feel inwardly, not because I am defeated by it. When I encounter various impressions from the senses, I remain free. I approve the best and follow what I approve.

You do not blame me for loving. Love, you say, leads up to Heaven and is both the way and the guide. Then bear with me if what I ask is lawful: Do not the heavenly spirits also love? And how do they express their love? By looks only? Or do they blend their radiance in a direct or virtual touch?"

The angel answered with a smile that glowed celestial rosy red, love's proper color: "Let it be enough that you know we are happy, and that without love there is no happiness. Whatever pure enjoyment you find in the body -- and pure you were created -- we enjoy in a higher degree. We find no barrier of membrane, joint, or limb to block us.

More easily than air mingles with air, spirits embrace. Total, they merge -- pure joining with pure in a union of desire, needing no physical channel as flesh must mix with flesh or soul with soul. But I can say no more now. The setting sun, beyond Earth's green cape and the Hesperian isles, is my signal to depart.

Be strong, live happy, and love! But first of all, love and obey him whose love is to obey and whose great command you must keep. Take care that passion does not sway your judgment into doing what your free will would not otherwise allow. The welfare or misery of you and all your descendants is placed in your hands. Be warned!

I shall rejoice in your perseverance, and so shall all the blessed. Stand firm! To stand or fall is free, within your own power to decide. You are perfect within and need no outside help. Resist every temptation to transgress."

So saying, he rose. Adam followed with a blessing: "Since we must part, go, heavenly guest, ethereal Messenger, sent by the sovereign goodness I worship! You have been gentle and kind in your condescension, and I shall honor you forever with grateful memory. Be good and friendly still to humanity, and return often!" So they parted. The angel flew up to Heaven from the thick shade, and Adam returned to his bower.

chapters.title: Book IX
paragraphs: No more of those friendly talks where God or angel guest sat with Man as a companion, sharing a country meal and allowing harmless conversation. I must now change my notes to tragic ones -- foul distrust and disloyal breach on Man's part: revolt and disobedience. On Heaven's part: alienation, distance, displeasure, anger, just rebuke, and the pronouncement of judgment. This brought into our world a universe of sorrow -- Sin and her shadow Death, and Misery, Death's herald. A sad task! Yet my subject is no less heroic than the wrath of fierce Achilles pursuing his enemy three times around Troy's walls, or the fury of Turnus over losing Lavinia,

or Neptune's grudge, or Juno's, that so long troubled the Greeks and Aeneas, Aphrodite's son. If my celestial patroness can provide me with a style equal to the subject -- she who deigns to visit me nightly, uninvited, and dictates to me while I sleep, or inspires my unpremeditated verse with ease --

since this subject for heroic song has pleased me through long deliberation and a late start -- I have no natural inclination to write about wars, which until now were the only topic considered truly heroic: the tedious butchery of imaginary knights in fictional battles. The better heroism of patience and martyrdom has gone unsung. Nor do I care to describe races, tournaments, embossed shields, elaborate horse trappings, gorgeous knights at jousts, or feasts served in great halls by stewards and seneschals.

Those are the skills of ceremony or minor office, not what truly gives heroic stature to a person or a poem. I, unskilled in such things and unstudied, have a higher subject remaining -- one sufficient in itself to earn that heroic name, unless it comes too late in an age too cold, or the climate or my years dampen the wings of inspiration. Much depends on whether the gift is truly mine, or hers who brings it nightly to my ear.

The sun had set, and after it the star of Hesperus, whose role is to bring twilight upon the earth -- that brief arbiter between day and night. Now from end to end, night's hemisphere had veiled the horizon round.

Satan, who had recently fled before Gabriel's threats out of Eden, now returned with his skill in deceit and malice sharpened, bent on humanity's destruction despite whatever heavier punishment might fall on himself. Fearlessly he came back. He had fled by night and returned at midnight, having circled the earth. He was cautious about daylight since Uriel, regent of the sun, had spotted his entrance and warned the Cherubim on guard. Driven away and full of anguish, he rode with darkness for seven continuous nights. Three times he circled the equator. Four times he crossed from pole to pole, traversing each great circle.

On the eighth night he returned. On the side opposite the entrance and the Cherubim's watch, he found an undetected way in by stealth. There was a place -- it no longer exists, for sin, not time, brought the change -- where the river Tigris, at the foot of Paradise, plunged underground into a gulf and part of it rose up again as a fountain near the Tree of Life.

Satan sank with the river and rose with it, wrapped in rising mist. Then he looked for a place to hide. He had searched the sea and land from Eden across the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, and beyond the river Ob to the far north.

Southward as far as the Antarctic. And in length, west from the Orontes River to the ocean at the Isthmus of Darien, then to the land where the Ganges and Indus flow. He had roamed the whole globe with careful investigation, and after deep consideration of every creature, decided which of all of them would best serve his deception. He chose the Serpent, the most cunning beast of all the field.

After long internal debate, turning over his conflicting thoughts, he made his final decision. The Serpent was the perfect vessel, the fittest agent of fraud, in whom to enter and hide his dark temptations from the sharpest observers. Whatever sly behaviors the snake displayed would seem natural, proceeding from its well-known native craftiness. In any other beast, such observed cleverness might raise suspicions of demonic possession beyond ordinary animal capacity.

So he resolved. But first, from inward grief, his bursting passion poured forth in these complaints: "More justly than Heaven, you, O Earth, deserve to be the seat of gods, built as though with improved design, reforming what was old! How like Heaven you are -- if not better! Why would God build something worse after something better?

Earthly Heaven, circled by other heavens that shine, bearing their bright, dutiful lamps -- light above light -- for you alone, it seems, concentrating all their precious beams of sacred influence. As God is the center of Heaven yet extends to all, so you, Earth, centered here, receive from all those spheres. Not in themselves but in you does all their known power appear -- productive in herb, plant, and the nobler births of creatures with graduated levels of life: growth, sense, reason, all summed up in Man.

With what delight I could have explored you, if I could feel joy in anything -- sweet variety of hill and valley, rivers, woods, and plains, now land, now sea, with shores crowned by forest, rocks, dens, and caves! But I find no place of rest or refuge in any of these. The more I see of pleasures around me, the more torment I feel within, besieged by the hateful opposition of contrary feelings. All good becomes poison to me. In Heaven, my state would be even worse.

But I seek to dwell neither here nor in Heaven -- not unless I can master Heaven's Supreme Ruler. I have no hope of becoming less miserable through what I seek, but I can make others as miserable as I am. Though it will rebound worse on me,

I find ease only in destroying. If I can ruin this one being -- Mankind, created for God's special favor -- or win him to whatever may cause his total ruin, then everything else that was made for him will quickly follow, linked as it is to his fortune for better or worse.

Into misery, then! The sole glory among the infernal powers shall be mine -- to have marred in one day what the so-called Almighty spent six nights and days creating, and who knows how long planning before that. Though perhaps not longer than it took me, in a single night, to free from servitude nearly half the angelic host and leave the ranks of his worshipers noticeably thinned. To be avenged and repair his reduced numbers -- whether because his former creative power has now weakened, or to spite us further -- he determined to elevate into our former places a creature formed from earth, endowed from such a base origin with the heavenly gifts that were our spoils. What he decreed, he accomplished. He made Man and built this magnificent world as his dwelling, pronounced him lord. And oh, the indignity!

He assigned angel wings and flaming ministers to watch and serve this earthly charge. It is the vigilance of these guardians I dread. To evade them, I glide wrapped in midnight mist, prowling through every bush and thicket where I might find the Serpent sleeping, in whose winding coils I can hide myself and my dark purpose.

O foul descent! That I, who once contended with gods to sit on the highest throne, am now forced into a beast -- mixed with bestial slime, this essence that aspired to the height of Deity now incarnated and made brutish!

But what will ambition and revenge not stoop to? Whoever aspires must descend as low as he once soared high, exposed sooner or later to the basest things. Revenge, at first sweet, soon turns bitter and recoils on itself.

Let it. I do not care, as long as it strikes the right target. Since I cannot reach the one above me, let it fall on the one who next provokes my envy -- this new favorite of Heaven, this creature of clay, this son of scorn, whom his Maker raised from dust, to spite us further. Spite is best repaid with spite."

So saying, through every thicket, damp or dry, creeping low like a black mist, he continued his midnight search for the Serpent. He soon found it sleeping, coiled in a labyrinth of many rings, its head in the center, well-stored with subtle cleverness.

It was not yet in any horrible den or dismal shade, nor was it harmful yet. On the grassy ground, fearless and unfeared, it slept. Satan entered through its mouth, possessing its brute senses, heart, and head. He inspired it with intelligent purpose, but did not disturb its sleep, waiting hidden for the approach of morning.

Now, when sacred dawn began to rise in Eden over the moist, incense-breathing flowers, and all things that breathe sent up silent praise from Earth's great altar to the Creator, filling his presence with grateful fragrance, the human pair came forth and joined their voices to the choir of creatures that lacked speech. Having done this, they shared the best hour for sweetest scents and air.

Then they discussed how to organize their day's work best, for their garden grew faster than two pairs of hands could manage. Eve spoke first: "Adam, we may labor as we will to tend this garden -- our pleasant appointed task -- but until more hands come to help us, the work outgrows our efforts. What we trim, prune, prop, or bind by day, one or two nights of wild growth undoes, defying our care and going back to wilderness. Let me suggest something.

Let us divide our work. You go where your choice leads or where need is greatest -- whether to train the woodbine around this arbor or direct the ivy where to climb. Meanwhile I will go to that bed of roses mixed with myrtle to find what needs attention until noon.

For while we work so near each other all day, no wonder if looks and smiles interrupt us, or if some casual conversation draws our attention away. Our work comes to little, though we started early, and the supper hour arrives unearned."

Adam gently answered: "Sole Eve, my companion beyond compare, above all living creatures dear! You have proposed well, and your thoughts show proper concern for how we might best fulfill the work God has assigned us. I shall not leave you unpraised for this, for nothing is lovelier in a woman than to care about domestic good and to promote good works in her husband.

Yet God has not imposed labor so strictly that he forbids us refreshment when we need it -- whether food or conversation between tasks, the food of the mind, or this sweet exchange of looks and smiles. Smiles flow from reason, which brutes lack, and they are love's nourishment.

Love is not the lowest purpose of human life. For God made us not for tedious toil but for delight, and delight joined with reason. These paths and bowers, I am confident our combined efforts will easily keep from wilderness, at least as wide as we need to walk, until younger hands before long come to help us. But if my company has grown tiresome and you could use a short absence --

sometimes solitude is the best society, and brief separation makes the return sweeter. But I have another concern: that harm may befall you if we separate. You know what we have been warned about -- the malicious enemy who envies our happiness, and who, despairing of his own, seeks to bring us grief and shame through sly attack. He is somewhere nearby, no doubt, watching with greedy hope for his best chance to catch us apart.
Our separation would make his task hopeless, for together we could quickly aid each other. Whether his plan is to turn us from God or to destroy our married love, which perhaps arouses his envy most,

or something worse -- do not leave the faithful side that gave you life and still protects you. A wife, where danger or dishonor lurks, is safest and most fitting by her husband's side, who guards her or endures the worst alongside her."

Eve, with the virgin dignity of one who loves but feels some injury, replied with sweet, firm composure: "Offspring of Heaven and Earth, Lord of all the Earth! That we have such an enemy who seeks our ruin, I learned from you and from the parting angel, whose words I overheard while I stood behind in a shady corner as the evening flowers were closing.

But that you should therefore doubt my firmness toward God or toward you, because we have an enemy who may tempt it -- this I did not expect to hear. You do not fear his violence, since we are spirits and cannot suffer death or pain from such attacks, nor can we fail to resist them.

Then it is his fraud you fear. This plainly implies that you equally fear my firm faith and love can be shaken or seduced by his deceit. How could such thoughts find a home in your heart, Adam -- such mistrust of her so dear to you?"

Adam replied with soothing words: "Daughter of God and Man, immortal Eve -- for such you are, sinless and blameless -- I am not distrusting you when I discourage your absence from my sight. I only wish to prevent the attempt itself from being made by our enemy.

For he who tempts, even unsuccessfully, dishonors the one tempted by implying they are thought corruptible. You yourself would resent such an insult with scorn and anger, even if the temptation failed. So do not misjudge me if I try to keep such an affront from you alone, which our enemy, though bold, would hardly dare attempt against us both together.

Or if he dared, the first assault would fall on me. Do not underestimate his malice and false cunning. He must be subtle indeed to have seduced angels. And do not think my help unnecessary. I draw strength from the influence of your presence. In your sight I become more wise, more watchful, more strong. Shame of being overcome while you watch would raise my utmost effort and unite all my powers."

"Why should you not feel the same when I am present, and choose your trial with me -- the best witness of your tested virtue?" So spoke Adam in his domestic care and married love. But Eve, who felt he attributed too little to her sincere faith, renewed her reply sweetly.

"If this is our condition -- to live in such a narrow space, hemmed in by a foe who may be subtle or violent, and we are not equipped to defend ourselves alone, wherever we meet him -- then how are we happy, living always in fear of harm?

But harm cannot come before sin. If our enemy merely tempts us, it only insults his own estimate of our integrity. That insult reflects no dishonor on us but turns foul on him. Why then should we avoid or fear it, when by proving his suspicion false we would gain double honor, inward peace, and the favor of Heaven as our witness?

And what is faith, love, or virtue if never tested -- if it can only exist when supported by someone else? Let us not think our Maker left our happy state so imperfect and insecure that it cannot withstand a challenge, whether we face it alone or together.

Fragile indeed would our happiness be if that were so. And Eden would be no Eden if so easily exposed." To this Adam replied fervently: "O Woman, all things are best as God's will ordained them. His creating hand left nothing imperfect or deficient in all his works -- much less in Man, or in anything that might secure his happy state. He is secure from outward force. The danger lies within himself, yet it lies within his own power to control.

No harm can come to him against his will. But God left the will free. For what obeys Reason is free, and Reason he made right. But he warned Reason to be always alert, lest it be surprised by some fair-appearing good and make a wrong judgment, misinforming the will to do what God has expressly forbidden.

It is not mistrust but tender love that urges me to remind you often, and you should remind me too. We stand firm yet are capable of swerving, since Reason might conceivably meet some plausible illusion devised by our enemy, and fall into deception without the strictest vigilance, as we have been warned.

Do not seek temptation. It is better to avoid it, and most likely to succeed if you stay with me. Trial will come without your seeking it. Would you prove your constancy? First prove your obedience. Who can verify the other quality without seeing you actually tested?

But if you think trial unsought may find us both more alert than my warning seems to suggest, then go. Your staying here against your will distances you from me more than going. Go in your native innocence. Rely on what virtue you have. Summon all of it!

For God has done his part toward you. Now do yours." So spoke the father of humanity. But Eve, though submissive, persisted with her final reply: "With your permission then, and forewarned especially by your own concluding words -- that our trial, when least expected, may find us far less prepared -- I go all the more willingly. And I do not much expect a foe so proud will first seek out the weaker target.

If he does, his failure will shame him all the more." So saying, she withdrew her hand softly from her husband's. Like a light woodland nymph -- an Oread or Dryad, or one of Diana's attendants -- she made for the groves. But Diana herself she surpassed in grace and goddess-like bearing, though not armed like Diana with bow and quiver, but with simple gardening tools that primitive art, not yet knowing fire, had formed, or that angels had brought.

She most resembled Pales or Pomona -- Pomona when she fled from Vertumnus, or Ceres in her prime, still a maiden untouched by the sorrow of Proserpine's loss. Adam's eyes followed her with ardent longing, delighted but wishing she would stay.
Again and again he urged her to return quickly. She as often promised to be back by noon at the bower, with everything prepared for their midday meal or afternoon rest.

O much-deceived, much-disappointed, hapless Eve! Your presumed return will prove tragically wrong. From that hour you never again found sweet rest or safe repose in Paradise. Such an ambush, hidden among sweet flowers and shades, waited with hellish venom to intercept your path, or send you back stripped of your innocence, your faith, and your happiness!

For now, since the first break of dawn, the Fiend, in the outward form of a mere serpent, had come forth. He was on his hunt for the only two human beings, but in them the entire future race -- his intended prey.

In bower and field he searched, wherever any garden plot or grove lay more pleasantly arranged, where the pair might be tending their plants or enjoying their favorite places. He searched by fountain and shady stream for both of them, but wished he might find Eve alone. He wished, but without hope of what so rarely happened. Then, to his wish and beyond his hope, he spied Eve alone -- veiled in a cloud of fragrance where she stood, half-hidden as the roses bloomed thickly around her, their blush matching her own glow.
