Or if you seek death as the ultimate escape from misery, thinking to dodge the penalty God pronounced -- do not doubt that God has armed his vengeance more wisely than that. I fear that death snatched prematurely will not exempt us from the pain we are doomed to suffer. Such defiant acts will only provoke the Highest to make death live within us. Let us seek some safer resolution instead. I think I see one, calling to mind part of our sentence -- that your offspring shall bruise the Serpent's head. What welcome amends! Unless I am wrong, this means our great enemy Satan, who used the Serpent to devise this deception against us. To crush his head would be real revenge indeed -- revenge that would be lost if we brought death upon ourselves or chose childless days. Our enemy would escape his ordained punishment, and we would double our own misery.

So let there be no more talk of violence against ourselves, or of willful childlessness. Both cut us off from hope and taste only of bitterness, impatience, and resentment -- rebellion against God and his just requirement laid upon us. Remember how mild and gracious he was when he heard and judged us. Without anger or scolding! We expected immediate annihilation, which we thought death meant that day. But look -- your pains were limited to childbearing, soon compensated by the joy of motherhood. And on me the curse fell slantwise, landing on the ground. I must earn my bread by labor. What harm in that? Idleness would have been worse.

My labor will sustain me. And to protect us from cold and heat, his caring hand has already provided for us, unsought. While pronouncing judgment, he pitied us and clothed us. How much more, if we pray to him, will his ear be open and his heart inclined to pity, teaching us how to avoid the harsh seasons -- rain, ice, hail, and snow?

The sky already shows us various weather on this mountain, while the winds blow moist and sharp, stripping the graceful leaves from these fair trees. This tells us to seek better shelter, some warmth to comfort our numbed limbs before the daylight star departs and cold night comes. We might learn to gather and focus the sun's rays with dry material,
or by rubbing two objects together, grind the air to fire -- as recently the clouds, colliding and pushed by winds, struck slanting lightning that kindles the resinous bark of fir or pine

and sends comfortable warmth from a distance, which might replace the sun. Fire and whatever else may remedy or cure the evils our own misdeeds have brought -- God will teach us if we pray and seek his grace. We need not fear that we cannot live this life in reasonable comfort, sustained by him with many blessings, until we return to dust, our final rest and native home.

What better can we do than go back to the place where he judged us, and fall on our faces before him in reverence? There let us humbly confess our sins and beg pardon, with tears watering the ground and sighs filling the air. Let these come continually from contrite hearts as signs of genuine sorrow and humble submission.

Without doubt he will relent and turn from his anger. In his expression, even when he seemed most angry and severe, what shone there but favor, grace, and mercy?" So spoke our penitent father. Eve felt no less remorse. They went immediately to the place where he had judged them and fell on their faces in reverence before him. They both confessed their sins humbly and begged for pardon, with tears watering the ground and sighs filling the air, sent continually from their contrite hearts as signs of genuine sorrow and humble submission.

chapters.title: Book XI
paragraphs: So they stood in their humblest state, praying. Prevenient grace, descending from the mercy seat above, had already removed the stony hardness from their hearts and grown new, tender flesh in its place. Now they breathed sighs too deep for words, inspired and winged for Heaven by the Spirit of prayer, flying faster than the loudest eloquence. Yet their bearing was not that of insignificant petitioners. Their plea seemed no less important than when that ancient pair of legend -- Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha, less ancient than Adam and Eve though called ancient -- stood devoutly before the shrine of Themis to restore the human race drowned by the flood. Their prayers flew up to Heaven without missing the way, not blown astray by malicious winds. They passed dimensionless through Heaven's doors, then were clothed with incense where the golden altar burned. Presented by their great Intercessor, they came before the Father's throne. The glad Son began to intercede.

"See, Father, what first fruits have sprung on Earth from the grace you planted in Man. These sighs and prayers, mixed with incense in this golden censer, I bring before you as your priest. They are fruits of a more pleasing flavor, sown by your hand with contrition in his heart, than anything all the trees of Paradise could have produced before the Fall, when he still tended them with his own hand in innocence. Now bend your ear to his prayer. Hear his sighs, though they have no words.

He does not know how to pray with proper words. Let me interpret for him. I am his advocate and propitiation. All his works, good and bad, graft onto me. My merit shall perfect the good ones, and my death shall pay for the bad.

Accept me, and in me receive from humanity the fragrance of peace. Let him live before you, reconciled. Let his remaining days, numbered though sorrowful, continue until death -- his doom, which I plead to soften, not to reverse -- yields him to a better life. There, with me, all my redeemed shall dwell in joy and bliss,

made one with me, as I am one with you." The Father, serene and cloudless, replied: "All your requests for Man, accepted Son, are granted. All your requests were already my decree. But he can no longer dwell in that Paradise. The law I gave to Nature forbids it.

Those pure, immortal elements that know no gross or discordant mixture reject him now that he is tainted. They purge him out as a disease, casting him into air as gross as himself, and to mortal food. This will best prepare him for the dissolution that sin first caused, distempered and corrupted all things, changing the incorrupt to corrupt. At first I endowed him with two fair gifts: happiness and immortality. The first he foolishly lost. The second, without the first, would only have made his misery eternal,

until I provided death as his final remedy. After a life of sharp trial, refined by faith and faithful works, he shall awaken to a second life in the renewal of the just, and be delivered up with Heaven and Earth renewed.

But let us call all the blessed to assembly throughout Heaven's wide realm. I will not hide my judgments from them -- how I proceed with humanity, just as they recently saw how I dealt with the sinful angels. Though the faithful stand firm, seeing this will make them stand firmer still."

He ended, and the Son gave the signal to the bright minister keeping watch. He blew his trumpet -- the same heard at Oreb when God descended, and perhaps to sound once more at the general judgment. The angelic blast filled every region. From their blessed bowers of ever-green shade, by springs and fountains, by the waters of life, wherever they sat in fellowship and joy, the sons of light hurried to answer the high summons.

They took their seats. Then from his supreme throne, the Almighty pronounced his sovereign will: "O Sons, Man has become like one of us, knowing both good and evil, since he tasted that forbidden fruit. But let him boast about his knowledge -- of good lost and evil gained!

He would be happier had it been enough for him to know good by itself, and evil not at all. He now grieves, repents, and prays with a contrite heart -- these are my promptings within him. But I know his heart, how fickle and vain it is when left to itself. Therefore, lest his now bolder hand also reach the Tree of Life, eat from it, and live forever -- or at least dream of living forever -- I decree to remove him. I will send him from the garden to till the ground from which he was taken, a more fitting soil.
Michael, take this charge. Choose from among the Cherubim your pick of flaming warriors, in case the Fiend, either on Man's behalf or to invade the vacant territory, causes new trouble.

Hurry, and drive out the sinful pair from the Paradise of God without hesitation. From hallowed ground expel the unholy. Announce to them and their descendants perpetual banishment from this place. Yet, lest they faint at the harsh sentence delivered too severely -- for I see them softened, weeping over their excess -- hide all terror from them.

If they patiently obey your command, do not dismiss them in despair. Reveal to Adam what shall come in future days, as I shall enlighten you. Weave into your account my covenant, renewed in the Woman's Seed.

So send them forth, sorrowful yet at peace. On the east side of the garden, where the ascent from Eden is easiest, station the Cherubim on guard, with a flaming sword waving wide. Keep all approaches far off, and guard every passage to the Tree of Life,

lest Paradise become a haven for foul spirits who would make all my trees their prey, using stolen fruit to deceive Man once again." He finished. The archangelic Power prepared for swift descent, along with a bright company of watchful Cherubim. Each had four faces, like a double Janus. Their entire forms were covered with eyes, more numerous than those of Argus and more wakeful than he, who was lulled to sleep by Hermes's charmed pipe and enchanted rod. Meanwhile, Leucothea woke to greet the world with sacred light, and fresh dews anointed the earth. Adam and first mother Eve had finished their prayers and found new strength from above -- new hope springing from despair, joy mixed with lingering fear.

Adam spoke these welcome words to Eve: "Eve, I readily believe that all the good we enjoy comes down from Heaven. But that anything from us could ascend to Heaven -- so powerful as to touch the mind of God or change his will -- that is hard to believe. Yet prayer, even one short sigh of human breath, can rise to the very seat of God. For since I sought through prayer to appease the offended Deity,

kneeling and humbling my whole heart before him, I thought I saw him approachable and mild, bending his ear. A growing conviction that I was heard with favor filled me. Peace returned to my heart, and to my memory came his promise that your offspring shall bruise our enemy.

That promise, which I had overlooked in my dismay, now assures me that the bitterness of death is past and we shall live. So hail to you, Eve, rightly named Mother of all living, since through you Man is to live, and all things live for Man."

Eve replied with sad, humble demeanor: "I am unworthy of such a title -- I, the transgressor, who was ordained as your help but became your snare. Reproach, distrust, and all blame belong more rightly to me.

But my Judge was infinite in pardon. I, who first brought death upon all, am graced to be called the source of life. Next after God, you are most generous, who honor me with such a title when I deserve far different. But the field calls us to our labor, now imposed with the sweat of our brows, though we have had a sleepless night. See, the morning has begun her rosy progress, smiling and unconcerned with our unrest. Let us go forth.

I will never again stray from your side, wherever our daily work leads, though it is now toilsome until day's end. While we dwell here, what can be burdensome in these pleasant surroundings? Let us live here, though in a fallen state, content."

So spoke much-humbled Eve. But Fate did not agree. Nature first gave signs, impressed on bird, beast, and sky. The sky suddenly darkened after the brief blush of dawn. In Eve's sight, the eagle, Jove's bird, swooped from its high flight and drove two brightly colored birds before it.

Down from a hill came the beast that rules the forest -- the first hunter -- pursuing a gentle pair of deer, the most graceful in all the woods. Their flight was aimed directly at the eastern gate. Adam watched and, following the chase with his eyes, not unmoved, spoke to Eve.

"O Eve, some further change awaits us. Heaven shows it through these silent signs in Nature -- forerunners of his purpose. Either to warn us, perhaps too confident, of our release from penalty because death has been delayed for some days -- how long we shall live and what until then, who knows? Or perhaps this tells us nothing more than what we already know: that we are dust, and to dust we must return, and be no more.

Why else this double display of flight pursued both in the air and on the ground at the same hour, both heading the same direction? Why does darkness come before midday in the east, while a more radiant morning light appears in the western cloud, drawing a white radiance across the blue sky and slowly descending with something heavenly?"
He was right. For by now the heavenly bands had descended from a sky of jasper and landed in Paradise on a hill. It was a glorious sight, though doubt and mortal fear that day dimmed Adam's eyes.

Not more glorious was the vision when angels met Jacob at Mahanaim, where he saw a field pavilioned with his bright guardian hosts. Nor was it more glorious than the scene at Dothan, where a camp of fire appeared against the Syrian king who had sent an army to capture one man -- undeclared war. The princely Hierarch left his forces in bright array on the hill to take possession of the garden. He went alone to find where Adam was sheltered. Adam saw him and spoke to Eve as the great visitor approached.

"Eve, expect great news now. It may soon decide our fate or impose new laws on us. I can see, from that blazing cloud veiling the hill, one of the heavenly host. By his walk, he is no ordinary one -- some great Potentate or one of the highest Thrones. Such majesty invests his coming! Yet he is not so terrifying that I should be afraid, nor so familiarly friendly as Raphael, in whom I would place great trust.

He is solemn and grand. To avoid offending him, I must meet him with reverence, and you should withdraw." He finished, and the archangel soon drew near. He came not in his celestial form but dressed as a man to meet a man. Over his gleaming armor flowed a military robe of purple, more vivid than the finest dyes of Meliboea or Tyre, worn by kings and heroes of old in times of truce. Iris herself had dipped the fabric.

His starry helmet, unbuckled, showed him in the prime of manhood where youth had just ended. At his side hung the sword -- Satan's great terror -- in a glistening zodiac-like belt. In his hand he held a spear. Adam bowed low. The angel, kingly, did not stoop from his stately bearing but made his announcement.

"Adam, Heaven's high command needs no introduction. Your prayers have been heard, and that is sufficient. Death, which was due by sentence when you sinned, has been delayed for many days granted to you in grace. In those days you may repent, and by many good deeds cover over one bad act. Then your Lord, appeased, may well redeem you entirely from Death's greedy claim.

But to remain in this Paradise any longer is not permitted. I have come to remove you and to send you from the garden to till the ground from which you were taken -- a more fitting soil." He said no more. Adam, struck by the news, stood with a chilling grip of sorrow that bound all his senses. Eve, who had been listening unseen, revealed her hiding place with an audible cry of grief.

"O unexpected blow, worse than death! Must I leave you, Paradise? Must I leave you, native soil, these happy walks and shades, fit home for gods? Here I had hoped to spend, quiet though sad, the remaining days that must end in death for us both. O flowers that will never grow in any other climate -- my early morning visits, my evening farewells -- I raised you with tender care from the first opening bud and gave you names. Who will now tend you, who will train you toward the sun, who will arrange your beds and water you from the sweet fountain?

And you, bridal bower, which I adorned with everything sweet to sight and smell! How shall I part from you? Where shall I wander down into a lower, unfamiliar world -- obscure and wild? How shall we breathe in different, less pure air, accustomed as we are to immortal fruits?"

The angel gently interrupted: "Do not grieve, Eve, but patiently accept the just loss of what was not truly yours. Do not set your heart too fondly on what does not belong to you. Your departure is not lonely: your husband goes with you, and you are bound to follow him.

Where he lives, consider that your native soil." Adam, recovering from the cold shock and collecting his scattered thoughts, humbly addressed Michael: "Celestial one, whether you are counted among the Thrones or named highest among them, for your form suggests a Prince above princes -- you have gently delivered your message, which might otherwise have wounded us in the telling and destroyed us in the execution. Whatever further sorrow and dejection our frailty can endure, your news brings it: departure from this happy place, our sweet retreat, the only comfort left to us, familiar to our eyes. Every other place seems inhospitable and desolate,

unknown to us and unknowing of us. If I could hope to change God's will by constant prayer, I would never stop wearing him down with my pleas. But prayer against his absolute decree avails no more than breath blown against the wind, stifled and blown back on the one who breathes it.

Therefore I submit to his great command. What grieves me most about leaving here is that I shall be hidden from his face, deprived of his blessed presence. Here I could worship in places marked by his visits. I could tell my children: 'On this mountain he appeared; under this tree he stood; among these pines I heard his voice; here at this fountain I spoke with him.'
How many grateful altars I would raise of grassy earth, piling up every gleaming stone from the stream as memorials for all ages. On them I would offer fragrant gums, fruits, and flowers.

In that lower world, where shall I look for his bright appearances or trace his footsteps? Though I fled from him in anger, now recalled to prolonged life and the promised offspring, I would gladly gaze upon even the farthest edges of his glory, and from a distance worship his steps."

Michael replied with kind regard: "Adam, you know that Heaven belongs to God, and all the Earth. Not only this rock but everywhere. His Omnipresence fills land, sea, and air, sustaining every living thing with his power and warming it with his warmth.

He gave you all the Earth to possess and rule -- no small gift. Do not suppose, then, that his presence is confined to the narrow bounds of Paradise or Eden. This might have been your capital, from which all generations would have spread, coming from all ends of the Earth to celebrate and honor you, their great ancestor.

But that privilege you have lost, brought down to live on the same level as your descendants. Yet do not doubt that in valley, plain, or anywhere else, God is present just as he is here, and will be found equally present. Many signs of his presence will still follow you, still surrounding you with goodness and fatherly love -- his face expressed in all things, the track of his steps visible in every divine act.

So that you may believe this and be strengthened before you leave, know that I am sent to show you what shall come in future days for you and your descendants. Expect to hear both good and bad -- heavenly grace contending with human sinfulness. From this you will learn true patience and how to balance joy with fear and devout sorrow. Trained equally to bear either state, prosperous or adverse, you will live your life most safely and be best prepared to endure your mortal passage when it comes. Climb this hill. Let Eve, whose eyes I have made drowsy, sleep below while you wake to visions of the future.

Just as you once slept while she was being formed." Adam gratefully replied: "I follow you, safe Guide, up whatever path you lead. I submit to the hand of Heaven, however it may discipline me. I will turn my exposed chest toward every trial, arming myself to overcome through suffering, and to win rest from the labor -- if I may so achieve it." So both climbed the hill together, in the visions of God. It was a hill, the highest in all Paradise. From its top, the hemisphere of Earth stretched out before them in the clearest view, reaching to the widest extent of sight.

No higher was that hill, nor wider the view around it, where the Tempter, for a different purpose, placed our second Adam in the wilderness to show him all the kingdoms of the Earth and their glory. From there the eye could command every famous city, ancient or modern, seat of the mightiest empires -- from the walls of Cambalu, seat of the Great Khan, and Samarkand by the Oxus, Tamerlane's throne, to Peking of the Chinese emperors. Thence to Agra and Lahore of the great Mughal, down to the golden Malay peninsula. Or where the Persian sat in Ecbatana or later in Isfahan. Or the Russian Czar in Moscow. Or the Sultan in Constantinople, Turkestan-born. Nor could his eye miss the empire of the Ethiopian Negus, from its furthest port of Arkiko, to the lesser maritime kingdoms of Mombasa, Kilwa, and Malindi, and Sofala -- thought to be the biblical Ophir -- to the realms of Congo and Angola at the southern tip.

Or from the Niger to the Atlas Mountains, the kingdoms of Fez, Susa, Morocco, Algiers, and Tlemcen. Then Europe, where Rome was destined to rule the world. Perhaps in spirit he also saw rich Mexico, seat of Montezuma, and Cusco in Peru, the richer seat of Atahualpa, and yet-unspoiled Guiana, whose great city was called El Dorado. But to prepare Adam for nobler visions, Michael removed from his eyes the film bred by the false fruit that had promised clearer sight. He purged his visual nerve with the herbs euphrasy and rue, for there was much to see.

From the well of life, three drops he instilled. So deep did these ingredients penetrate, reaching even to the innermost seat of mental vision, that Adam, now forced to close his eyes, sank down. All his faculties fell into a trance.

But the gentle angel quickly raised him by the hand and recalled his attention: "Adam, now open your eyes. First see the effects that your original crime has caused in some who spring from you -- who never touched the forbidden tree themselves, nor conspired with the Serpent,

nor committed your sin. Yet from that sin they inherit corruption, producing even more violent deeds." He opened his eyes and saw a field. Part was arable farmland, where sheaves of grain had just been reaped. The other part was sheep pasture with folds.

In the middle stood a rustic altar as a landmark, built of grassy turf. A sweaty reaper brought his first fruits from his tilled field -- green ears and yellow sheaves, unchoosen, just as they came to hand. Then a shepherd came, more humble, with the firstlings of his flock, the finest and best. Sacrificing, he laid the entrails and their fat on the cleft wood, with incense sprinkled over them. He performed all the proper rites.

His offering was quickly consumed by a favorable fire from Heaven, with a bright flash and grateful steam. The other's offering was not, for his was not sincere. At this, he raged inwardly. As they talked together, he struck his brother in the midsection with a stone that knocked the life out of him. The brother fell, and deadly pale, groaned out his soul as blood gushed forth.

Adam was deeply troubled at heart by this sight, and in distress cried hastily to the angel: "O Teacher! Some great catastrophe has happened to that gentle man who sacrificed properly! Is this how piety and pure devotion are repaid?"

Michael, also moved, replied: "These two are brothers, Adam. They are to come from your body. The unjust has killed the just out of envy that his brother's offering was accepted by Heaven. But the bloody deed will be avenged, and the other's faith, though approved, will not lose its reward, even though you see him die here, rolling in dust and blood." Our forefather said:

"Alas! Both for the deed and for its cause! But have I now seen Death? Is this how I must return to native dust? O terrifying sight, foul and ugly to look at, horrible to think about, and how much more horrible to experience!"

Michael answered: "You have seen Death in his first form on Man. But Death has many shapes, and many paths lead to his grim cave -- all of them dreadful. They are more terrible at the entrance than inside.

Some, as you saw, shall die by violence. Others by fire, flood, or famine. But far more by intemperance in eating and drinking, which shall bring upon the Earth a host of terrible diseases. A monstrous parade of sickness shall appear before you, so that you may know what misery Eve's lack of self-control shall bring upon humanity." Immediately a scene appeared before his eyes -- a sad, foul, dark place.

It seemed a hospital, packed with every kind of diseased person -- all the agonies of ghostly spasms, racking torture, heart-sick pain, fierce seizures, convulsions, epilepsy, violent coughs, kidney stones, ulcers, colic, demonic frenzy, moping melancholy, moon-struck madness, wasting atrophy, consumption, and widespread plague, dropsy, asthma, and joint-racking rheumatism.

Terrible was the suffering, deep the groans. Despair was the busiest attendant, moving from bed to bed among the sick. Over them all, triumphant Death shook his dart but delayed the final stroke, though often begged for as their chief relief and only hope.

Such a deformed sight -- what heart of stone could watch it dry-eyed for long? Adam could not but wept, though he was not born of woman. Compassion overwhelmed his manliness and gave him up to tears for a time, until firmer thoughts restrained the excess.

Barely recovering his voice, he renewed his grief: "O miserable humanity! To what a wretched state are we degraded! What a terrible fate reserved for us! Better to have remained unborn. Why is life given only to be so cruelly torn from us? Rather, why is it forced on us? If we knew what we were receiving, we would either refuse the offer of life or soon beg to lay it down,

glad to be dismissed in peace. Can the image of God in Man, once created so noble and upright, though flawed since, be reduced to such hideous sufferings under inhuman pains? Why should Man, still retaining some of the divine likeness, not be free from such deformities, and exempt for the sake of his Maker's image?"

Michael replied: "Their Maker's image abandoned them when they degraded themselves by serving ungoverned appetite. They took on the image of what they worshiped -- a bestial vice, leading primarily to the same kind of sin as Eve's.

Therefore their punishment is fitting. It does not disfigure God's likeness but their own -- or if his likeness, only as they themselves have defaced it. They pervert Nature's healthful rules into loathsome sickness, and deservedly so, since they did not honor God's image within themselves."

"I accept it as just," said Adam, "and I submit. But is there no other way to reach death besides these painful passages -- some way we might come to death and return to our native dust?" "There is," said Michael, "if you carefully follow the rule of moderation: temperance in what you eat and drink, seeking nourishment rather than gluttonous pleasure. After many years have passed,

you may live until, like ripe fruit, you drop gently into your mother's lap, gathered easily and not roughly plucked -- mature for death. This is old age. But then you must outlive your youth, your strength, and your beauty, which will fade to withered, weak, and gray. Your senses will grow dull. All taste for pleasure will be lost. Instead of the hopeful, cheerful energy of youth, a melancholy chill will reign in your blood, weighing your spirits down and finally consuming the vital essence." Our ancestor replied:

"From now on I neither flee death nor seek to prolong life much. I am more concerned with how to leave it most fairly and easily -- this burdensome load I must carry until my appointed day of surrendering it. I will patiently await my dissolution." Michael answered:

"Neither love your life nor hate it. But whatever life you live, live it well. How long or how short, leave to Heaven. Now prepare yourself for another sight." He looked, and saw a spacious plain with tents of various colors. By some tents, herds of cattle grazed. From others came the sound of harp and organ, played by musicians whose nimble touch ran through all the scales -- fugues fleeing and pursuing each other across the full range of notes.

In another area stood a man at a forge, laboring over two massive lumps of iron and brass he had melted -- found perhaps where accidental fire had burned through woods on mountain or in valley, the molten ore running into a cave's mouth or washed out of underground streams. He drained the liquid metal into molds and formed first his own tools, then whatever else could be wrought or engraved in metal. Beyond these, on the other side, a different kind of people descended from the high neighboring hills to the plain. By their appearance they seemed just men, devoted to worshiping God rightly and understanding his works, and to preserving freedom and peace among people. They had not been long on the plain when from the tents appeared

a group of beautiful women, richly and alluringly dressed, adorned with jewels. To the harp they sang soft love songs and danced forward. The men, though serious, let their eyes rove without restraint. They were quickly caught in love's net, and each chose the one he liked best.

Now they spoke of love, and soon the evening star appeared. Then, all inflamed with passion, they lit the wedding torches and invoked Hymen -- the first time marriage rites were formally celebrated. With feasting and music, all the tents resounded.

Such a happy scene of love and youth -- not lost in dissolution -- with its songs, garlands, flowers, and charming music, captured Adam's heart. He was naturally inclined to admit delight, and expressed himself this way:

"True opener of my eyes, blessed first angel! This vision seems much better and more hopeful of peaceful days than the two before. Those were full of death and pain, or worse. Here Nature seems fulfilled in all her purposes."

Michael answered: "Do not judge what is best by pleasure, though it may seem natural. You were created for a nobler end: holiness, purity, and conformity with the divine. Those pleasant tents you saw belong to the race of the one who killed his brother. Though they seem skilled in arts that polish life -- rare inventors --

they are unmindful of their Maker, though his Spirit taught them, and they acknowledge none of his gifts. Yet they shall produce a beautiful offspring. For that lovely group of women who seemed like goddesses -- so cheerful, smooth, and gay, yet empty of all the goodness that constitutes woman's true domestic honor and praise,

bred and trained only for lustful appetite, for singing, dancing, dressing up, fluttering their eyes and tongues -- to these that sober race of men whose devout lives earned them the title Sons of God shall surrender all their virtue, all their reputation. They will give up everything ignobly to the wiles and smiles of those fair atheists. They swim in joy now, but before long they shall swim in tears -- and the world with them, weeping for a world of sorrow."

Adam, bereft of his brief joy, said: "What pity and shame that those who started so well should turn aside to tread crooked paths or faint halfway! But I still see the same pattern of Man's sorrow: it always begins from Woman."

"It begins from Man's own weak yielding to her," said the angel. "He should better maintain his place by wisdom and the superior gifts he has received. But now prepare for another scene." He looked and saw wide territory spread before him -- towns and rural settlements between them.

Cities with tall gates and towers appeared. Armed crowds gathered with fierce, warlike faces, threatening war. Giants of mighty bone and bold enterprise -- some wielding weapons, some curbing foaming horses -- stood in single combat or in battle formation, both cavalry and infantry, not merely parading.

One band raided a herd of fine cattle from a rich meadow, or drove off fleecy flocks of sheep and bleating lambs across the plain. The shepherds barely escaped with their lives and called for help, which led to a bloody fight.

Armies clashed in cruel tournament. Where cattle had recently grazed, the blood-soaked field now lay scattered with corpses and weapons, deserted. Others laid siege to a strong city, assaulting it with siege engines, scaling ladders, and mines. Defenders on the walls fought back with javelins, stones, and burning sulfur.

Slaughter raged on both sides with gigantic deeds. In another part, heralds called a council in the city gates. Gray-haired elders and soldiers assembled, and speeches were made. But soon factional opposition arose. At last one middle-aged man stood up, distinguished in wise bearing, and spoke eloquently of right and wrong, justice, religion, truth, peace, and divine judgment. The crowd shouted him down, both old and young, and would have seized him violently had not a descending cloud snatched him away unseen. So violence, oppression, and the law of the sword spread through all the plain, and no refuge could be found.

Adam dissolved in tears and sadly turned to his guide, lamenting: "O, what are these -- Death's ministers, not men? Who deal death so inhumanly to their fellow humans and multiply the sin of the one who first killed his brother ten thousand times over! They massacre their own brothers -- men slaughtering men! But who was that just man who would have perished in his righteousness, had Heaven not rescued him?"

Michael replied: "These are the offspring of those ill-matched marriages you saw, where good was mixed with bad -- unions that should never have been joined. Their imprudent mixing produced monstrous births of body and mind.

Such were those giants, men of high reputation. For in those days only might was admired. Valor and heroic virtue meant the ability to conquer nations in battle and bring home spoils through immense slaughter. This was considered the highest achievement of human glory. The greatest conquerors, who triumphed through mass killing, were called patrons of humanity, gods, and sons of gods.

They should rightly be called destroyers and plagues of men. Such is the fame earned on Earth. What truly deserves fame remains hidden in silence. But the one you saw -- the seventh from you in descent, the only righteous man in a corrupt world, hated for daring to stand alone for justice and to speak unwelcome truth, declaring that God would come to judge them with his saints -- God received him, as you saw, caught up in a gentle cloud with winged steeds, to walk with God in the heights of salvation and bliss, exempt from death. This was to show you what reward awaits the good. The rest shall see what punishment follows.

Now turn your eyes in that direction and see what comes next." He looked, and saw the face of the world completely changed. The brazen throat of war had ceased to roar. Everything had turned to revelry and entertainment -- feasting, dancing, luxury, and riotous behavior.

Marriage had degenerated into promiscuity, adultery, and rape, as beauty lured them. From their cups, civil quarrels arose. At length a revered old man came among them and loudly condemned their behavior, testifying against their ways. He frequented their assemblies, wherever they gathered for celebrations or festivals, and preached conversion, repentance, and the urgency of imminent divine judgment.

But all in vain. When he saw they would not listen, he stopped arguing. He moved his tents far away. Then, from the mountain, he cut tall timber and began building a vessel of enormous size, measured by cubits in length, breadth, and height.

It was sealed with pitch, with a door in its side, and stocked with large provisions for both man and beast. Then a wonder appeared! Every kind of beast, bird, and insect came in pairs of seven, entering in proper order. Last came the old man and his three sons with their four wives, and God sealed the door.

Meanwhile the south wind rose and, with black wings hovering wide, drove all the clouds together from under Heaven. The hills sent up vapor and moist exhalation. Now the thickened sky stood like a dark ceiling. Down rushed the rain, continuous and violent, until the Earth could no longer be seen. The floating vessel rode high, tilting over the waves with its beaked prow, secure. Every other dwelling was overwhelmed by the flood. The waters rolled deep, swallowing everything and everyone with all their splendor. Sea covered sea, shoreless. In the palaces where luxury once reigned, sea-monsters now bred and made their lairs. Of all humanity, so recently numerous, only those few survived, embarked in one small vessel.

How you grieved then, Adam, to see the end of all your offspring -- such a sad depopulation! Another flood overwhelmed you too -- a flood of tears and sorrow that nearly drowned you, until gently raised by the angel, you stood on your feet again, though comfortless, like a father mourning all his children destroyed at once before his eyes.

And you could barely speak to the angel, uttering this complaint: "O visions I wish I had never foreseen! Better to have lived in ignorance of the future, bearing only each day's share of trouble. These sorrows, meant for many ages, now fall on me all at once through my foreknowledge. They torment me before they exist, born prematurely and aborted by the mere thought that they must one day be real. Let no one seek to be told what shall befall him or his children. Evil is certain enough, and foreknowledge cannot prevent it.

The future evil will be felt no less in anticipation than in reality. But that concern is now past. There is no one left to warn. Those few survivors will eventually die of hunger and exhaustion, wandering that watery desert. I had hoped, when violence ended and war ceased on Earth, that peace would reign and happy days would crown the human race.

But I was badly mistaken. Now I see that peace corrupts no less than war destroys. How can this be? Explain, heavenly guide, and tell me whether the human race will end here." Michael answered: "Those you saw last in triumph and luxurious wealth were the same first seen in acts of outstanding military prowess and great exploits, but empty of true virtue.

Having spilled much blood and caused great devastation subduing nations, earning fame and high titles and rich plunder, they eventually traded their martial pursuits for pleasure, ease, and sloth -- excess, and lust. Their pride and indulgence spawned hostile conflict even in peacetime.

The conquered peoples, enslaved by war, lost all their virtue along with their freedom. They lost their reverence for God, since their pretended piety had brought them no help against invaders. Growing cold in their faith, they learned to live only for worldly comfort, dissolute or merely secure, enjoying whatever scraps their lords left them. The Earth bore more than enough -- enough to test whether anyone would practice moderation.

So all degenerated, all became depraved. Justice, temperance, truth, and faith were forgotten. One man alone, the only son of light in a dark age, stood against the general example, against custom, and against a hostile world. Fearless of reproach, scorn, or violence, he warned them of their wickedness. He set before them the paths of righteousness, showing how much safer and more peaceful they were. He denounced the coming wrath if they did not repent. They mocked him. But God watched this one just man alive. By his command, that man built a miraculous ark, as you saw, to save himself and his household from the universal destruction of a world given over to ruin.

No sooner had he and his chosen company of people and animals been safely lodged in the ark than all the floodgates of Heaven opened over the Earth, pouring rain day and night. Every fountain of the deep burst forth, heaving the ocean beyond all bounds until the waters rose above the highest hills. Then this mount of Paradise, by the force of waves, was torn from its place, pushed by the flood down the great river to the open sea. There it took root as a bare, salty island -- the haunt of seals, whales, and screaming sea-birds.

This teaches you that God does not attribute holiness to any place unless it is brought there by the people who worship him there. And now see what shall follow next." He looked and saw the ark riding on the flood, which had now receded. The clouds had fled, driven by a keen north wind that blew dry, wrinkling the surface of the waters as the deluge decayed.

The clear sun gazed hot on the wide, watery surface and drew moisture from it as from a drink after thirst. This caused the waters to shrink from standing lake to trickling ebb, flowing softly toward the deep, whose sluices were now shut as Heaven had closed its windows.

The ark no longer floated but seemed grounded, resting firmly on the top of some high mountain. Now the hilltops appeared like rocks above the receding water. Rapid currents rushed from them toward the retreating sea.

A raven flew forth from the ark, and after it a dove -- the surer messenger -- was sent out twice to look for a green tree or dry ground on which to land. The second time it returned with an olive leaf in its beak -- a sign of peace.

Soon dry ground appeared. The ancient patriarch descended from his ark with all his company. With uplifted hands and devout eyes, grateful toward Heaven, he looked up and saw overhead a dewy cloud. In the cloud appeared a bow, bright with three bands of lifted color, signaling peace from God and a new covenant.

At this, Adam's heart, which had been so sorrowful, greatly rejoiced. His joy burst forth: "O heavenly teacher, who can reveal future things as present! I am revived at this last sight, assured that humanity shall survive, with all creatures, and their line shall be preserved.

I now grieve far less for one whole world of wicked people destroyed than I rejoice for one man found so perfect and just that God honors him by raising another world from him and forgetting all his anger.

But tell me, what do those colored streaks in Heaven mean, stretched across the sky like the brow of an appeased God? Or do they serve as a floral border to bind the edges of that same watery cloud, to prevent it from dissolving again and flooding the Earth?"

The archangel replied: "You guess well. So willingly does God put aside his anger, though late repenting of having made Man, who proved so depraved. Grieved at heart when he looked down and saw the whole Earth filled with violence, all flesh corrupting its way -- yet those removed, such grace shall one just man find in his sight that he relents, choosing not to destroy humanity entirely.

He makes a covenant never again to destroy the Earth by flood, nor to let the sea exceed its boundaries, nor rain to drown the world, whether with human beings or animals. But when he brings a cloud over the Earth, he will set his triple-colored bow within it, as a reminder of his covenant. Day and night, seed-time and harvest, heat and frost shall continue in their course -- until fire purges all things new, both Heaven and Earth, where the just shall forever dwell."

chapters.title: Book XII
paragraphs: Like a traveler who pauses at noon during his journey, though eager to continue, the archangel paused here between the world destroyed and the world restored, in case Adam might wish to interpose something. Then, with a smooth transition, he resumed his account.

"So you have seen one world begin and end, and Man, as from a second stock, continue anew. Much more you have yet to see. But I notice your mortal sight is beginning to fail. Divine visions inevitably strain and weary human senses.

From now on I will narrate rather than show you what is to come. So listen carefully. This second source of humanity, while still few in number and while the dread of past judgment remains fresh in their minds, shall live with some respect for what is just and right, fearing the Deity.

Working the soil and reaping plentiful harvests of grain, wine, and oil, and frequently sacrificing cattle, lambs, or goats with generous wine-offerings and sacred feasts, they shall spend their days in blameless joy. They shall live long in peace, organized by families and tribes under patriarchal rule -- until one shall rise, a man of proud and ambitious heart. Not content with fair equality and brotherly governance, he will seize undeserved dominion over his fellow humans, completely driving out harmony and the law of nature from the Earth.

Hunting -- and his game shall be men, not beasts -- with war and treacherous snares against all who refuse to submit to his tyrannical empire, he shall be called a mighty hunter before the Lord, as if in defiance of Heaven, or claiming authority from Heaven as second sovereign.

From rebellion he shall derive his very name, though he accuses others of it. He and a crew of like-minded tyrants, marching westward from Eden, shall find a plain where a black, tar-like spring boils up from underground -- the mouth of Hell itself.

With brick and that material they plan to build a city and tower whose top may reach to Heaven, seeking to make a name for themselves lest, dispersed in foreign lands, their memory be lost -- careless whether their fame is good or evil.

But God, who often descends unseen to visit humanity and walks through their dwellings to observe their doings, soon comes down to see their city before the tower can obstruct Heaven's towers. In mockery he sets upon their tongues a varied spirit that completely erases their native language, replacing it with a confused babble of unknown words.

Immediately a hideous uproar of gibberish rises loud among the builders. Each calls to the other but is not understood. Until, hoarse and all in a fury, as if being mocked, they rage. Great laughter echoed in Heaven at the sight and sound of this strange chaos. So the building was abandoned, left ridiculous, and the work was named Confusion."

Adam, fatherly displeased, said: "O detestable son! To aspire above his brothers, seizing authority God never gave him! God gave us dominion only over beast, fish, and bird -- absolute power over them by his gift. But Man over men he did not make lord. He reserved that title for himself alone, leaving humans free from human tyranny.

But this usurper's proud aggression does not stop at men. His tower challenges God himself -- siege and defiance against the Almighty! Wretched fool! What food will he carry up there to feed himself and his reckless army, where the thin air above the clouds will starve his lungs, if not his stomach?"

Michael replied: "You are right to detest that man who brought such trouble upon the peaceful state of humanity, seeking to suppress rational liberty. Yet know this: since your original fall, true liberty has been lost. Liberty always lives inseparably with right Reason, and has no separate existence apart from her.

When Reason in Man grows dim or is disobeyed, unruly desires and upstart passions immediately seize control from Reason, reducing Man to inner servitude -- Man who was formerly free. Therefore, since he permits unworthy powers to rule within himself over free Reason, God, in just judgment, subjects him outwardly to violent tyrants as well.

These often enslave his external freedom just as undeservedly. Tyranny must exist, though it gives the tyrant no excuse. Yet sometimes nations will sink so low from virtue -- which is Reason -- that nothing but justice, accompanied by some fatal curse, deprives them of their outward liberty,

since they have already lost their inward liberty. Witness the irreverent son of Noah, who built the ark. For the shame he brought upon his father, his vicious race heard the heavy curse: 'Servant of servants.' So this later world, like the former, will tend always from bad to worse, until God at last, wearied by their wickedness, withdraws his presence from them and turns his holy eyes away, resolving henceforth to leave them to their own polluted ways.

And he will select one particular nation from all the rest, to be invoked by him alone -- a nation sprung from one faithful man. This man still lives on the other side of the Euphrates, raised in idol worship. Can you believe that people should grow so foolish, while the patriarch who escaped the flood still lives, as to forsake the living God and worship their own handiwork in wood and stone as gods? Yet God the Most High condescends to call this man by a vision, summoning him from his father's house, his family, and his false gods, to a land God will show him. From him God will raise a mighty nation and shower such blessings on him that through his offspring all nations shall be blessed. He obeys at once,

not knowing what land he goes to, yet firmly believing. I can see him -- though you cannot -- with what faith he leaves his gods, his friends, and his native land of Ur of the Chaldeans. He is now crossing the river toward Haran, followed by a large caravan of herds, flocks, and many servants.

Not wandering in poverty, but trusting all his wealth to God who called him, he enters an unknown land. Now he reaches Canaan. I see his tents pitched near Shechem and the neighboring plain of Moreh. There by promise he receives the gift for his descendants of all that land, from Hamath in the north to the southern desert.

I call these places by their future names, though they are not yet named. From Hermon in the east to the great western sea -- Mount Hermon there, the sea yonder. See each place as I point them out. On the shore, Mount Carmel. Here, the double-sourced Jordan River, the true eastern boundary. But his descendants shall settle as far as Senir, that long ridge of hills.

Consider this: all nations of the Earth shall be blessed through his offspring. By that offspring is meant your great Deliverer, who shall crush the Serpent's head -- which I shall explain to you more plainly soon. This blessed patriarch, who shall in due time be called faithful Abraham, leaves a son, and from that son a grandson.

Like Abraham in faith, wisdom, and renown, the grandson, along with his twelve sons, departs from Canaan to a land later called Egypt, divided by the Nile. See where it flows, emptying through seven mouths into the sea. He goes to live in that land, invited by a younger son whose worthy deeds raise him to be second in command in Pharaoh's kingdom. There the patriarch dies, and his descendants grow into a nation. Viewed with suspicion by a later king, they are treated as unwelcome guests too numerous to accommodate. He makes them slaves, treating them cruelly, and kills their infant sons.

Until two brothers -- called Moses and Aaron -- are sent by God to claim his people from bondage. With glory and plunder they shall return to their promised land. But first, the lawless tyrant who refuses to acknowledge their God or heed his message must be compelled by terrible signs and judgments.

The rivers must turn to blood. Frogs, lice, and flies must fill his palace and the entire land. His cattle must die of plague and disease. Boils and sores must cover his flesh and all his people. Thunder mixed with hail, and hail mixed with fire, must tear the Egyptian sky and roll across the ground, devouring everything in its path.

Whatever the hail does not destroy -- herb, fruit, or grain -- a dark swarming cloud of locusts must descend and eat, leaving nothing green on the ground. Darkness must cover all his territory, a palpable darkness blotting out three days.

Last, with one midnight stroke, all the firstborn of Egypt must die. Thus with ten plagues the river-dragon is finally tamed and submits to let his captive workers depart. He humbles his stubborn heart repeatedly, but each time, like ice freezing harder after a thaw, he hardens again. In his final rage, pursuing those he had just dismissed, the sea swallows him and his entire army. But the Israelites pass through safely, as if on dry land, between two crystal walls of water.

The waters stand divided, held back by the rod of Moses, until the rescued people gain the far shore. Such wondrous power God will lend to his holy servant, though the power operates through an angel who goes before them. A cloud by day, a pillar of fire by night --

this cloud and pillar of fire shall guide them on their journey and move behind them to block the Egyptian king's pursuit. All night he will chase them, but darkness will shield them until the morning watch.

Then through the fiery pillar and the cloud, God will look out and throw the entire enemy host into confusion, breaking their chariot wheels. At his command, Moses once more stretches his powerful rod over the sea. The sea obeys his rod.

The waves roll back over the enemy's battle ranks and overwhelm their army. The chosen people advance safely toward Canaan from the shore, though not by the most direct route. They avoid the land of the Canaanites, lest the alarm of war terrify them -- inexperienced as they are -- and fear send them back to Egypt, choosing the shame of slavery over the hardship of battle. Untrained in arms, where rashness does not lead the way, life, whether noble or base, is sweeter.

In the wide wilderness they shall also gain something by this delay. There they shall establish their government and choose their great senate from the twelve tribes, to rule by ordained laws. God himself, descending from Mount Sinai -- whose gray summit shall tremble as he comes down -- will personally ordain their laws in thunder, lightning, and loud trumpet blasts. Some laws will govern civil justice. Others will establish religious rites of sacrifice, foreshadowing through types and symbols the destined Offspring who shall crush the Serpent, and the means by which he shall accomplish humanity's deliverance. But the voice of God is terrifying to mortal ears. They will beg that Moses report God's will to them, so the terror may cease. God grants their request, teaching them that there is no access to God without a mediator -- whose high office Moses now represents in figure, prefiguring the one greater Mediator to come. Moses shall foretell his day, and all the prophets in their ages shall sing of the times of the great Messiah. With laws and rites established, such delight God takes in obedient humanity that he will set up his tabernacle among them.

The Holy One shall dwell with mortal men. By his instruction they shall build a sanctuary of cedar overlaid with gold. Within it, an ark containing his testimony -- the records of his covenant. Above it, a mercy seat of gold, set between the wings of two bright Cherubim. Before it, seven lamps burn like a zodiac representing the heavenly fires. Over the tent, a cloud shall rest by day and a fiery glow by night.

Except when they journey. At length, conducted by God's angel, they come to the land promised to Abraham and his descendants. The rest would take too long to tell: the many battles fought, the many kings destroyed, the many kingdoms conquered,

or how the sun shall stand still in mid-heaven for an entire day, and night's course be suspended, at the command of a man's voice: 'Sun, stand still over Gibeon, and moon, over the Valley of Aijalon, until Israel has conquered!' That commander shall be called the third from Abraham, son of Isaac. From him and his whole line, the nation shall win Canaan."

Here Adam interposed: "O messenger sent from Heaven, enlightener of my darkness! You have revealed gracious things, especially those concerning just Abraham and his offspring. My eyes are truly opened now, and my heart is greatly eased.

I was perplexed before, wondering what would become of me and all mankind. But now I see his day -- the day of the one in whom all nations shall be blessed. An undeserved favor to me, who sought forbidden knowledge by forbidden means!

But I still do not understand why so many and such varied laws are given to those among whom God will deign to dwell on Earth. So many laws suggest so many sins among them. How can God live among such people?"

Michael answered: "Do not doubt that sin will reign among them, born as they will be from you. The law was given to them precisely to expose their natural depravity, by stirring up sin against the law to fight. When they see that the law can reveal sin but not remove it -- except through the weak, shadowy rituals of animal sacrifice, the blood of bulls and goats -- they will conclude that some more precious blood must be shed for humanity.

The just dying for the unjust. Through that righteousness, credited to them by faith, they will find justification before God and peace of conscience -- which the law with its ceremonies cannot provide. Man cannot perfectly keep the law's moral demands, and failing to do so, he cannot live.

So the law appears imperfect, given only as a temporary measure to prepare them, in the fullness of time, for a better covenant. It is a discipline leading from shadows to truth, from flesh to spirit, from the imposition of strict law to the free acceptance of abundant grace, from fearful obedience to the trust of children, from works of law to works of faith.

Therefore Moses, though highly beloved of God, shall not lead his people into Canaan, being only the minister of law. But Joshua -- whom the Gentiles call Jesus -- bearing that same name and office, shall defeat the adversary Serpent and bring back humanity, long wandered through the world's wilderness, safely to the eternal Paradise of rest.

Meanwhile, settled in their earthly Canaan, they shall dwell and prosper for a long time. But when national sins disrupt their public peace, provoking God to raise up enemies against them, he shall save them when they repent -- first through Judges, then under Kings. The second king, renowned for both piety and mighty deeds, shall receive an irrevocable promise that his royal throne shall endure forever. All prophecy shall sing the same: from the royal house of David -- for so I name this king -- shall rise a Son, the Woman's Seed foretold to you, foretold to Abraham as the one in whom all nations shall trust, and foretold to kings as the last and greatest King, for of his reign there shall be no end.

But first a long succession must follow. His immediate successor, famed for wealth and wisdom, shall enshrine the long-wandering Ark of God, which until then had dwelt in tents, in a glorious temple. His successors will be a mixed lot: some good, more bad -- the list of the bad being much longer.

Their gross idolatries and accumulated sins will so anger God that he will abandon them. He will expose their land, their city, his temple, and his holy ark to scorn and plunder by that proud city whose high walls you saw left in confusion -- Babylon, as it was called.

There in captivity he lets them dwell for seventy years. Then, remembering mercy and his covenant sworn to David -- established as firm as the days of Heaven -- he brings them back. Returned from Babylon by leave of the foreign kings whom God disposed, they first rebuild the house of God. For a time they live modestly in a humble state. But as they grow in wealth and numbers, they become factious.

Dissension first springs up among the priests -- men who serve the altar and should most strive for peace. Their quarrels bring pollution upon the temple itself. At last they seize the royal scepter, disregarding the heirs of David.

Then they lose it to a foreigner, so that the true Anointed King, the Messiah, might be born while barred from his rightful throne. Yet at his birth, a star never before seen in Heaven proclaims his coming and guides wise men from the East who inquire where he is, bringing gifts of incense, myrrh, and gold.

His birthplace is announced by a solemn angel to simple shepherds keeping watch by night. They joyfully hurry there and hear a choir of angels singing his carol. A virgin is his mother, but his father is the power of the Most High. He shall ascend the hereditary throne and extend his reign to Earth's widest boundaries, and his glory shall fill the Heavens."

He paused, seeing Adam so overcome with joy that it was like grief dissolved in tears, unable to find words. At last Adam breathed these words: "O prophet of glad tidings, finisher of our utmost hope! Now I clearly understand what my most careful thoughts have long searched for in vain.

I understand why our great Expectation should be called the Seed of the Woman. Hail, Virgin Mother, high in Heaven's love! Yet from my own body you shall come, and from your womb the Son of God Most High. So God unites himself with Man!

Now the Serpent must surely expect the fatal bruising of his head. Tell me when and where the fight shall take place, and what blow shall bruise the Victor's heel." Michael answered: "Do not imagine their conflict as a physical duel with literal wounds to head or heel. The Son does not join Manhood to Godhood to gain more physical strength against your enemy. Nor is Satan overcome that way. Satan's fall from Heaven was a deadlier blow than any wound of head or heel. Satan is already disabled, unable to give you your death-wound.

Your Savior shall heal what Satan has done -- not by destroying Satan himself, but by destroying Satan's works in you and in your offspring. And this can only happen by fulfilling what you lacked: perfect obedience to the law of God, even at the cost of suffering death --

the penalty due for your transgression, and due for all the sins that will grow from yours. Only so can high Justice be satisfied. He shall fulfill God's law completely, both through obedience and through love, though love alone fulfills the whole law. He shall bear your punishment, coming in the flesh to live a life of reproach and endure a cursed death.

He shall proclaim life to all who believe in his redemption. His obedience, credited to them by faith, along with his merits -- not their own legal works -- shall save them. For this, he shall be hated, blasphemed, seized by force, tried, and condemned to a shameful, accursed death -- nailed to a cross by his own nation, killed for bringing life.

But on the cross he nails your enemies: the law that stood against you and the sins of all humanity, crucified with him. These shall never again harm those who rightly trust in his satisfaction. So he dies, but soon revives. Death shall not hold power over him for long. Before the third morning light returns, the stars of dawn shall see him rise from his grave, fresh as the dawning light. Your ransom is paid, redeeming Man from death -- his death for Man. As many as accept the offered gift of life and do not neglect it, embracing the benefit through faith backed by works -- this God-like act cancels your doom, the death you should have died, lost forever in sin. This act shall crush Satan's head, defeating Sin and Death, his two main weapons,

and shall fix their stings far deeper in Satan's head than any temporal death shall bruise the Victor's heel or the heels of those he redeems. For them, death is like a sleep -- a gentle passage to immortal life. Nor after his resurrection shall he remain on Earth longer than a certain time, appearing to his disciples -- men who followed him during his life. To them he shall leave the charge of teaching all nations what they learned from him and his salvation. Those who believe and are baptized in the flowing stream -- the sign of washing them from sin's guilt to pure life, prepared in mind, if necessary, for a death like their Redeemer's.

All nations they shall teach. For from that day, salvation shall be preached not only to the descendants of Abraham's body, but to all who share Abraham's faith throughout the world. So in his offspring all nations shall be blessed.

Then he shall ascend to the Heaven of Heavens with victory, triumphing through the air over his enemies and yours. There he shall surprise Satan, prince of the air, drag him in chains through all his realm, and leave him there confounded.

Then the Son shall enter into glory and resume his seat at God's right hand, exalted above all names in Heaven. From there he shall come again, when this world's dissolution is ripe, with glory and power to judge both the living and the dead.

To judge the unfaithful dead, but to reward his faithful ones and receive them into bliss, whether in Heaven or on Earth. For then the whole Earth shall become Paradise -- a far happier place than this Eden, with far happier days."

So spoke the archangel Michael. Then he paused, as at the world's great conclusion. Our forefather, overflowing with joy and wonder, replied: "O infinite Goodness! Immeasurable Goodness! That all this good shall come out of evil, and evil shall be turned to good -- more wonderful than when Creation first brought light out of darkness! I am full of doubt whether I should now repent of the sin I committed and caused, or rejoice far more that so much greater good shall spring from it --

more glory to God, more goodwill from God to humanity, and grace abounding over wrath. But tell me, if our Deliverer must ascend back to Heaven, what will happen to the few faithful he leaves behind among the unfaithful masses, the enemies of truth? Who will guide and defend his people? Will they not deal even worse with his followers than they dealt with him?"

"You can be sure they will," said the angel. "But from Heaven he will send to his own a Comforter, the promise of the Father. The Holy Spirit shall dwell within them. The law of faith, working through love, shall be written upon their hearts to guide them in all truth. He shall also arm them with spiritual armor, able to resist Satan's attacks and quench his fiery darts.

Whatever human persecution they face, they shall not be afraid, even in the face of death. Against such cruelties they will be inwardly consoled and supported in ways that will astonish their proudest persecutors. For the Spirit, poured first on his Apostles whom he sends to spread the good news to the nations, and then on all who are baptized, shall endow them with wondrous gifts -- the power to speak all tongues and perform all miracles, just as their Lord did before them. In this way they shall win great numbers from every nation to joyfully receive the news brought from Heaven. At length, their ministry completed and their race well run, their teaching and story committed to writing, they shall die. But in their place, as they forewarned, wolves shall succeed as teachers -- grievous wolves who will twist all the sacred mysteries of Heaven to serve their own greed and ambition. They will corrupt the truth with superstitions and human traditions, leaving it pure only in those written records -- though understood only through the Spirit.

Then they shall seek to claim religious authority through official names, places, and titles, joining these with political power while pretending to act spiritually. They will appropriate to themselves the Spirit of God, which was promised equally to all believers. From this pretense, they will impose spiritual laws by political force on every conscience -- laws that no one will find authorized in scripture or inscribed by the Spirit on the heart. What will they be doing but forcing the Spirit of Grace itself and binding Liberty, its companion? They will tear down the living temples that faith has built -- temples of individual conscience. For on Earth, who can claim to be infallible against faith and conscience? Yet many will presume to do so.

Heavy persecution shall therefore arise against all who persist in worshiping in spirit and truth. The majority will consider outward rituals and impressive ceremonies sufficient for religion. Truth shall retreat, bristling with slanderous darts. Works of genuine faith will rarely be found. So the world will go on, hostile to good and favorable to the wicked,

groaning under its own weight until the day of deliverance for the just arrives, and vengeance for the wicked, at the return of the one promised to help you -- the Woman's Seed, once only dimly foretold, now more fully known as your Savior and Lord.

Last, revealed from Heaven in clouds, in the glory of the Father, he shall dissolve Satan and his corrupted world. Then from the burning mass, purged and refined, he shall raise new Heavens and a new Earth, founded in righteousness, peace, and love, for ages without end,

bringing forth fruits of joy and eternal happiness." He ended. Adam replied: "How quickly your prophecy, blessed Seer, has measured this passing world and the entire race of time until time itself stands still! Beyond that is nothing but the abyss of Eternity, whose end no eye can reach.

Greatly instructed, I shall leave here greatly at peace in my thoughts, filled with as much knowledge as this vessel can hold. It was my folly to aspire beyond that. From now on I learn that the best course is to obey, and to love with reverent fear the only God. I will walk as if always in his presence, ever observing his providence and depending on him alone. He is merciful above all his works, always overcoming evil with good. By small things he accomplishes great ones, overthrowing the worldly strong by the worldly weak, and the worldly wise by simple humility. Suffering for the sake of truth is the highest form of courage, leading to the ultimate victory. And for the faithful, death is the gateway to life.

I have learned this from his example, whom I now acknowledge as my Redeemer, forever blessed." The angel replied last: "Having learned this, you have attained the highest sum of wisdom. Hope for nothing beyond it, even if you knew every star by name and all the powers of Heaven, all secrets of the deep, all of Nature's works, or the works of God in Heaven, air, Earth, or sea, and enjoyed all the world's riches and ruled its entire empire. Only add to your knowledge corresponding deeds. Add faith, add virtue, patience, and temperance. Add love, which shall come to be known by the name of charity -- the soul of all the rest. Then you will not be reluctant to leave this Paradise. You will possess a Paradise within you, far happier. Let us now descend from this mountaintop of contemplation, for the precise hour demands our departure. See, the guards I stationed on that hill are expecting the signal to move. In front of them, a flaming sword waves fiercely in a circle as the signal to leave.

We may stay no longer. Go, wake Eve. I have calmed her too with gentle dreams that promise good things, composing all her feelings to peaceful acceptance. At the right time, share with her what you have heard.

Especially what concerns her faith to know: the great deliverance that shall come through her offspring -- for by the Woman's Seed salvation comes to all humanity. So may you live, which will be for many days, both of you united in one faith, though sorrowful with good cause over past evils, yet far more encouraged by meditating on the happy ending."

He ended. They both descended the hill. Adam ran ahead to the bower where Eve lay sleeping, but found her already awake. She greeted him with words that were not sad: "I know where you have been and where you went, for God is present even in sleep. He has sent dreams that are favorable, foretelling some great good.

Since with sorrow and heartbreak I fell exhausted into sleep. But now lead on. I will not delay. To go with you is to stay here. To remain here without you is to leave unwillingly. You are everything to me under Heaven, every place -- you, for whose willing crime I am banished from here.

I carry this further consolation with me: though everything is lost through me, I am given such undeserved favor that through me, the Promised Seed, shall restore all." So spoke our mother Eve. Adam heard, well pleased, but did not answer. For now, too near at hand, the archangel stood. From the opposite hill, the Cherubim descended to their assigned stations in full bright array, gliding over the ground like evening mist rising from a river and gathering speed at a laborer's heel as he walks homeward. High in front advanced the brandished sword of God before them, blazing fierce as a comet. Its scorching heat and vaporous radiation, like the burning Libyan wind, began to parch that once-temperate climate. At this, the hastening angel caught our lingering parents by each hand and led them directly to the eastern gate and down the cliff to the plain below. Then he vanished.

They looked back. All the eastern side of Paradise, so recently their happy home, was engulfed in waving flame. The gate was thronged with terrifying faces and fiery weapons. They shed some natural tears, but quickly wiped them away.
The whole world lay before them, where to choose their place of rest, with Providence as their guide. Hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, through Eden they took their solitary way.
